title: How a Puerto Rico Lease Continues After Its Term
bodyText:
In Puerto Rico a residential lease does not end by itself when its term runs out. Under the 2020 Civil Code it continues on the same terms (same rent, same rules) until you or the tenant gives notice ending it; the Code sets no notice period, so the lease should set one (the Ending the Lease section does). If the lease names no term at all, the law treats it as a one-year lease.

Two side effects matter: a guarantor's (fiador's) obligations end when the continuation begins, so a guaranty does not cover rent or damage after the original term unless the guarantor signs again; and a tenant who stays after a valid notice has ended the lease can be removed only through a court eviction (desahucio).

Leases that were already running when the 2020 Code took effect (in November 2020) stay under the 1930 Civil Code, where a fixed term ends on its last day without notice and a tacit renewal arises only if the tenant stays 15 days with your acquiescence and you made no prior demand, renewing month by month for a monthly rent; the same end of a guaranty applies there. If you are unsure which Code governs an older lease, sign a new written lease or give written notice well ahead of the date you want possession.

title: No Just-Cause Requirement to End a Lease
bodyText: Puerto Rico law does not require a landlord to have a reason (just cause) to end a private residential lease once its term is over. When the term ends the lease continues on the same terms, and either you or the tenant may end it by notice; the Civil Code sets no notice period, so use the one your lease states. During the term you may end the lease only for the tenant's breach (after a written demand warning that you will end it, or on the Code's own grounds such as abandonment, a change of use or two consecutive unpaid rental periods) or under an early-termination term the lease contains. A tenant who does not leave can be removed only by a court eviction (desahucio). Some tenancies carry outside limits: subsidized housing under Puerto Rico Department of Housing programs must follow those programs' eviction rules (a project in the older adults' rent subsidy program must first go through mediation, at its own cost, and the Department's complaint process before it ends the lease or files an eviction); federally assisted housing has its own good-cause and notice rules; covered properties need the federal 30-day notice to vacate; if the court finds the family insolvent, it notifies the Departments of the Family and of Housing, and the removal may not be carried out unless officials of both departments are present; if the tenant is a veteran, an older adult or a person with a disability, the court notifies the relevant agency; in these cases, and to be safe also for an insolvent family, the removal period after the judgment is notified is 20 days that cannot be extended; and a protective order under the domestic-violence law or the older-adults law can order the abuser out of a shared home whatever right the abuser claims to it (the domestic-violence order can also order rent payments to continue). No general Puerto Rico statute protects a tenant from a retaliatory notice. Older adults and people with disabilities have a statutory right to be free from reprisal for exercising their civil rights, and one law bars long-term care establishments from retaliating against residents who complain to the Ombudsman for older adults; the Civil Code also bars the abusive exercise of a right. The 2020 COVID-19 economic law's eviction measures are not in force.

title: Renting to Students: DACO License
bodyText:
Puerto Rico regulates student housing as a licensed business. If you rent a unit to three or more college, technical or other post-secondary students, or rent rooms to students in a home where you live, you need a license from the Department of Consumer Affairs (DACO) before you rent, renewed every year, and DACO may inspect.

You may not sign a lease for such housing without the license and permits, every lease must contain the certification in the Student Housing Certification section, and you must post DACO's list of requirements in a visible place.

DACO's student-housing regulation also requires a written contract filed with your license application, house rules and an emergency plan, a copy of the municipal Public Order Code for each student, and at least 30 days for a student to move out (Regulation No. 6628, listed as in force in the Department of State's regulation registry). DACO can fine up to $10,000 for each violation. Renting a whole unit to one or two students when you don't live there is not a student housing business.

title: Payment Methods and the Card Surcharge Ban
bodyText:
Puerto Rico law does not tell you which rent payment methods you must accept: we found no statute that requires you to take cash, requires a paper option, or bars you from requiring payment through an online portal or electronic transfer. The lease decides, because a money debt is paid in the kind the parties agreed.

One rule does apply: if a tenant chooses to pay by credit or debit card or another valid payment method, you may not add a surcharge for using it. Puerto Rico's card-surcharge law covers any "sale or lease of goods and services" and defines a surcharge as any increase over the regular price imposed by the merchant or lessor; breaking it is a crime punishable by a fine of up to $500, up to six months in jail, or both.

If your card processor charges you a fee, absorb it or do not accept cards; do not pass it on as a "convenience fee". Payment costs other than a card surcharge (for example a money-order fee the tenant pays its own bank) fall on the tenant under the Civil Code.

title: No Rule on Algorithmic Rent-Setting
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute on setting rents with algorithmic pricing software or on landlords sharing rent data. Puerto Rico's general antitrust law still applies: it makes every contract, combination or conspiracy that unreasonably restrains trade in Puerto Rico illegal and a misdemeanor, and federal antitrust law (Sherman Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1) applies in Puerto Rico too. Setting your own rent with a pricing tool is not addressed by any Puerto Rico statute; agreeing with competing landlords, directly or through a shared tool that pools their private rent data, is the risk. Take advice before using a tool that relies on competitors' non-public data. This covers Puerto Rico statutes we could search.

title: No Puerto Rico Rule on Application Fees
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute that caps, bans or regulates rental application or screening fees, requires a refund of an unused fee, or requires a written disclosure of screening criteria before you take a fee. You may charge a reasonable application fee, but say in writing before you take it what it covers and whether it is refundable, and charge every applicant the same way. If the applicant pays by credit or debit card, you may not add a card surcharge. If you deny an application or change its terms because of a credit or background report, federal law (the Fair Credit Reporting Act) requires you to give the applicant an adverse-action notice. This covers Puerto Rico statutes we could search.

title: How Payments Are Applied in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Under the Civil Code a tenant who owes you several amounts may say, when paying, which one the payment covers, and you must follow that choice. If the tenant says nothing, the lease's order of application governs; without one, a debt that bears interest takes payment first to the interest, and otherwise the payment goes to the most burdensome debt that is due, or pro rata if the debts are alike. Give a receipt that states how you applied each payment: once a tenant accepts a receipt that applies the payment, the tenant cannot later challenge that application without a reason that invalidates it. Accepting a payment does not by itself waive unpaid amounts if your receipt says what remains due (see the receipts guidance).

title: Collection Fees on Unpaid Rent
bodyText:
No Puerto Rico statute sets or bans a fee a landlord may charge for collecting past-due rent or damages. If you hand a debt to a collection agency, Puerto Rico's Collection Agencies Act bars the agency from adding any extra charge, its own collection costs or any other expense, including attorney's fees the parties did not agree to, unless a final court judgment authorizes it. A lease may make the tenant reimburse your actual, reasonable collection costs up to a stated cap; the library offers an optional collection-cost clause that keeps the agency limit. It does not fix the costs in advance or stop the tenant from disputing them.

The Act covers businesses that collect debts for others; it does not cover you collecting your own rent, or attorneys and real estate brokers collecting as part of their own business. A licensed agency must also send a written demand by certified mail before suing.

title: Amounts Due at Signing in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico sets no cap on what you may collect at signing: no statute limits first or last month's rent paid up front or the size of a security deposit. Rent is payable in arrears unless the lease says otherwise, so if you want the first month's rent at signing and each later month in advance, the lease must say so (the library's rent clause does). Give a receipt for each amount you collect at signing, and do not add a surcharge if the tenant pays by card.

title: Itemize Every Mandatory Fee
bodyText:
Puerto Rico's purchase-receipt transparency law covers anyone who offers goods or services for rent, and we treat it as covering residential landlords. Under it: every charge that is not optional must be itemized, explained and shown with its final cost next to the rent in every document you give the tenant or use to persuade a prospect (ads, quotes, the lease, invoices and receipts); you may not add a separate charge for a basic service the tenant needs in order to get the home itself; and no document may carry a "service charge" line, or any other line for a mandatory charge the tenant did not expressly agree to.

If you run a leasing office, post a visible sign at its entrance listing any mandatory charges beyond rent. DACO may fine up to $5,000 per violation.

Puerto Rico's Consumer Bill of Rights also says consumers are entitled to a detailed account of all costs, to a copy of a contract before signing with time to read it, and not to be asked to sign a contract with blanks. Give the tenant the full lease, with every blank filled, before signing.

Puerto Rico has no separate all-in advertised-rent rule. We could not read DACO's Commercial Practices Regulation (Reg. No. 9158), and DACO's 2024 list of regulations in force shows none under the transparency law.

title: No Fees for Services You Do Not Provide
bodyText: Do not charge a tenant for a service that does not exist or that the tenant cannot verify receiving. Puerto Rico's purchase-receipt transparency law, which we treat as covering residential landlords, bars charging money for services that are nonexistent or cannot be verified by the consumer, bars a "service charge" line or any other line for a mandatory charge the tenant did not expressly agree to, and bars a separate charge for a basic service the tenant needs in order to receive the home itself. DACO may fine up to $5,000 per violation. Every fee in your lease should name the service or feature it pays for, and you should actually provide it.

title: Fees and Rent in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico law has no definition of rent that sweeps in fees, and no statute lets a lease turn a fee into rent by calling it "additional rent". Rent is the price the parties agree for the use of the home. The nonpayment eviction rests on unpaid "rent or price agreed", and the landlord's right to end the lease for nonpayment counts missed rent periods. Late fees are penalty clauses, which courts read narrowly, and a form lease is read against the landlord who drafted it, so a label that turns fees into rent may not hold. The library does not call fees rent. Collect unpaid fees in an ordinary money claim; the joinder the eviction statute allows (as an exception, and only if you ask) covers only the unpaid rent on which a nonpayment eviction rests, not fees. If you want a lease that treats a recurring charge for use of part of the property (such as monthly parking) as part of the rent, state it as part of the Monthly Rent rather than as a separate fee, and take advice first. In a nonpayment case the tenant can defend only with a receipt or another document showing payment (the court may also hear evidence that the tenant contributed to the property as a co-owner), so issue receipts for every payment.

title: Passing Government Fees to Tenants
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute that imposes a registration or licensing fee on long-term residential rentals, and none that says whether you may pass a government fee on to a tenant. By default the tenant pays the charges and taxes that belong to the tenant's own use of the home, and you bear the charges on your property and your rental business, such as property tax and any municipal business-volume tax on your rental income. A lease may shift a specific government fee to the tenant if the tenant expressly agrees to it in the lease; the library offers an optional clause for a fee a municipality assesses on the rental. Puerto Rico's 78 municipalities may adopt their own fees by ordinance.

title: Passing Government Fines to Tenants
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute that bars, or expressly allows, passing to a tenant a fine a municipality or agency imposes on you. General contract law decides it. A tenant who breaks the lease answers for the loss the breach causes, which can include a fine you had to pay because of the tenant's conduct, and a tenant answers for the people the tenant brings in. You cannot make the tenant pay for fines that arise from your own duties as landlord, such as keeping the home in repair, and a form-lease clause that shifts your own liability to the tenant is especially annullable. The library offers an optional clause limited to fines caused by the tenant's household or guests. Fines a condominium association imposes are a separate matter.

title: Late Fees in Puerto Rico
bodyText:
A late fee is lawful in Puerto Rico as a penalty clause, and Puerto Rico sets no maximum and no required grace period for dwelling rent. A court must enforce the agreed fee and may reduce it only if it is extremely out of proportion to the rent. The tenant is in default from the due date without any demand, because rent has a fixed date. Write the fee clearly: courts read penalty clauses narrowly and a form lease against the landlord.

Unless the lease clearly says otherwise, the agreed late fee takes the place of interest as compensation for the delay, so do not also charge default interest for the same late payment. You may collect both the late fee and the unpaid rent. State the grace period in calendar days, and use a flat fee rather than a charge that grows month by month like interest: agreed interest is capped by Puerto Rico's interest law (see the interest guidance).

When you accept a late or partial payment, write on the receipt what remains unpaid (including the late fee): under the Civil Code, a receipt for the latest payment given without any reservation creates a presumption that earlier payments were made.

title: No Late Fee Limit
bodyText: Puerto Rico sets no maximum late fee, no required grace period and no notice requirement for late fees on dwelling rent; the amount and timing are what your lease says. Statutory late-charge caps exist only for self-storage units, rent-to-own contracts for household goods and other leases of movable goods, none of which reaches a home lease. A court must enforce the agreed fee but may reduce it if it is extremely out of proportion to the rent, so keep it modest and state it clearly in the lease. No Puerto Rico rule gives seniors, benefit recipients or federal workers a special grace period.

title: No Rule Comparing Fixed-Term and Periodic Terms
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute that bars charging a periodic or indefinite-term tenant more, or imposing heavier terms, than a fixed-term tenant (or the reverse), and none that caps a rent difference between lease types. A lease may be for a fixed or an indefinite term; a lease of real property with no agreed term is treated as one for a year. When a fixed term ends and neither side gives notice, the lease continues on the same terms, so a continued tenancy keeps the fixed-term rent and terms until a new agreement is made. Charge different rents for different lease lengths only by offering each option before signing, and apply the same choice to every applicant.

title: Deadlines for Suing a Tenant
bodyText: In Puerto Rico a claim for unpaid rent or other money owed under a lease is a personal action that must be brought within four years. For rent, each month's installment has its own clock, which starts on the date that installment was due. A claim for damage the tenant caused outside the lease (a tort) must be brought within one year of learning of the damage and who caused it. The clock restarts from zero when you file suit, when you send the tenant a written demand for payment, or when the tenant acknowledges the debt; send a dated written demand well before four years run. A demand on one of several tenants who are jointly and severally liable restarts the clock against all of them. A lease cannot lengthen these periods, and a tenant's advance waiver of the defense is ineffective. For a lease that began under the 1930 Civil Code (before November 28, 2020), a rent claim already running at that date kept the old five-year period unless it was interrupted afterwards, in which case the four-year period applies from the interruption. Whether a partial payment counts as an acknowledgment is decided by the courts; do not rely on it alone.

title: No General Rent Control in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no general rent control or rent-stabilization law: the old Reasonable Rents Act of 1946 was repealed in 1995, and the parties set the rent. Two kinds of special limits remain. First, some tax-incentive and housing programmes tie benefits to rent limits: for example, an owner who takes the Río Piedras rehabilitation tax benefits and leases the property must keep the reasonable rents set by regulation while enjoying the benefits, and subsidy and tax-credit programmes set maximum rents for participating units. Check the terms of any incentive, decree or subsidy you hold. Second, when the Governor or the President declares an emergency or disaster, the prices of essential goods and services are frozen automatically and DACO may issue freeze orders; DACO's emergency price regulation reaches anything leased or rented that people need because of the emergency and bars raising rental prices while a freeze order is in force; it does not name housing, so do not raise rent while a declared emergency or a DACO freeze order is in force.

title: Rent Concessions and the Continued Lease
bodyText: No Puerto Rico statute regulates rent concessions such as a free first month or a reduced rent for a period. A concession is part of the price you and the tenant agree, so write it into the lease with its amount and the exact rental periods it covers. This matters in Puerto Rico because when a fixed term ends and neither side gives notice, the lease continues on the same terms: a concession written as a standing reduction (for example "Monthly Rent is $100 less") would carry into the continued lease, while one limited to named months would not. Show any concession on the receipt for the months it applies to.

title: Collecting Rent for a Defective or Closed Unit
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute that flatly bars you from demanding or collecting rent while a unit has code violations. Three rules limit it. First, if a municipality orders a dwelling vacated and closed as unfit for human habitation, a sign is posted saying its use as a dwelling is illegal, and anyone who rents it out is liable to the fine the municipal ordinance sets: you may not rent a closed unit. Second, the lease is a contract of reciprocal obligations: if you fail to deliver or repair the home as the Civil Code requires, the tenant may withhold performance while you do not perform, may reduce the rent in proportion to what you still owe when your performance is partial or defective, and may end the lease or ask for a proportional rent reduction in the cases the lease chapter lists. Separately, an owner who rents a vacant home the Secretary of Health declared unfit before making the ordered repairs commits a crime and forfeits the rent for that period (see the guidance on renting a home declared unfit). Third, a tenant may ask a municipal judge for a provisional order in a dispute over urgent repairs to a dwelling. In a nonpayment eviction the tenant may defend only with a receipt or other proof of payment (the court may also hear evidence that the tenant contributed to the property as a co-owner), but that does not stop a separate claim for the landlord's breach. Make repairs promptly after notice.

title: Rent Changes During the Lease
bodyText:
In Puerto Rico the rent is set by agreement of the parties (or by a third party they name), so you may change it during the lease only as the lease itself provides: a schedule of fixed new amounts, or an adjustment by a published index stated in the lease. A clause letting you raise the rent on notice alone is especially annullable in a form lease, because it lets the drafter change a core term unilaterally; the library does not offer one.

A scheduled or index clause keeps working if the lease continues after the term ends, because the continued lease runs on the same terms; if you want a different rent after the term, give notice ending the lease and agree a new one. Puerto Rico has no tenant anti-retaliation statute, and no statute limits how much or how often rent may rise between leases, but a rent-limit condition in a tax incentive or subsidy you hold still applies.

title: Raising the Rent in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute that sets a notice period or form for a rent increase. Because the rent is part of the agreement, you cannot raise it during a fixed term unless the lease schedules the increase, and when the term ends the lease continues on the same terms, at the same rent, until either side gives notice ending it. To change the rent at the end of the term, give the tenant written notice ending the lease at the end of the term together with an offer of a new lease at the new rent, well ahead of time (the library suggests at least 30 days; the law sets no period), and sign the new rent in writing. Do not write a lease that renews or raises the rent automatically if the tenant stays silent: that is especially annullable in a form lease. During a declared emergency or disaster, prices of essential goods and services are frozen; check DACO's current orders before raising rent then. Subsidized tenancies follow their programme's notice rules.

title: Rent in Installments and Partial Payments
bodyText: Puerto Rico lets the lease set how rent is paid, including in installments within the month. Without such a term you do not have to accept a partial payment: a creditor cannot be made to accept part of what is owed unless the contract or the law expressly allows it. If you agree to installments, put the schedule in the lease so that an installment paid on time is not a late or partial payment. If you accept a partial payment outside the schedule, say on the receipt what remains unpaid, because a receipt for the latest installment given without any reservation creates a presumption that earlier installments were paid. Under the Civil Code the landlord may end the lease for nonpayment when the tenant fails to pay the agreed rent for two consecutive periods; the rental period is the one the lease sets, not each installment.

title: Paying Rent in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico rent is payable in arrears unless the lease says otherwise, and at the tenant's home municipality unless the lease names a place, so the lease should state that rent is due in advance, the due date, and where and how it is paid (the library's rent and payment-method clauses do). A due date that falls on a holiday moves to the next business day. Two statutes let rent go elsewhere than to you. A tenant may pay overdue property taxes on the property and deduct the amount from the rent, and a tenant who redeems the property after a tax sale may deduct what it paid. If you own a condominium unit and fall behind on maintenance fees, the court may order your tenant to pay the rent into court for the condominium until your debt is covered. Keep property taxes and condominium fees current.

title: Rent Receipts in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Give a written receipt for every rent payment, in any form, and keep a copy. Under the current Civil Code a tenant who pays part of what is owed may demand a receipt and may ask that it record reservations; for leases that began before November 28, 2020 under the old Civil Code, the landlord must sign and give a receipt for each payment. Puerto Rico's purchase-receipt laws also require businesses that sell goods or services to consumers to issue durable receipts showing the date, the service, who received the payment, the amount and the method, with DACO fines; we treat them as reaching landlords who rent as a business. Receipts matter more in Puerto Rico than elsewhere: in a nonpayment eviction the tenant may defend only with a receipt or other document showing payment (the court may also hear evidence that the tenant contributed to the property as a co-owner), and a receipt for the latest payment given without any reservation creates a presumption that earlier installments (and any interest) were paid. When you accept a late or partial payment, write on the receipt what is still owed. If you refuse a proper payment without reason, the tenant may deposit it in court and be released.

title: Reporting Rent to Credit Bureaus
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no rent-reporting programme law: nothing requires you to offer positive rent reporting, and nothing bars you from offering it. If you report a tenant's payments to a credit bureau in the ordinary course of your business, Puerto Rico's credit-reporting law treats you as an information furnisher: each time you report a late payment or other adverse information you must notify the tenant in writing within 30 days, stating the days in arrears and warning that the delinquency is being reported, and repeat the notice every 90 days. Tell tenants in writing before you start reporting, and get their consent if you use a reporting service. A licensed collection agency you hire may not report the debt to a credit bureau. Federal credit-reporting law (the Fair Credit Reporting Act) also applies to furnishers.

title: Sales Tax and Room Tax on Rent
bodyText: Puerto Rico's sales and use tax (IVU) treats a lease of real property as a taxable service, but rent a tenant pays for a home that is the tenant's principal residence, or for student lodging, is exempt. Rent for a dwelling that is not the tenant's principal residence (for example a second home or a unit rented to a business for its staff) may therefore be subject to IVU, which you would have to collect and report as a merchant; take tax advice before renting on that basis. Rentals of less than 90 days are short-term rentals subject to the room occupancy tax (7 percent for short-term rentals) collected through the Tourism Office, with registration; this library's leases are for longer residential tenancies. No Puerto Rico statute bars passing a tax through to the tenant, but any tax you charge must be itemized and agreed.

title: List Every Required Fee in the Lease
bodyText: Puerto Rico requires, under the purchase-receipt transparency law we treat as covering landlords, that every charge that is not optional be itemized, explained and shown with its final cost in the documents you give the tenant, and that no mandatory charge be collected unless the tenant expressly agreed to it. List every required fee in the lease with its amount and purpose (the library's fees-and-charges clause does). Puerto Rico sets no notice period for adding a fee later, because you cannot add one on your own: a change to a signed lease needs the same form as the lease itself, and a form-lease clause letting you change terms alone is especially annullable. Add a fee during the tenancy only by a written amendment the tenant signs.

title: Bounced Rent Checks in Puerto Rico
bodyText:
Puerto Rico's Commercial Transactions Act lets the payee of a check returned for insufficient funds, a closed account or lack of authority to overdraw charge the writer a $10 administrative charge, plus the unpaid amount and interest at the legal rate from the first return; use that figure for checks. No Puerto Rico statute sets a fee for a failed electronic or card payment, so the lease sets it, and a court may cut it only if it is extremely out of proportion.

Writing a bad check with intent to defraud is a crime, but no one can be prosecuted unless the holder first gave the writer personal notice or certified-mail notice with return receipt demanding payment within at least 10 days (15 days if the writer lives in another municipality); payment before the probable-cause hearing ends criminal liability. Do not threaten criminal charges to collect rent; send the statutory notice only if you mean to file.

Keep the fee for a failed electronic or card payment close to what your bank or payment processor charges you.

title: Government Shutdowns and Rent
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute that delays rent, bars late fees or limits eviction for federal or Puerto Rico government workers during a government shutdown. The lease's ordinary rent, late-fee and default terms apply. Consider a written payment plan for a tenant who shows a shutdown-related pay delay; a plan you sign is an agreed change to the lease, and a receipt should record what remains owed.

title: Puerto Rico Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: Puerto Rico sets few fixed money limits on a residential lease. No statute caps the security deposit, the late fee, the application fee or the rent itself, and none requires a grace period. The limits that do exist: a check returned for insufficient funds may carry an administrative charge of $10 plus legal-rate interest; no surcharge may be added for paying by credit or debit card; a collection agency may not add its collection costs or any extra charge to a debt without a final judgment; default interest is the agreed rate or, without agreement, the legal rate set by the Office of the Commissioner of Financial Institutions, computed as simple interest; and a court may cut any agreed penalty (such as a late fee) that is extremely out of proportion. Every mandatory fee must be itemized and agreed, and rent limits can come with a tax incentive, subsidy or declared emergency.

title: No Subsidy Proration Rule
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no special rule for reducing rent when part of a subsidized unit becomes uninhabitable. The general Civil Code rules apply to every tenancy: if you fail to keep the home fit for the agreed use the tenant may end the lease or ask for a proportional rent reduction, and may reduce its own performance in proportion when yours is partial or defective. For a subsidized tenancy, the programme's contract (for example a federal housing-assistance payments contract) may also stop or reduce the subsidy while the unit fails inspection; and an eviction of a tenant in a Puerto Rico Department of Housing subsidy programme must follow that programme's regulations.

title: Late Fees and the Subsidy Portion of Rent
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute on late fees connected to the part of rent a housing subsidy pays. A late fee is a penalty for the tenant's own delay, and penalty clauses are read narrowly, so apply your late fee only to the tenant's own share: write the lease so the fee is triggered by late payment of the tenant's portion, never by a late or missing subsidy payment. Subsidy programmes often bar such fees in their own lease addenda, and those addenda control for the programme. An eviction of a tenant in a Puerto Rico Department of Housing subsidy programme must follow that programme's regulations.

title: Passing Property Tax Increases to the Tenant
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute on passing real property tax (CRIM) or insurance increases to a residential tenant. By default the tax on the property is yours, and the tenant pays only the charges and taxes that belong to the tenant's own use. A lease may make the tenant pay a stated share of an increase over a base year if the share and the calculation are fixed in the lease, the tenant gets the bill and the calculation, and any reduction or refund is shared back; the library's optional tax-and-insurance clause does this. A clause letting you set the share later, or add a new pass-through by notice, is especially annullable in a form lease. Keep the taxes current: if they go unpaid, a tenant may pay them and deduct the amount from the rent.

title: Interest on Unpaid Rent and Damages
bodyText:
In Puerto Rico a tenant who is late paying money owes interest as damages: the rate agreed in the lease or, without one, the legal rate, which is the judgment rate set by the Office of the Commissioner of Financial Institutions, always computed as simple interest. Rent is in default from its due date without any demand; other amounts (such as repair costs) are in default from your written demand.

No lease clause is needed for the legal rate, but a higher agreed rate must be in writing and is capped by Puerto Rico's interest law at 8 percent a year (9 percent when the amount owed is $3,000 or less) unless the Financial Board has set other maximum rates for the transaction. Do not stack an agreed interest rate on a late fee for the same late payment unless the lease says so clearly. A court also adds judgment interest, and prejudgment interest against a party that litigated obstinately.

title: Move-In and Move-Out Condition Records
bodyText:
Puerto Rico does not require a move-in inspection, a signed inventory or any particular condition form, and sets no move-out inspection procedure. But the tenant must return the home in the condition it was received, except for ordinary wear and the passage of time, so what the home was like at move-in decides every damage claim.

The current Civil Code no longer carries the old Code's presumption that a tenant received the home in good condition (that presumption, and the rule that the tenant answers for deterioration unless it proves it was not at fault, still govern leases begun before November 28, 2020). Under the current Code you should be ready to prove the move-in condition yourself.

Use the library's move-in condition report (Existing Condition section) with dated photos, give the tenant a copy and invite the tenant to add comments and sign it; do the same at move-out. Write it as a record of fact; do not word it as the tenant giving up the right to dispute it.

title: Preset Cleaning and Repair Charges
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no security-deposit statute, so nothing in statute lets or forbids a lease listing preset cleaning, carpet or repair charges. Two Civil Code rules shape what works. You cannot charge for ordinary wear and the passage of time, because the tenant's duty is to return the home in the condition received except for that wear; a flat cleaning or repainting fee charged whatever the condition is therefore risky. The Civil Code allows parties who negotiate a contract to calculate damages in advance, so that the landlord need not prove the loss and the tenant cannot show it was smaller. In a form lease that kind of clause is especially annullable because it restricts the tenant's evidence, so the library does not offer a schedule of preset cleaning or repair deductions. Charge the actual reasonable cost of repairing damage beyond ordinary wear, with receipts, and take advice before adding your own schedule.

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds
bodyText: If you hold a tenant's deposit in the course of your rental business and the tenant does not collect the refund, the money does not become yours. Under Puerto Rico's unclaimed-money law you are a "holder": once the refund is due and you have told the former tenant it is available, it is presumed abandoned if five years pass without the tenant claiming it or writing to show interest. Holders must report presumed-abandoned money each year to the Office of the Commissioner of Financial Institutions by August 10 (as of June 30), publish the annual notice the law requires, and turn the money over to the Commissioner; fines run up to $5,000 per violation. Do not put a clause in the lease that lets you keep an unclaimed refund. Keep a dated record of every attempt to return a deposit.

title: No Right to Pay the Deposit in Installments
bodyText: Puerto Rico gives tenants no statutory right to pay a security deposit in installments, and sets no deposit statute at all, so you may require the full deposit at signing. You do not have to accept part of what is owed unless the lease allows it. If you agree to installments, write the schedule into the lease or a signed addendum.

title: Last Month's Rent and the Deposit
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no rule on collecting last month's rent in advance or on treating it as part of the deposit: rent may be agreed payable in advance, so last month's rent collected up front is advance rent if the lease says so. Keep it separate from the security deposit in the lease and on the receipt. A tenant cannot simply apply the deposit to the last month's rent: legal set-off needs both debts to be money that is liquid, due and payable, and a deposit refund is not due or liquid until the tenancy ends and the deductions are known. If you want to allow it, say so in writing.

title: Move-Out Notice and the Deposit Refund
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no deposit statute, so no rule makes the refund depend on, or forbids conditioning it on, advance notice of move-out, a forwarding address or a joint move-out inspection. What the lease says governs. Ask for a forwarding address in writing at move-out, offer a joint walk-through, and return the deposit, with a written list of any deductions, promptly after the tenant surrenders the home; the library suggests within 30 days, which is a practice, not a Puerto Rico rule. Do not keep the deposit as a penalty for short notice unless the lease clearly provides an agreed charge, which a court may reduce if extremely out of proportion.

title: Deposits After a Domestic-Violence Move-Out
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no deposit statute and no special rule on when a deposit is returned after a tenant leaves because of domestic violence; the lease and the general rules apply. Return the departing victim's share as soon as the deductions are known, and do not hold it hostage to the other occupants' move-out. Victims of domestic violence may get reasonable housing-deposit costs, up to a capped amount, from Puerto Rico's crime-victim compensation programme; a tenant may pay you a new deposit with those funds.

title: Deposits After Eviction or Abandonment
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no expedited or special deposit procedure for a tenant who is evicted or abandons the home, and no deposit statute. Apply the deposit, as the lease allows, to rent and damage the tenant owes once possession is back with you, give the former tenant a written accounting, and return any balance; if you cannot reach the tenant, keep the record, because an unclaimed balance may become reportable unclaimed money. You may return a deposit early at any time. A court in a nonpayment eviction may join a claim for unpaid rent, and the judgment can account for the deposit.

title: Deposit Alternatives and Fees in Lieu of a Deposit
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute on deposit-alternative programmes or fees charged in place of a security deposit, and no deposit statute. If you offer one, make it a real choice: offer every applicant the same option of a traditional deposit, say in writing that the fee is not a deposit and is not refundable, what it covers, and that the tenant still owes for damage and unpaid rent. Puerto Rico's purchase-receipt transparency law requires any mandatory charge to be itemized and expressly agreed. If the programme is insurance or a surety bond, the provider must be authorized under Puerto Rico's Insurance Code; check its authorization. If you will report a tenant's unpaid damage claim to a credit bureau or send it to a collector, follow the credit-reporting notice and collection-agency rules.

title: Furnished Rentals
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no special rule for furnished dwelling rentals and no separate furniture-deposit rule. The Civil Code's lease rules cover the furniture as part of what is leased: the tenant must care for it, tell you of any damage, and return it in the condition received except for ordinary wear and the passage of time. List each item and its condition in the lease or a signed inventory (the library's optional furnishings clause does). Puerto Rico's movable-goods lease law is aimed at businesses that lease movable goods and excludes leases of less than a year; we read it as not reaching furniture rented with a home.

title: Holding Deposits Before the Lease
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute on holding deposits taken from an applicant before the lease is signed. The Civil Code supplies the rules, and they cut both ways. Money given so that either side may back out by losing it is earnest money (arras): if the applicant backs out, it loses the money, but if you back out, you must return it plus the same amount again. To avoid that, put the holding deposit in a short signed writing that says what it is: that it holds the unit for the applicant until a stated date, that it will be applied to the first month's rent or the security deposit if the lease is signed, that it is refunded in full if you decline the applicant or do not offer the lease on the stated terms, and what happens if the applicant does not sign by that date. Give a receipt. A promise to sign a lease later is a preliminary contract that a court can enforce, so state clearly whether you are committing to lease the unit.

title: No Inspection-Notice Penalty
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no deposit statute, so there is no required notice of move-in or move-out inspection rights and no penalty (such as forfeiting the right to withhold, or double damages) for failing to give one. Your claims against the deposit rest on ordinary proof of the home's condition, so a joint move-in and move-out report is still your best evidence.

title: Nonrefundable Fees and Deposits
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no deposit statute and no rule on nonrefundable deposits, so whether money is refundable depends on what the lease says. Money given to secure the tenant's performance or against damage is a refundable security deposit unless the lease clearly says otherwise; a form lease is read against the landlord who drafted it. If you charge a nonrefundable fee (for example a pet fee), name it as a fee, state its amount and what it pays for, and list it with the other required fees, as Puerto Rico's purchase-receipt transparency law requires for mandatory charges. Do not call a nonrefundable amount a "deposit".

title: No Separate Nonrefundable-Deposit Notice
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no rule requiring a separate written notice, when you collect money, that part of it is nonrefundable. State any nonrefundable fee in the lease's fee list and show it separately on the receipt; label the rest as the refundable security deposit.

title: No Security Deposit Cap
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no security-deposit statute and sets no maximum deposit, no tier by tenancy type, no limit on extra deposits for pets or alterations, and no rule on raising a deposit later. The deposit is whatever the lease sets. Two general rules still apply: a court may undo or adjust a contract in which one side knowingly exploits the other's need, inexperience or dependence to gain a grossly disproportionate advantage, and fair-housing law bars deposits that differ by a protected characteristic. A larger deposit for a tenant with a service or assistance animal, or as a condition of a disability accommodation, is barred by federal fair-housing rules. Raise a deposit during the lease only by a signed amendment.

title: Where to Hold the Deposit
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no security-deposit statute, so an owner who rents directly faces no rule on where to keep a deposit, no separate-account or bank requirement and no bond. Keep it in a separate, clearly labelled account anyway and record it on the receipt, because you must be able to return it. Licensed real estate brokers and real estate companies are different: when a broker acts as intermediary in a lease or in administering property, the Real Estate Brokers Act requires deposits received from clients to be placed in a special escrow account at a bank in Puerto Rico, kept separate from the broker's operating and personal accounts, with records of each deposit and whom it belongs to. If a broker or management company collects your tenants' deposits, confirm it uses that account.

title: No Interest Due on the Deposit
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute requiring interest on a security deposit. The Civil Code does not classify a lease security deposit, and two of its rules point different ways: someone who receives a thing for safekeeping must return it with its fruits and may not use it, but money the holder is allowed to use becomes a loan, and a loan bears no interest unless the parties expressly agree. To remove the doubt, say in the lease whether you may hold the deposit with your other funds and whether any interest is paid; the library offers an optional clause that does both.

title: Waiving Deposit Rights
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no deposit statute, so no statute makes deposit rights non-waivable; the lease governs the deposit. General limits still apply: a person may waive legal rights only where the waiver is not prohibited or contrary to law, morals or public order and does not harm third parties; liability for fraud can never be waived; and in a form lease a clause that excludes or limits the landlord's liability, or restricts the tenant's defenses or evidence, is especially annullable. So do not write that the tenant gives up the right to the deposit's return, to an accounting or to dispute deductions, and do not make the whole deposit a forfeit for any breach; a fixed forfeiture is a penalty a court may reduce if extremely out of proportion.

title: The Deposit When You Sell
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute on what happens to a security deposit when the landlord sells the property. A sale does not shorten the lease unless the lease provides otherwise, so the buyer takes the property with the tenancy. No statute moves the duty to return the deposit to the buyer: you, as the landlord who received it, remain liable to the tenant unless the tenant agrees to look to the buyer instead, because a new debtor can replace the old one only with the creditor's consent. At closing, transfer the deposit (or credit it) to the buyer, have the buyer assume the return duty in writing, give the tenant written notice with the buyer's name and address, and ask the tenant to sign a release of you; keep the records.

title: No Statutory Deposit Penalty; General Contract Damages Apply
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no security-deposit statute, so there is no statutory penalty such as double or triple damages or automatic forfeiture for mishandling a deposit. The deposit is governed by your lease and Puerto Rico's general contract law. If you keep deposit money the lease does not entitle you to keep, the tenant can sue for the amount withheld plus damages; once you are in default (after the tenant demands it, or from a fixed return date your lease sets), you also owe interest at the rate your lease sets or, if none, the legal rate fixed for court judgments. If you withhold deliberately and in bad faith, you answer for all the damages that flow from it, and no lease clause can waive that liability. The same rules apply to a fixed term, to a lease continuing on the same terms after the term ends, and to an oral lease. Return the balance promptly with a written, itemized list of what you kept and why.

title: Deposit Return: No Statutory Deadline in Puerto Rico
bodyText:
Puerto Rico has no statute that sets a deadline for returning a security deposit, requires an itemized statement, or makes the tenant give a forwarding address. Your lease sets those terms, so state a clear return period in it. You may keep only what the lease allows, and for damage only what goes beyond normal deterioration from time and ordinary use, since the tenant must return the home in the condition received except for that deterioration. If you keep money without basis, the tenant can sue for it with damages and interest. Send a written, itemized list with the balance and keep move-in and move-out photos.

If you hold deposits in the course of a business and a refund goes unclaimed for five years after it fell due and after you told the tenant it was available, Puerto Rico's unclaimed-money law presumes it abandoned and requires a yearly report to the Office of the Commissioner of Financial Institutions.

These rules apply to every kind of tenancy.

title: No Deposit-Standards Disclosure Rule in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no rule requiring you to post or hand out the standards you use to set deposit amounts, even if you charge different tenants different deposits; it has no security-deposit statute at all. Fair housing law still applies: the federal Fair Housing Act bars setting a deposit differently because of a protected trait, so base any difference on written, neutral screening criteria and apply them the same way to every applicant.

title: Using the Deposit: The Lease Decides; No Fixed Charge Schedule
bodyText:
Puerto Rico has no statute listing what a security deposit may be used for; your lease decides. The shared clause lets you apply the deposit to unpaid rent and other defaults and to damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, which matches the tenant's duty under Puerto Rico's Civil Code to return the home in the condition received except for deterioration from time and ordinary use.

Puerto Rico law allows contracts to fix damages in advance, so that the creditor need not prove the loss and the debtor cannot show it was smaller. In a form lease the tenant had to accept as written, however, a clause that restricts the tenant's defenses or evidence is especially open to annulment, so the library offers no fixed schedule of cleaning or repair charges to be kept from the deposit. Charge actual, documented costs instead. A landlord who still wants a fixed schedule should take legal advice before adding one.

This covers Puerto Rico statutes only: municipal ordinances, DACO regulations and case law were not searched.

title: No Separate Utility-Deposit Rule in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no rule for a separate utility deposit that you hold, and no special refund deadline for one. If you collect money to secure utility charges the tenant owes you under the lease, treat it as part of the security deposit: say in the lease what it secures and when it will be returned, and return any balance with a written, itemized statement. Deposits that the electric or water provider charges the tenant are between the tenant and the provider; Puerto Rico's consumer bill of rights entitles the tenant to the provider's guidance on them, and to service on showing legal authorization to occupy the home, such as the lease.

title: Alterations and Improvements Under Puerto Rico Law
bodyText:
Under Puerto Rico's Civil Code a tenant may not make improvements that the lease prohibits, that change the substance or form of the property, or after you have justifiably asked for the property back. A tenant who does make useful or decorative improvements cannot make you pay for them, but may remove them at the end if that can be done without damaging the property, unless the lease says otherwise; the library's alterations clause requires your written consent and keeps approved alterations with the property, which Puerto Rico law allows.

The tenant must put up with urgent improvements you have to make during the lease, and you may not make improvements that reduce the use the tenant agreed to.

Federal fair housing law separately lets a tenant with a disability make reasonable modifications at the tenant's own expense; you may, where reasonable, require the interior to be restored at the end. These rules apply to every kind of tenancy.

title: No Bed Bug or Pest Statute in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute on bed bugs or other pests in rental housing: nothing sets inspection or treatment deadlines, assigns treatment costs or spells out a tenant's duty to cooperate. The Civil Code's general rules apply: the tenant must keep up the home and tell you about any condition you need to repair, and you must make necessary repairs within a reasonable time after the tenant tells you. To inspect, you need a justified reason and seven days' prior notice. The library's optional pest clause adds reporting, preparation and fault-based cost terms.

title: No Professional Carpet Cleaning Rule in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute on professional carpet cleaning at move-out: nothing requires it and nothing forbids a lease term requiring it. The tenant must return the home in the condition received except for deterioration from time and ordinary use, and what the parties agree in the lease binds them. If the carpets were professionally cleaned right before the tenancy, the library's optional carpet clause lets you require professional cleaning at the end and charge the actual reasonable cost against the deposit if the tenant does not do it. Without such a clause, charge only for soiling beyond ordinary use.

title: Cold-Weather Vacating Notice: Not Applicable in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no freezing season and no statute requiring a tenant to warn you before vacating in cold weather, so this topic does not apply. A tenant's duty to tell you about conditions that need repair still applies all year (see the library's maintenance rows).

title: Construction Worker Wage Liens on Your Property
bodyText:
Puerto Rico gives construction workers a lien for their unpaid wages on the building they worked on, whether the work was directed by the owner or done through contractors, and the lien is paid ahead of the owner's other debts. A worker must first demand payment from the owner, may sue within one year after the work ends, and can recover costs and attorney's fees from the owner. A creditor financing construction work can also note its claim in the Property Registry while the work lasts.

The law does not say whether work a tenant orders on its own can burden your property, and no court decisions were searched, so assume it can. Require your written consent before any work, and if you allow tenant work, use the library's optional no-liens clause so the tenant pays everyone, tells contractors it is not acting for you, and clears any claim quickly.

title: Noise and Nuisance Rules in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no landlord-tenant noise statute, but a tenant's disturbing conduct can be a nuisance: anything harmful to health, offensive to the senses or that interferes with the comfortable use of property gives neighbors a court action to stop it and recover damages, and a municipal judge can issue a provisional order in a neighbor dispute over such disturbances. In a condominium unit, no occupant may make noise or nuisances that disturb other owners or neighbors, and the unit owner answers to the other owners for violations by anyone occupying the unit, including a tenant. The library's no-disturbance clause makes these limits lease terms; a tenant who breaches them is in breach of the lease, and the tenant may not change the agreed use of the home.

title: Extended Absence: No Statutory Notice Duty in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute requiring a tenant to tell you before an extended absence. Puerto Rico's Civil Code does require the tenant to use the home, and lets you end the lease if the tenant abandons it or stops using it, so an absence-notice term helps you tell a vacation from an abandonment before you act. The library's absence clause asks the tenant to notify you of any absence over seven days and lets you recover actual damages for a willful failure. Entering during an absence still needs a justified reason and seven days' notice under the entry rules.

title: Family Child Care in a Rental Home
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute requiring you to allow a tenant to run a family child care home, and none that limits a lease term restricting one. Puerto Rico's Department of the Family licenses a family child care home (a family that regularly cares for up to six unrelated children for part of the day), and the licensing law bars selling or leasing a licensed establishment, or the property where it operates, to anyone without the Department's certificate of eligibility. If you know a tenant will run licensed child care in the home, ask for the license or eligibility certificate and get legal advice before signing. Your lease's residential-use clause binds the tenant, who may not change the agreed use of the home; say in the lease whether in-home child care is allowed.

title: Home Businesses in a Rental Home
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute making a home-based business a permitted use of a rented home, and none that stops a lease from restricting one. The tenant may not change the use agreed in the lease, even if the change does not harm you, and you may end the lease if the tenant does; in a condominium, each apartment may be used only as the deed allows. Say in the lease whether work from home or a home business is allowed, for example allowing office work with no customer visits, signs or inventory. Zoning and permit rules and condominium bylaws may also limit business use.

title: Co-Tenant Liability Must Be Stated Expressly in Puerto Rico
bodyText: In Puerto Rico, co-tenants are not each liable for the whole rent unless the lease says so expressly. Without that clause, the debt is presumed divided, and each co-tenant owes only an equal share. The library's joint-and-several clause supplies the express term, so you can collect the full rent or damages from any one of the tenants. Be careful when one co-tenant pays only that person's share: if you demand or acknowledge a payment of that person's share without a reservation, Puerto Rico law treats it as a waiver of full liability for that person, though the others remain liable for the rest. When you accept a partial payment from one co-tenant, write on the receipt that it is accepted without waiving joint and several liability.

title: Yard Upkeep and Irrigation in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute on landscaping or irrigation in rentals. Its Civil Code makes the tenant keep up and maintain the property and tell you about conditions that need repair, so a lease term giving the tenant reasonable yard upkeep is lawful, and no separate signed agreement or payment is needed for it. Put the tasks in the lease itself; a chore added after signing changes the contract and needs the same form as the original lease. In a condominium, common gardens are the condominium's responsibility, not the tenant's.

title: No Lien for a Tenant's Unpaid Utility Bills
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute that turns a tenant's unpaid water, sewer, electric or garbage bill into a lien on your property. Water and electric balances are the personal debt of the customer named on the account: the water and electric authorities may not bill a former tenant's balance to the next customer at the same home or refuse that customer service because of it, unless the new customer is part of the same household or otherwise benefited from the old service. Keep each tenant's utilities in the tenant's own name. If an account is in your name, you are the customer and owe the bill yourself. Garbage fees are set by municipalities, whose ordinances were not searched.

title: Occupants and Survivors in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute limiting how many people may live in a rented home; fire-safety occupancy rules for buildings exist in regulations that were not searched. Listing every occupant in the lease matters in Puerto Rico for another reason: when a tenant of a home dies, family members who lived there for the six months before the death, or another person who lived there for that time, may take the tenant's place under the lease. Federal fair housing law bars limits that discriminate against families with children, so any occupancy limit you set should be reasonable and applied the same way to everyone.

title: Agreed Use of the Home in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico's Civil Code makes the tenant keep to the use agreed in the lease, even if a different use would not harm you, and lets you end the lease if the tenant changes that use. The library's residential-use clause states that use; a tenant who runs a business or another non-residential activity in breach of it gives you a statutory ground to end the lease. In a condominium, each apartment may be used only as the deed allows and never for unlawful purposes. Renting rooms to students can make you a licensed student-housing business; see the student housing rows.

title: Smoking and Cannabis Rules for Puerto Rico Rentals
bodyText:
Puerto Rico's public smoking law does not apply inside people's homes, so a smoking rule for a rental unit comes only from the lease. The library's smoking clause, which bans tobacco, marijuana and vaping everywhere on the property, is lawful in Puerto Rico.

The public smoking law does ban smoking, including electronic cigarettes, in elevators of residential buildings, and in the indoor common areas of apartment and other multi-unit residential buildings wherever one or more employees work there (a doorman, guard, cleaner or maintenance worker), though not outdoors away from the work area.

Puerto Rico's medical cannabis law allows patients to use cannabis only in homes and private places, but it protects patients from discrimination only in employment; no housing protection was found, and cannabis remains illegal under federal law. If a tenant asks to use medical cannabis as a disability accommodation, get legal advice before answering.

title: Subletting Under Puerto Rico Law
bodyText: In Puerto Rico a tenant may sublease all or part of the home unless the lease expressly prohibits it, and where the lease is silent you may refuse a subtenant or assignee only if that person lacks the tenant's financial qualifications or the planned use would cause you economic harm. The library's clause prohibits subleasing and assignment expressly and lets you agree case by case in writing. If a sublease does happen, the tenant stays liable to you, and you may sue the subtenant directly for unpaid rent and other breaches. In a condominium, the condominium itself may limit short-term rentals only through its deed or bylaws, but your lease can still forbid your tenant from offering the home as a short-term rental. Subletting rooms to students can bring the student-housing licensing rules into play.

title: Tenant Must Report Claims Against the Property
bodyText: Puerto Rico's Civil Code requires the tenant to tell you about any usurpation of, disturbance of, or easement imposed or attempted on the leased property, as well as any damage you need to repair. The library's clause applies that duty to court proceedings: a tenant who is served with or learns of a proceeding to recover the property or its possession must tell you at once and hand you any written notice. These rules apply to every kind of tenancy.

title: Tenant's Insurance and Your Repair Duties
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute on whether you may require a tenant to make a claim on the tenant's own renter's insurance. You may require the tenant to carry insurance for the tenant's own belongings and liability, but you may not use the tenant's policy to cover your own repair duties: you must make necessary repairs within a reasonable time after notice, and in a form lease a clause that excludes or limits your liability is especially open to annulment. If the tenant caused the damage, you may recover the cost from the tenant directly; whether the tenant then claims on its own policy is the tenant's choice.

title: Tenant Upkeep and Repair Duties in Puerto Rico
bodyText:
Puerto Rico's Civil Code requires the tenant to keep up and maintain the property, to tell you about damage or conditions you need to repair, to make urgent necessary repairs at your cost after telling you, and to return the property in the condition received except for normal deterioration from time and ordinary use.

You must make the improvements necessary for the agreed use and carry out necessary repairs within a reasonable time after the tenant tells you. If the tenant fails to conserve the property, you may end the lease; if you fail to keep it fit for use, the tenant may. Damage the tenant causes is the tenant's breach, and you may recover the cost. Puerto Rico's current Civil Code does not make a tenant answer automatically for damage by household members or guests, so the lease should say so. These rules apply to every kind of tenancy.

title: Tenant Duties Under Puerto Rico Law
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no landlord-tenant act; the tenant's duties are set by the Civil Code. The tenant must take and use the property; keep to the agreed use; keep up and maintain the property; make urgent necessary repairs at your cost after telling you; pay rent and the utilities and charges of the tenant's own use on time; tell you about any usurpation, disturbance or damage you need to repair; let you inspect for a justified reason on seven days' notice; return the property as received except for normal deterioration; give you proof of rent payments; and refrain from improvements the lease forbids. In a condominium the tenant must also follow the Condominium Act's use rules, and the water authority can remove a sewage nuisance at the owner's, agent's or tenant's cost.

title: Who Pays Utilities in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Under Puerto Rico's Civil Code the tenant pays, on time, the utilities and charges that come with the tenant's own use of the home, unless the lease says you provide them. The library's utilities clause states that rule; list in the lease any utility you will provide. The tenant needs the lease to open water and electric accounts, and a former tenant's unpaid balance cannot be billed to the next customer. If the lease makes you provide a service such as water, electricity or an elevator, willfully cutting it off is a crime in Puerto Rico (a fine of $25 to $500, up to 90 days in jail, or both), unless the tenant is at least three months behind on rent after a certified-mail demand giving five working days to pay and warning that the services will be cut.

title: Submetered Utilities: No Interruption Rules; Resale Is Regulated
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute setting rules for interrupting electricity, water or gas that a landlord submeters and bills to tenants. Two cautions apply. First, Puerto Rico's energy law treats anyone engaged in reselling electric power as an electric service company subject to the Energy Bureau; the Energy Bureau's rules require a certification from anyone who offers billing or resale of electricity, with no exception for landlords, so do not submeter or rebill electricity to tenants. Second, if the lease makes you supply a service, willfully cutting it off is a crime (a fine of $25 to $500, up to 90 days in jail, or both), unless the tenant is at least three months behind on rent after a certified-mail demand giving five working days to pay and warning that the services will be cut. Never cut a tenant's service to collect a debt.

title: Proof of Utility Payments
bodyText: Puerto Rico's Civil Code makes the tenant pay the utilities of the tenant's own use and give you proof of rent payments. The library's clause extends the proof duty, by agreement, to utilities that are the tenant's responsibility under the lease, which is lawful. Unpaid water and electric balances follow the customer named on the account, not the property, so proof of payment mainly protects you when the account is in your name or when service to the home is at risk.

title: Keeping Utility Service On
bodyText: Puerto Rico's Civil Code makes the tenant pay the utilities of the tenant's own use and keep up the property, so a lease term forbidding the tenant to let water, electricity, gas, sewer or trash service be cut off is lawful. It applies for as long as the lease runs, including when the lease continues on the same terms after the end of the original term. Remember that the duty runs both ways: if the lease makes you supply a service, cutting it off willfully is a crime in Puerto Rico except in the narrow case of three months' unpaid rent after a certified-mail demand.

title: Smoke Alarms and Fire Safety in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico's fire code (Fire Bureau Regulation No. 7364, which adopts the national NFPA 1 fire code and the Life Safety Code) requires smoke alarms in homes. In a one- or two-family home: outside each sleeping area, on every level including any basement, and in every bedroom except in existing homes; existing homes may use battery-powered alarms. In an apartment building: in each unit outside each sleeping area and on every level, plus in every bedroom in new buildings without sprinklers, and in new construction the alarms within a unit must be interconnected. Apartment residents must get emergency instructions each year showing where the alarms are and what to do in a fire. The code makes the owner, operator or occupant responsible for compliance without dividing the duty, and calls for monthly testing of smoke alarms. It has no carbon monoxide alarm rule. Building-wide rules also apply: a building more than 75 feet tall built before 1987 and used for housing must have one of the approved fire-protection systems, such as sprinklers in selected areas plus smoke detectors in common areas; a building over four floors needs emergency lighting and exit signs; and every multi-story building, including condominiums, must keep an automatic fire extinguisher on each floor and keep escape stairs lit and clear. Violations are crimes. Install working smoke alarms where the code requires them before the tenant moves in, add carbon monoxide alarms where there is a gas appliance, generator or attached garage, and have the tenant test the alarms monthly and report any alarm that does not work.

title: No Alternate-Housing Duty in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute requiring you to provide or pay for alternate housing while the home is being repaired or after a fire or other casualty. If you fail to keep the home fit for the agreed use, the tenant may end the lease; if your improvements deprive the tenant of part of the home, the tenant may instead ask for a proportional rent reduction for the time of the deprivation. A municipal judge can also issue a quick provisional order in a landlord-tenant dispute over urgent repairs. Offering a rent reduction or a short alternative stay in writing can head off a dispute, but the law does not require it.

title: Excluding Appliances You Will Not Maintain
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute saying that appliances left at the property are presumed to be yours to maintain, and none barring you from excluding them. What you lease is what the lease describes, and you must deliver it fit for its use and repair it. Because a form lease is read against the landlord, list in the lease any item you leave but will not maintain, as the library's optional exclusion clause does. Never exclude an item whose defect could seriously affect health or safety, such as a gas appliance or water heater.

title: Appliances Included in a Puerto Rico Lease
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute listing appliances you must supply. Appliances listed in the lease are part of what you lease: you must deliver them fit for use and repair them within a reasonable time after the tenant tells you of a problem, and the tenant must take care of them and return them in the condition received except for normal wear. List every appliance and piece of equipment in the lease, and use the optional exclusion clause for anything you leave but will not maintain.

title: Common-Area Lighting in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico requires the owner of a building of more than four floors built before 1987 to keep automatic emergency lighting in the hallways, stairs, corridors and lobbies leading to exits, and every multi-story building, including condominiums, must keep its escape stairs lit and clear. These are your duties as owner and a lease cannot shift them. No statute says who pays for common-area lights wired to a tenant's electric meter. If a tenant's meter serves outside or shared lights, say so in the lease and state whether the tenant pays for them; otherwise the lease will be read against you.

title: Renting a Home Declared Unfit
bodyText: If Puerto Rico's Secretary of Health declares a vacant home unfit and orders repairs, you may not rent it, extend a lease or let anyone occupy it until the repairs are made; doing so is a crime (a fine of $50 to $100, 30 to 90 days in jail, or both), and once convicted you lose any right to rent from the day you received the Secretary's notice until the repairs are done. Separately, a municipality that finds a dwelling unfit can order you to repair it or vacate and close it, and once it is closed, renting or letting anyone occupy it as a home is illegal and draws the fine the municipal ordinance sets. A lease of a home that the law forbids occupying is open to being declared void, and the tenant may end the lease because you must deliver and keep the home fit for use. Stop charging rent from the date occupancy becomes unlawful, and check the municipal ordinance.

title: Habitability: What Puerto Rico Has and Lacks
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no habitability statute or housing code for private rentals of the kind other states have: no statutory list of required conditions, no rent-escrow procedure, no statutory non-waiver rule and no repair-and-deduct statute. Its Civil Code still requires you to deliver the home fit for its use, make the improvements needed for that use and make necessary repairs within a reasonable time after notice. The tenant must make urgent repairs at your cost after telling you, and may end the lease if you fail to keep the home fit for use. Other routes exist: a municipal judge can issue a quick provisional order on urgent repairs, municipalities can order unfit dwellings repaired or closed, the Department of Health can inspect and close unsanitary buildings, renting a vacant home the Secretary of Health has declared unfit before making the ordered repairs is a crime that costs you the rent for that period, and willfully cutting a service the lease includes is a crime. In a form lease, a clause limiting your liability is especially open to annulment.

title: Which Defects Matter Under Puerto Rico Law
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no habitability statute setting a materiality threshold. The Civil Code measures your duty by the use agreed in the lease: you must deliver the home suitable for that use and repair damage within a reasonable time after the tenant reports it, and the tenant may end the lease if you fail to keep the home fit for the agreed use, if a hidden defect breaches the Civil Code's guaranty, or, after a demand with warning, if you fail to perform a principal obligation. A minor defect that leaves the home fit for living does not by its terms justify ending the lease, but you must still repair it within a reasonable time.

title: Changing Repair Duties by Agreement in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no habitability statute with its own rule on modifying the landlord's duties. Under the Civil Code, rights may be waived unless the waiver is prohibited or against law, morals or public order, so a specific, negotiated arrangement, such as the tenant handling listed chores for a rent reduction, is lawful. But in a form lease, a clause that excludes or limits your own responsibility is especially open to annulment, so the library does not shift your basic duties to deliver the home fit for use and make necessary repairs. Liability for deliberate bad-faith breach can never be waived.

title: No Habitability Presumption in Puerto Rico Evictions
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statutory presumption that a landlord breached a habitability duty. In an eviction for nonpayment, the tenant may offer only a receipt or other document showing payment (the court may also hear evidence that the tenant contributed to the property as a co-owner), so condition complaints generally have to be raised another way, such as a separate claim. Keep repair requests and your responses in writing: they are your best evidence if the tenant later claims the home was unfit.

title: No General Fitness Statement Required
bodyText: Puerto Rico does not require a lease to state that you will deliver the home fit for habitation; the Civil Code imposes the duty anyway, since you must deliver the property in a condition suitable for its use. The one exception is a licensed student-housing business, whose leases must contain a clause certifying that the lodging complies with the student-housing law; see the student housing rows.

title: Disability Accommodations in Puerto Rico Rentals
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute spelling out a private landlord's duty to make reasonable accommodations or allow reasonable modifications for a tenant with a disability. The federal Fair Housing Act applies in Puerto Rico and does: you must allow reasonable modifications at the tenant's expense (you may require restoration of the interior where reasonable) and make reasonable exceptions to your rules, including for assistance animals. Puerto Rico's own disability laws define reasonable accommodation to include housing, bar excluding people from programs and activities because of a disability, and give people with disabilities a right to adapted housing that the government must promote; how far they reach a private landlord is unsettled. Treat every accommodation request seriously, answer in writing, and get advice before refusing one.

title: Leasing the Same Home Twice
bodyText: If you lease the same home to two people, Puerto Rico's Civil Code decides who gets it: first, the tenant whose lease is properly recorded in the Property Registry; if neither is recorded, the one who took possession first; if neither has taken possession, the one whose lease bears the earliest certain date.
