The tenant who loses may end the lease and recover damages from you, and a deliberate double lease makes you answer for all the resulting damages. Check that a home is free before signing a new lease, especially when a prior tenant's lease continues on the same terms after its term ended.

title: Background Checks for Building Staff
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute requiring a residential landlord or property manager to run background checks on its employees. Condominiums are the exception: every condominium management contract must require the managing agent to present a negative criminal-record certificate, and if the agent is a company, the certificate must cover its principal officer and every person who works directly in administering the condominium. That duty belongs to the condominium, not to an owner renting a unit. Screening anyone who will hold keys or enter tenants' homes is still good practice; follow Puerto Rico and federal limits on using criminal records in employment.

title: Health Inspections and Unfit-Dwelling Orders
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no local health-district rental codes and no rule that you hand tenants health rules on request. Health oversight is island-wide: the Department of Health may inspect any building's sanitary conditions, close a building that poses an imminent public-health problem, and fine owners, agents or managers after written notice and time to correct. If the Secretary of Health declares a vacant home unfit and orders repairs, you may not rent it or let anyone live there until the repairs are made; doing so is a crime and costs you the rent for the whole period from the notice until the repairs are done.

title: Heating: Not Applicable in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no space-heating requirement for rentals, so this topic does not apply. One related rule does: if the lease includes hot water, willfully cutting it off is a crime in Puerto Rico, except where the tenant is at least three months behind on rent after a certified-mail demand giving five working days to pay.

title: Tenant Remedies When the Landlord Breaches
bodyText: If you breach the lease, a Puerto Rico tenant may end it when you fail to keep the home fit for the agreed use, fail in your warranties against eviction or hidden defects, or deprive the tenant of part of the home through your improvements; in the last case the tenant may instead take a proportional rent reduction. The tenant may also recover damages, end the lease out of court for breach of a principal obligation after a written demand warning that the lease will be ended, make urgent repairs at your cost after telling you, and ask a municipal judge for a quick provisional order on urgent repairs. A tenant who simply stops paying rent faces a hard eviction case, since in a nonpayment eviction the tenant may offer only proof of payment (the court may also hear evidence that the tenant contributed to the property as a co-owner). Answer repair requests promptly and in writing.

title: Landlord Repair Duties Under Puerto Rico Law
bodyText: Under Puerto Rico's Civil Code you must deliver the home suitable for its use, make or pay for the improvements that use requires, carry out necessary repairs within a reasonable time after the tenant tells you of damage, avoid improvements that reduce the agreed use, and take the home back when the lease ends. The tenant must report damage and may make urgent repairs at your cost after telling you. Municipal and Department of Health orders, quick provisional orders by a municipal judge, and the crime of willfully cutting included services back up these duties. The library's maintenance clause states your repair duties and asks for written repair requests; act on any request you actually receive, however it is made.

title: No Statutory List of Shiftable Duties
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no minimum-standards statute that lists particular duties, such as common-area garbage removal, that a lease may move to the tenant on conditions. Under the Civil Code a negotiated, specific arrangement is lawful, but in a form lease a clause that shifts or limits your own responsibilities is especially open to annulment. Use the library's tenant repair agreement for listed tasks with something given in return, and keep your basic duties to deliver and keep the home fit for use.

title: No Puerto Rico List of Other Facilities You Must Supply
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute listing specific facilities you must supply inside a rental home, such as locks, window screens, a mailbox, hot water or trash containers. Your duties come from the Civil Code: deliver the home suitable for its use and make or pay for the improvements that use requires, so whatever the home needs for its agreed residential use, and everything the lease lists, is your responsibility. If the lease, expressly or by implication, has you supply hot or cold water, light, power, elevator or telephone service or another service or facility, willfully failing to supply it when it is needed is a crime in Puerto Rico. Building-wide fire-safety rules are covered in the library's fire-safety row. Check them for your building.

title: Promises to Repair
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no rule that your promise to clean, repair or improve a home must be in writing, carry a completion date or be made before the lease is signed. A lease needs no special form (only a lease of more than six years must be in writing), and a later change to a lease follows the same form as the original. What you agree to binds you, written or not, and breaking partial agreements reached while negotiating is a breach of good faith. Clauses in a form lease are read against you as the drafter. Put every promised cleaning, repair or improvement in the lease or a signed addendum, with what will be done and by when. DACO's commercial-practices regulation could not be read and may also reach promises made to tenants.

title: Quiet Enjoyment in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico's 2020 Civil Code has no separate covenant of quiet enjoyment, but the tenant gets the same protection in other ways. A lease gives the tenant the use and enjoyment of the home for its term. If you fail in your warranty against eviction (someone with a better right takes the home) the tenant may end the lease, and the Code's warranty rules make you answer for a physical disturbance that comes from you, though not for a third party's mere physical interference. In a form lease, a clause limiting your liability for these warranties is especially open to being annulled, so the library offers none. Willfully and intentionally interfering with a tenant's peaceful enjoyment is also a crime in Puerto Rico for you, your agent, manager, administrator, superintendent, caretaker or janitor (a fine of $25 to $500, up to 90 days in jail, or both). The tenant must tell you of any usurpation or disturbance of the property. A lease that was already running when the 2020 Code took effect stays under the 1930 Code, which bound the landlord to keep the tenant in peaceful enjoyment for the whole term.

title: Rent Collection and Your Repair Duties
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute saying whether a lease, an assignment, a deed, a trust or a mortgage may let someone collect the rent without the landlord's repair duties. Under the Civil Code those duties are yours as the landlord, whether you lease as the owner, a usufructuary or an administrator with power to lease, and a sale of the property does not shorten the lease. Assume that assigning the rent to a lender or having a manager collect it leaves every repair duty in place, and do not sign any lease or rent assignment that tries to separate the two.

title: Government Inspections of Rental Homes
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no rental registration or periodic rental inspection program set by statute. Inspections come from two other sources. The Department of Health may inspect any building for sanitary conditions, but except in a true emergency it inspects a home only with the permission of its lawful occupant, which for a rented home is the tenant; if the tenant refuses, the inspector may get a magistrate's order. A municipality that adopts an unfit-dwelling ordinance may let its official enter to inspect, causing the least inconvenience possible to the occupants. DACO has power to require registration of properties offered for rent, but no such regulation appeared on its 2024 list of regulations in force. A lease term cannot replace the tenant's permission or the magistrate's order, so the library offers none. Check your municipality's ordinances.

title: No Small-Landlord Remedy Exemption
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no rent-escrow procedure for repairs and no notice that lets a landlord with few units opt out of a tenant's repair remedies. A tenant's repair remedies come from the Civil Code and the provisional-remedies law (urgent repairs at your cost after notice, ending the lease or a rent reduction for your breach, and a quick order from a municipal judge on urgent repairs), and they apply to every landlord whatever the number of units. There is nothing to put in the lease.

title: How Tenants Give Repair Notice in Puerto Rico
bodyText: In Puerto Rico your duty to make necessary repairs within a reasonable time starts when the tenant tells you about the damage, and no law says how the tenant must tell you: a call, a text, a conversation or a letter all count. The tenant must report damage and conditions you need to repair, and may make urgent repairs at your cost only after telling you. The library's maintenance clause asks the tenant for prompt written notice; treat that as a request. Act on any notice you actually receive, keep a record of it, and never refuse a repair because the request was not in writing. In a form lease, a term that only written notice counts, or that limits how the tenant may prove notice, is especially open to being annulled.

title: No Security-Device or Re-Keying Statute
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute requiring you to install deadbolts, peepholes, window latches or security bars, or to re-key the locks between tenants. You must still deliver a home suitable for its use, which in practice means exterior doors and windows that close and lock. Re-keying or changing the locks at each turnover is good practice, and a domestic-violence victim may be advised to change the locks (see the library's domestic-violence lock-change row).

title: Staff Certification in Older-Adult Housing
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no work-card rule for staff of ordinary 55-plus apartments. But if your property is an égida (a housing complex for older adults that provides services) or otherwise provides care or services to people 60 or older, every person providing those services, and every employee or contractor with habitual contact with the residents, must first obtain the Department of Health's SICHDe certification showing no conviction for the listed crimes, and is subject to routine criminal-history updates. Whether a senior building that only leases units and provides no services is covered is not settled; if you provide any on-site services, get the certification for every staff member who deals with residents.

title: Services You Provide Under a Puerto Rico Lease
bodyText: In Puerto Rico the tenant pays the utilities and charges that come with the tenant's own use of the home unless the lease says you provide them, so list every service you will provide. Once the lease, expressly or by implication, has you supply water, light, power, elevator, telephone or another service, willfully failing to supply it when it is needed is a crime (a fine of $25 to $500, up to 90 days in jail, or both), with a narrow exception after three months of unpaid rent and a certified-mail demand. Under the Civil Code no one answers for events that could not be foreseen or avoided, so an outage you could not prevent is not your breach. See the library's utilities rows for who pays and for keeping service on.

title: No Stove or Refrigerator Requirement
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute requiring you to supply a stove or refrigerator. If the lease includes one, it is part of what you lease: deliver it working and repair it within a reasonable time after the tenant reports a problem. List every appliance in the lease, and use the library's appliance-exclusion clause for anything you leave in the home but will not maintain.

title: Repair Orders for Unfit Homes; No Receivership
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no rental receivership: no court or agency appoints a receiver to collect rents and fix a private rental. Repair orders come from two places. A municipality that adopts an unfit-dwelling ordinance may, after notice and a hearing, order you to repair a home or, at your option, vacate and close it; if you do not comply it can close the home, fine anyone who rents it, and for a dangerous building have it repaired or demolished, with the cost becoming a lien collected like a special tax. The Department of Health can also close an unfit home and order repairs; renting it before the repairs are made is a crime and costs you the rent for that period. These rules apply whatever the number of units. Check your municipality's ordinance.

title: Cable, Satellite and Internet Access
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute giving tenants a right to cable, satellite or internet service in a rental building, requiring you to let providers wire the building, or barring a rent difference for subscribers. Federal rules on satellite dishes and antennas, and on cable and broadband service in apartment buildings, may still apply; check them before limiting a tenant's dish or choice of provider. In a condominium, the building's rules also govern installations on common elements.

title: Tenant Repair Remedies in Puerto Rico
bodyText:
A Puerto Rico tenant whose home needs repairs may make urgent repairs at your cost after telling you, end the lease if you fail to keep the home fit for the agreed use, take a proportional rent reduction while your own improvements deprive the tenant of part of the home, withhold performance while you fail to perform, and ask a municipal judge for a quick provisional order on urgent repairs.

Puerto Rico has no repair-and-deduct statute and no rent escrow while a home is unfit, and a tenant who stops paying rent can be evicted in a case where only proof of payment counts (the court may also hear evidence that the tenant contributed to the property as a co-owner). Damage the tenant, an occupant or a guest causes is the tenant's to repair or pay for.

title: Utilities You Agree to Pay
bodyText: If the lease says you pay a utility, that service becomes one the lease requires you to supply, and in Puerto Rico willfully failing to supply it when needed is a crime (a fine of $25 to $500, up to 90 days in jail, or both), except in the narrow case of three months' unpaid rent after a certified-mail demand giving five working days to pay. Keep the accounts paid and never cut a listed service to pressure a tenant. Including a utility in a fixed rent is not reselling it; charging tenants separately for electricity, by meter, formula or reimbursement of a bill, may make you an electric service company that needs the Energy Bureau's certification, so the library does not do it.

title: Splitting Utility Bills Among Tenants
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute barring or regulating a lease term that splits a building's utility bill among tenants by a formula. Apportioning water or gas is a matter for the lease; state the method, the share and how the tenant sees the bill. Electricity is different: Puerto Rico's energy law treats anyone engaged in billing or reselling electric power as an electric service company regulated by the Energy Bureau, and its rules require that company to hold a certification, with no exception for landlords. Do not divide an electric bill among tenants or charge for electricity separately; include it in the rent or have each tenant hold the account.

title: No Utility Shutoff-Notice Authorization
bodyText: Puerto Rico law has no procedure for you to receive copies of a tenant's utility disconnection notices. Utility suspension notices go only to the customer on the account. If you need warning of a shutoff, ask the tenant to share notices or require the tenant to keep service on (see the library's service-continuity row); a utility's own customer rules may let the tenant add you as a contact.

title: Utilities in Your Name
bodyText: If a utility account for your rental is in your name, you are the customer: the utility must give you its billing-objection period and written suspension notices, may not cut service on a Friday, weekend, holiday or the working day before a holiday, and may not cut residential electric or water service for nonpayment from a storm or hurricane warning until ten days after the emergency ends. Puerto Rico gives your tenants no right to notice of a shutoff caused by your unpaid bill and no right to pay it and deduct it from rent. But if the lease includes the service, letting it be cut by willfully not paying can be a crime, and the tenant may withhold performance or end the lease. Keep landlord-held accounts current.

title: Utility Shutoff Rules in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico's utilities must follow set steps before cutting water or electric service for nonpayment. The customer gets time to pay or object to a bill and ask for an investigation (20 days for water and other public utilities, 30 days for electricity), then a written suspension warning, and a cutoff only after the warning period and a 48-hour notice; service is never cut on a Friday, weekend, holiday or the working day before a holiday. From a tropical-storm or hurricane warning, or an emergency declaration for one, no residential electric or water service may be cut for nonpayment until ten days after the emergency ends. These rules protect whoever holds the account: you, for accounts in your name, or your tenant. They do not let you cut a tenant's service yourself.

title: No Submetering Disclosure Statute
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute requiring a lease disclosure when you submeter or separately bill tenants for utilities, and none setting billing limits or late-fee caps for those charges. If you bill water or gas separately, the lease should state the method, the rate source and when payment is due. Do not submeter and rebill electricity without advice: Puerto Rico's energy law treats anyone engaged in billing or reselling electric power as an electric company regulated by the Energy Bureau.

title: No Cutoff for Untransferred Utilities
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no rule letting you cut off utilities still in your name because the tenant did not transfer them. A willful cut of a service the lease has you supply, or willful interference with the tenant's peaceful enjoyment, is a crime. Use the library's optional clause: the tenant transfers named services by a deadline and repays the provider's actual charges until then (electricity excepted: it goes in the tenant's name from the first day of the term, and you never charge for it), and you never cut service to force the transfer.

title: Lock Changes for Domestic-Violence Victims
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute letting a domestic-violence victim change a rental's locks or requiring you to change them. A court protection order can order the abuser out of a shared home whatever right the abuser claims to it, and can order that rent keep being paid; the court's safety-plan guide may advise the victim to change every lock. If a tenant with a protection order asks, change or allow a change of the locks promptly, keep a key yourself, and give no key to a person the order excludes. Federal law (VAWA) adds rules for federally assisted housing.

title: Inspections on Seven Days' Notice
bodyText: In Puerto Rico you may inspect the home for a justified reason, such as a periodic condition check, a reported problem or move-out, on at least seven days' prior notice. Count the seven days by excluding the day you give notice and including the last day (move it if the last day is an official holiday). The library's entry clause uses written notice stating the reason and date. Keep inspections to a real purpose and a reasonable hour.

title: No Key-Control Mandate
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no rule requiring a key-control policy, a key log or background checks for employees who can enter tenants' homes, at any size of complex. Good practice is still to keep keys locked and logged, re-key after a key is lost or an employee leaves, and screen anyone who holds keys. In a condominium, an outgoing managing agent must hand over the building's keys against a receipt.

title: Entry Rules in Puerto Rico
bodyText:
In Puerto Rico the tenant must let you in for a justified reason on at least seven days' prior notice, and must put up with urgent improvements that cannot wait until the lease ends; the library's entry clause sets this out, with an emergency exception for real dangers.

If a tenant refuses a proper entry, demand it in writing; the refusal is a breach of the lease that can support a damages claim, but it is not on the Civil Code's list of grounds for ending the lease. Entering without a justified reason or proper notice, or using entry to harass, can be a crime (willful interference with the tenant's peaceful enjoyment) and an abuse of right that costs you damages.

No Puerto Rico rule treats a repair request as permission to enter without notice, and none lets a separate form shorten the seven days. In a condominium, the building's repairs also give a right of entry; health inspectors need the tenant's permission or a magistrate's order.

title: Scheduled Service Visits
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no rule letting you skip the seven-day entry notice for regular services such as filter changes or pest treatment, even if the lease says so. You can still plan them: send one written notice, at least seven days ahead, listing the dates and hours of the scheduled visits, and the library's entry clause covers them as justified entries.

title: Showing the Home on Shorter Notice
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no rule letting a tenant give up the seven-day notice for showings in advance, and the library does not shorten it. Showing the home to prospective tenants or buyers is a justified reason for entry on seven days' notice; for a showing on shorter notice, ask the tenant each time and proceed only with the tenant's agreement for that showing.

title: Smart Locks and Electronic Entry
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute on smart locks or app-based or biometric entry systems in rentals. A remote unlock is still an entry: give the seven days' notice for a justified reason. Tell tenants what access data the system records and who can see it, keep a physical way in for emergencies, and dispose of tenant data securely when it is no longer needed.

title: Belongings Left Behind in Puerto Rico
bodyText:
Puerto Rico has no statute setting a procedure for belongings a tenant leaves behind. The Civil Code lets someone acquire movables that are truly abandoned, but things whose owner is unknown must be handed to the municipality, and belongings are not abandoned just because a tenant left them. At a court eviction the marshal removes the occupants and supervises the removal of their belongings, which your helpers carry out. Never remove a tenant or the tenant's things yourself without a court order. Before disposing of anything, give the tenant written notice and a reasonable time to collect it; the library's optional clause sets this up.

No Puerto Rico statute sets the collection period; the library's clause suggests at least 15 days after your notice.

title: When a Tenant Abandons: Rent and Re-Letting
bodyText: If a Puerto Rico tenant abandons the home, you may end the lease under the Civil Code, or keep it in force and claim the rent and other damages the tenant's breach causes. No statute requires you to re-let, but your damages are limited to what was foreseeable and you must act in good faith; make reasonable efforts to re-let and credit any rent you receive. In a lease that has continued past its term on the same terms, either side may end it by notice, so your claim is limited accordingly.

title: Attorney's Fees in Puerto Rico Lease Disputes
bodyText: In a Puerto Rico court case the winning party recovers its costs, and a party (or lawyer) who litigated with obstinacy or frivolousness must be ordered to pay attorney's fees. No statute requires a lease fee clause to be mutual or caps the fees a landlord may recover, but whether a lease can shift fees beyond those court rules depends on court decisions that were not searched. The library's default clause lets the prevailing party recover reasonable fees only to the extent Puerto Rico law allows; keep it mutual.

title: The Federal 30-Day Notice and Puerto Rico Law
bodyText: If your Puerto Rico rental has a federally backed mortgage or is in a covered federal housing program, federal law requires a 30-day notice to vacate before you file a nonpayment eviction. Puerto Rico itself has no notice-to-quit statute: to end a lease for breach out of court you must demand performance under warning that the lease will be ended, and a lease continuing after its term ends on notice. For a covered property, give the federal 30-day notice as well, and file only after it runs.

title: Fire and Other Casualty in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico's Civil Code has no fire or casualty article in its lease chapter. The general rules apply: if the home is destroyed without anyone's fault the lease obligations end; if it is partly destroyed the lease can continue for the usable part at a proportionally lower rent; a temporary impossibility suspends performance; and the tenant may end the lease if you fail to keep the home fit for its use. If the tenant, an occupant or a guest caused the damage, the tenant answers for it. The library's optional clause lets you end the lease after a serious casualty by written notice and states how rent is reduced.

title: Converting a Rental Building to Condominiums
bodyText: Puerto Rico law now in force gives tenants no special notice, waiting period or right to buy when a rental building is converted to a condominium, and no rule against converting rental housing to transient use. The repealed condominium law let DACO protect tenants living in a building before conversion. DACO's current condominium regulation (No. 9386, in force since July 2022, which replaced No. 6728) requires a building that is wholly or partly rented to be registered with DACO before conversion, but gives tenants no notice or right to buy. Give tenants generous notice anyway.

title: Criminal Activity at a Puerto Rico Rental
bodyText: In Puerto Rico it is a crime to lease a house or building for use for prostitution, or, as owner, administrator or manager, to permit people to be there habitually to practice it. No statute makes you evict for other crimes or sets a special procedure. The library's criminal-activity clause makes criminal activity on the property a serious breach you can act on through the default clause, with a written demand warning that you will end the lease. It does not apply when the tenant or a household member is the victim, or to calls for police or emergency help.

title: Cure Periods and Grounds for Ending a Lease
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statutory cure periods. To end a lease for a tenant's breach out of court, the tenant must be in default and you must demand performance under warning that you will end the lease; the lease ends when the demand's deadline passes. You may also end it on the Civil Code's own grounds: abandonment or change of use, failure to conserve the home, or two consecutive unpaid rental periods. The cure periods in the library's default clause are contract terms; the eviction itself always needs a court case.

title: Delivering Default Notices on Paper
bodyText: Give default, cure and eviction-related notices to a Puerto Rico tenant on paper, by hand or by certified mail with return receipt, even if the lease lets you e-mail other notices. Puerto Rico's electronic-transactions law expressly does not cover notices of default, eviction or the right to cure on a lease of a principal residence, so an e-mailed default notice may not count. Keep proof of delivery: the default clause's demand, warning that you will end the lease, is what lets the lease end when its deadline passes.

title: After a Hurricane or Other Disaster
bodyText:
After a hurricane or other declared disaster, Puerto Rico law does not end the lease automatically. If the disaster destroys the home, the lease obligations end; if it makes the home temporarily unusable, the tenant may suspend paying rent while it lasts, and a partial loss can lead to reduced rent for the usable part.

Residential electric and water service may not be cut for nonpayment from a storm warning until ten days after the emergency ends. Prices of essential goods and services are frozen automatically while a declared emergency lasts; DACO's emergency price regulation treats anything leased or rented that people need because of the emergency as an essential article, and its freeze orders bar raising rental prices; it does not name housing, so do not raise rent while a declared emergency or a DACO freeze order is in force (see No General Rent Control in Puerto Rico).

Talk to tenants early about repairs, rent for the affected period and whether either side wants to end the lease.

title: No Drug-Free Housing Addendum Rule
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute requiring or regulating a drug-free housing addendum. The library's criminal-activity clause already makes illegal drug activity on the property a serious breach. In federally assisted housing, follow the federal program's own lease rules.

title: Domestic Violence and Eviction in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute barring the eviction of a tenant because of domestic violence against the tenant. But a protection order can order the abuser out of a shared home whatever right the abuser claims and can order that rent keep being paid, and a person sued for eviction who claims a community of property through contributions to the shared home may require an ordinary court action instead of the quick eviction case. Federal law protects victims in covered federally assisted housing. Do not evict a victim for the abuser's acts; act against the abuser and keep accepting rent from the victim.

title: No Domestic-Violence Lease-Termination Statute
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute letting a domestic-violence, sexual-assault, trafficking or stalking victim end a lease early. A court protection order can remove the abuser from the home and order rent to keep being paid. You may agree with a victim to end the lease early, and doing so promptly and without a fee is good practice. Federally assisted housing has its own federal rules for victims.

title: No Domestic-Violence Documentation Rule
bodyText: Puerto Rico law sets no list of documents a domestic-violence victim must give a landlord, because Puerto Rico has no statutory right to end a lease on that ground. If you agree to release a victim from a lease, a copy of a court protection order is the usual proof; keep it confidential.

title: Ending a Lease Early in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico lets the parties agree in the lease to end it early. The library's early-termination clause gives a fixed-term tenant that option on 30 days' written notice for a flat fee of one month's rent, after which no later rent is owed; in Puerto Rico the fee is a penalty clause a court may reduce only if it is extremely disproportionate. Puerto Rico's consumer-contract law lets a consumer end an adhesion contract the same way it was made, so if the lease was signed online or by e-mail, accept the tenant's early-termination notice the same way. That law does not shorten the term or cancel the agreed fee.

title: Eminent Domain and the Lease
bodyText: In Puerto Rico a tenant's interest in leased property can itself be expropriated, so the tenant may be entitled to its own share of compensation. If the whole property is taken, the lease ends because you can no longer give the tenant its use; if only part is taken, the lease can continue for the rest, with the rent adjusted. You are not liable to the tenant for the taking. The library does not offer a clause giving you the tenant's share of the award.

title: Entity Landlords in Eviction Court
bodyText: Puerto Rico's eviction law lets the parties in cases before a municipal judge appear on their own behalf or through a lawyer, and the court's guides say the same. No statute or court rule found says whether a corporation or LLC landlord may appear through a non-lawyer manager or officer; that turns on court decisions that were not searched. If your landlord is an entity, appear through an attorney.

title: Environmental Events and the Lease
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute letting you or the tenant end a lease because of an environmental or public-health event, such as contamination, a chemical spill or flooding, or a government order to vacate. The Civil Code's general rules decide: a permanent impossibility ends the lease obligations, a temporary one suspends them, and either side may withhold its own performance while the other cannot perform. The library's optional casualty clause covers damage to the home.

title: Delays and Protections in Puerto Rico Evictions
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no general hardship delay for evictions. If the court finds the household is a family of proven insolvency, or the tenant is a veteran, an older adult or a person with a disability, it notifies the agencies that help them and the removal period after judgment is 20 days that cannot be extended; an insolvent family cannot be removed unless Family and Housing officials are present. A tenant may appeal within five days but must post a bond, or in a nonpayment case deposit the rent owed and keep depositing rent as it comes due. The courts also ran a temporary program pausing nonpayment cases for 60 days while a rent-assistance application was pending; check whether it still applies.

title: How Eviction Works in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Every eviction in Puerto Rico goes through court (desahucio); removing a tenant yourself is illegal. You file the complaint (court form OAT-931) with the summons (OAT-972); the hearing must be held within ten days of filing, in person or by videoconference, and the judge must decide within ten days after it. In a nonpayment case the tenant may defend only with a receipt or other document showing payment (the court may also hear evidence that the tenant contributed to the property as a co-owner), and you may join a claim for the rent owed. The tenant may appeal within five days by posting a bond or, in a nonpayment case, depositing the rent. Once the judgment is final you ask the court for the removal order (OAT-1742); the marshal carries it out with you present, your helpers remove belongings under the marshal's supervision, and you may change the locks. Removal waits 20 days, counted from the court's notice of the judgment to the agencies that help them, for veterans, older adults, people with disabilities and (on the cautious reading) families of proven insolvency, and an insolvent family cannot be removed unless officials of the Departments of the Family and of Housing are present.

title: Eviction Records in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute or court rule sealing eviction records or removing them from public view. The courts' temporary eviction-prevention program let a tenant in a qualifying nonpayment case ask that the case be marked confidential in the court system while it was paused for rent assistance. Assume an eviction case you file will otherwise be public.

title: Serving Eviction Papers in Puerto Rico
bodyText: A Puerto Rico eviction summons is served on the tenant personally or on an agent the tenant has authorized or the law designates; if the tenant is not found where the case is brought, the summons may be served on whoever looks after the property for the tenant there. Puerto Rico has no rule letting the lease name someone to accept court papers, and the library does not offer one: a defective service can undo the whole case.

title: No Fast-Track Eviction for Crime
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no special fast-track eviction for violent crime or drug activity. Every eviction uses the same quick court procedure, with a hearing within ten days of filing. Use the library's criminal-activity and default clauses to end the lease for criminal activity, then file the eviction.

title: Tenants When the Property Is Foreclosed
bodyText: No Puerto Rico statute requires you to tell a tenant or applicant that the property is in foreclosure, and none gives a tenant notice or keeps the lease in force at a foreclosure sale. Under Puerto Rico's Registry Act, the buyer at a mortgage-foreclosure sale is put in possession by the court marshal, and after 20 days the court may order the removal of everyone occupying the property by the owner's order or tolerance, which can include your tenant, without a separate eviction suit. A lease recorded in the Property Registry before the mortgage survives the sale; most residential leases are not recorded (only leases of six years or more, or those the parties agree to record, can be). Federal law fills much of the gap: the Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act applies in Puerto Rico and generally requires whoever takes title at foreclosure to honor a bona fide tenant's lease to the end of its term (a buyer who will live in the home may end it early) and to give at least 90 days' written notice to vacate. If your mortgage is in default, tell your tenant early and in writing; a tenant who loses the home because of your default can claim damages from you under the lease.

title: No Statutory Right to Pay and Stay After Termination
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute that lets a tenant who is behind on rent undo the end of the lease, or stop your eviction case, simply by paying what is owed before the hearing or before removal. Under the Civil Code, once you have demanded payment in writing with a warning that you will end the lease, and the time you gave has run out, the lease is ended; a later payment does not bring it back unless you agree. Before that point, if the tenant offers the full amount and you refuse it without reason, you are in default and the tenant can deposit it in court. In a nonpayment eviction the tenant may defend only with a receipt or other document proving payment (the court may also hear evidence that the tenant contributed to the property as a co-owner), and to appeal a judgment the tenant must post a bond or deposit the rent owed and each later rent as it falls due. If you take money after the lease has ended, say in writing whether you are reinstating the lease or applying the money to what is owed for the time the tenant stayed.

title: Guarantors and the End of the Term
bodyText:
In Puerto Rico a guaranty (fianza) of a lease must be in writing, or it is void. A guarantor owes no more than the tenant owes, plus reasonable collection costs and fees, and is not bound by a court judgment against the tenant unless notified of the suit. Unless the guaranty says the guarantor is bound jointly and severally with the tenant (solidariamente) or expressly gives up the benefit of excusión, you must first pursue the tenant's own property before collecting from the guarantor.

Most important for renewals: when the lease term ends and the lease continues on the same terms, the Civil Code says obligations a third party gave to secure the lease end. So a guarantor normally does not cover rent or damage after the original term.

If you want a guarantor beyond the term, have the guarantor sign a new guaranty for each new term, or use the optional Guaranty clause, which asks the guarantor to cover the continuation expressly up to a stated maximum; a guaranty for an open-ended period can be withdrawn by the guarantor for future obligations at any time, and a general guaranty does not cover new obligations the tenant takes on more than five years after the guaranty was signed.

title: No Waiver of Homestead or Collection Exemptions
bodyText: A Puerto Rico lease cannot waive a tenant's protection from collection. The homestead right in a person's own principal residence cannot be waived by agreement, and any contrary agreement is void; and no statute lets a tenant give up, in a lease, the exemptions that protect household goods and appliances (up to $10,000 combined), clothing, a month's food, work tools, a work vehicle, most recent wages and certain insurance and retirement funds from seizure to pay a judgment. A form-lease clause waiving those exemptions would likely be annulled, so the library does not offer one; take advice before adding your own. One rule helps you as an owner: if you rent out your own principal home temporarily because work, study, military or diplomatic service, or a family member's illness forces you to move, you keep its homestead protection, as long as you do not acquire another principal residence.

title: No Statutory Early Termination for Illness or Disability
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute that lets a tenant end a lease early because of illness, disability or age, or to move into a care facility or a relative's home. During a fixed term the tenant can end the lease only for your own breach, as the Civil Code allows, or under an early-termination term in the lease or a later agreement with you. Once the term has ended and the lease is continuing on the same terms, either of you may end it by notice. If an older or disabled tenant asks to leave early for health reasons, consider agreeing in writing: federal fair-housing law can require reasonable accommodations for a disability, and a written early-termination agreement avoids a dispute. If the tenant dies, the lease does not end by itself: family members, or another person who lived with the tenant for the six months before the death, may take the tenant's place.

title: No Landlord Lien on Tenant Belongings
bodyText: Puerto Rico law gives a residential landlord no lien on, and no right to hold or seize, a tenant's furniture or other belongings for unpaid rent. The old 1930 Civil Code gave rent a preference over the tenant's movables on the property, but the 2020 Civil Code repealed it, and a right to keep someone's property until they pay exists only where a law grants it; none grants it to a landlord. Do not take or lock up a tenant's belongings to force payment: that can be a crime of willfully interfering with the tenant's peaceful enjoyment. Collect unpaid rent through a court judgment, which you can enforce against property that is not exempt from seizure. The library offers no lien or security-interest clause.

title: Landlord's Remedies When the Lease Ends for Breach
bodyText:
When a tenant breaches, Puerto Rico's Civil Code lets you end (resolve) the lease, after a written demand warning that you will do so unless the tenant cures within the time you give, or on the Code's own grounds such as two consecutive unpaid rental periods, and claim damages: unpaid rent, interest at the agreed or legal rate, and the other losses the breach caused. Rent already paid for past periods stays paid. You recover possession only through a court eviction (desahucio).

In a nonpayment case the court may, if you ask, let you add the claim for the unpaid rent to the eviction case; otherwise sue separately, and a claim of $15,000 or less (not counting interest) can go through the summary collection procedure. Puerto Rico has no statute measuring rent owed after the lease ends; claim rent up to the day you get the property back, plus losses you can prove, and keep records of your efforts to rent it again.

title: Fixing a Tenant's Breach at the Tenant's Cost
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no landlord-tenant statute that lets you fix a tenant's breach, such as damage the tenant caused or upkeep the tenant neglected, and add the cost to the rent. The Civil Code's general rule is that when someone fails to do what an obligation requires, the work is done at that person's cost, but it is not settled whether you need a court order first. The optional Landlord's Right to Cure clause sets an agreed procedure: written notice, time to fix it, then you do the work and the tenant repays the reasonable cost. Treat the cost as an amount owed under the lease, not as rent, and give the seven days' notice the Civil Code requires before entering for anything but an emergency.

title: Agreed Charges for Breach: Penalty Clauses
bodyText:
Puerto Rico's Civil Code lets a lease set a fixed charge for a breach or for late performance, such as a late fee, an early-termination fee or a holdover charge (a penalty clause). Courts must enforce it, but may reduce it in cases of extreme economic disproportion, it is read narrowly, and you may not collect both the charge and full performance except for late performance.

The Code also allows a different kind of clause that fixes damages in advance so that you need not prove your loss and the tenant cannot show the loss was smaller. That kind is lawful between parties who negotiate, but in a form lease a clause limiting the tenant's evidence is especially open to annulment, so the library does not offer it: its fees stay penalty clauses, and its cost schedule lets the tenant show a lower actual cost. Take advice before adding your own pre-set damages clause.

Your security deposit is not an agreed damages amount; you may keep only what the lease allows.

title: No Lockouts for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: You may not lock out a tenant for unpaid rent in Puerto Rico, and a lease clause cannot give you that right. A tenant in possession is protected by the Civil Code and can get a fast court order (a possessory injunction) restoring possession, and unlawfully dispossessing someone of real property is a misdemeanor under the Penal Code. A landlord or manager who willfully interferes with a tenant's peaceful enjoyment also commits a separate misdemeanor (fine up to $500, up to 90 days in jail, or both). That last law stops applying when the tenant has not paid for three consecutive months or more after a certified-mail demand giving five working days to pay, but that exception does not authorize a lockout: the other rules still apply. The only lawful way to remove a tenant is a court eviction (desahucio), carried out by the court marshal.

title: Tenants Under 21 and Minors in Eviction Cases
bodyText: In Puerto Rico a person becomes an adult at 21, not 18. Until then, unless emancipated (by marriage, by the parents' grant or by a court), a person cannot alone make a binding contract about his or her property or personal interests, so a lease signed only by an 18-, 19- or 20-year-old may be challenged. For a tenant under 21, have a parent or guardian sign as tenant or guarantor, or see proof of emancipation. No Puerto Rico statute bars naming a minor in an eviction case, but name only the adult tenants: the court's eviction complaint form asks for removal of the defendant and anyone occupying the property in the defendant's name, and both that form and the motion for the removal order ask you to say whether minors, people 60 or older, people with disabilities or other vulnerable persons live there.

title: Notice Before a Nonpayment Eviction
bodyText: Puerto Rico's eviction statute requires no particular notice before you sue a tenant for unpaid rent: there is no statutory pay-or-quit notice, no required wording and no rule letting the lease serve as or waive such a notice. But two rules make a written demand the safe course. To end the lease yourself for a breach, the Civil Code requires that you demand payment and warn that you will end the lease if the tenant does not pay within the time you give; the lease ends when that time runs out. And the court's own eviction complaint form states that you asked the tenant to vacate and pay and the tenant refused. So, before filing, send a dated written demand stating the amount owed, the time to pay, and that the lease will end if the tenant does not; keep proof of delivery. For a property covered by the federal CARES Act, federal law also requires 30 days' notice to vacate before a nonpayment eviction. Rent with a fixed due date earns default interest from that date without a demand. Deliver the demand on paper, by hand or by certified mail with return receipt: Puerto Rico's electronic-transactions law does not cover default, cure or eviction notices on a lease of a principal residence, so an e-mailed demand may not count.

title: No Statutory Rule on Notice Fees
bodyText: No Puerto Rico statute bans, caps or authorizes a fee for preparing or serving a notice on a tenant, such as a demand for unpaid rent. The library does not offer a separate notice fee: the written demand before ending a lease is your own legal step, and the late fee already compensates you for late payment. Charge only fees your lease states clearly and that match a real cost, and recover court costs through the court in an eviction case.

title: Waiving or Shortening Notices
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statutory notice to quit that a lease could shorten or waive: the eviction statute requires no notice before you sue. What the law does require is a written demand, warning that you will end the lease, before you end a lease yourself for the tenant's breach; the lease ends when the time you give runs out. The library does not offer a clause waiving that demand, because in a form lease a clause taking away the tenant's chance to cure is likely to be annulled. You can lawfully keep things short instead: the lease may set brief cure periods for its demand, and it sets how much notice either party gives to end the lease once the term is over, since the Civil Code sets none. A period of less than seven days excludes weekends and official holidays unless you state an exact deadline date. Whatever the lease says about e-mail, give a demand or other default notice on paper, by hand or by certified mail: the electronic-transactions law does not cover those notices on a lease of a principal residence.

title: Nuisance Complaints and Your Rental
bodyText: In Puerto Rico anything injurious to health, offensive to the senses or that keeps neighbors from the comfortable use of their property is a nuisance (estorbo) that anyone harmed can sue to stop, with damages; a municipal judge can also resolve these disputes provisionally. The Department of Health can order the owner, agent or tenant of a property to remove a health nuisance and, if no one does, remove it at that person's expense, with a lien on the property for the cost. A tenant who creates a nuisance breaches the lease, and you can end the lease for it after a written demand, or right away if the tenant has changed the agreed use. Act promptly on complaints: property used in committing a felony can be subject to government forfeiture, and an owner must challenge a forfeiture within 30 days of notice. No Puerto Rico statute lets a court take your rents or end your lease in a nuisance case.

title: Ending a Lease Early to Move In
bodyText: Puerto Rico law gives you no right to end a fixed-term lease early because you or a relative want to move in, and selling the property or the landlord's death does not shorten the term either, unless the lease says otherwise. The Civil Code does let the parties agree in the lease on early termination, so if you may need the home back, use the library's optional Owner Occupancy clause, which lets you end a fixed term on written notice if you or a named family member will live there. Use it only for a genuine move-in: the right is tied to that fact, and a right exercised in bad faith invites a challenge. After the fixed term ends and the lease continues on the same terms, either party may end it by notice without giving a reason.

title: No Possession Bond Procedure
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no procedure by which a tenant posts a bond, or confesses judgment, to secure giving up possession at the end of the term. The only possession-related bond is the one a tenant must post, or the rent the tenant must deposit with the court, to appeal an eviction judgment. A lease clause in which the tenant agrees in advance to a judgment or to removal would likely be annulled. Use the security deposit and, where needed, a written guaranty, and recover possession through a court eviction.

title: Delay in Delivering Possession
bodyText: Under Puerto Rico's Civil Code your first duty is to deliver the home in a condition suitable for its use. If you cannot deliver on the start date, the tenant need not pay rent until you do, and may end the lease after demanding delivery and giving you time to deliver; if the delay is your fault, for example because you rented to someone else or did not remove a prior occupant, the tenant can also claim damages. You are not liable for damages for a delay caused by an event you could not foresee or avoid, but the tenant can still end the lease. The library's Delay in Possession clause applies these rules: no rent until possession, and the tenant may cancel with a full refund if possession is not delivered within 30 days. If a former tenant or occupant will not leave, only a court eviction can remove them, so start that process early.

title: The Tenant's Belongings at Removal
bodyText:
In Puerto Rico the court marshal, not you, removes a tenant after an eviction judgment becomes final, on a court order you request. You must be there, with a locksmith if needed, and the people you bring move the tenant's belongings out under the marshal's supervision.

If the court found the family insolvent, or the tenant is a veteran, an older adult or a person with a disability, the court sends the judgment to the agencies that help them and the removal cannot happen until 20 days after that notice; for an insolvent family, officials of the Departments of the Family and of Housing must also be present.

No statute tells you how long to store belongings left behind, or what to do with pets, and you have no right to keep belongings for unpaid rent. Make a written, photographed inventory, keep the items safe, and follow the lease's Abandoned Property section (written notice and a collection period) if it has one, and call animal control or a shelter for any animal left behind. A person who re-enters after removal can be reported to the police.

title: Illegal Use of the Premises
bodyText: No Puerto Rico statute makes a residential lease void because the tenant uses the home for a prohibited purpose. The lease does not end by itself: you may end it, because the Civil Code lets a landlord end the lease when the tenant changes the agreed use, and illegal activity is also a breach you can act on after a written demand. One older law matters if the activity is illegal numbers gambling (bolita): after a conviction, if the premises keep being used for it, a prosecutor may ask the court to close and clear the premises for a month and return them to the owner, and people found in possession, including tenants, are presumed responsible for what is found. Property used to commit a felony can also be subject to government forfeiture, so act on reports of crime at the property quickly.

title: Partial Payments, Third-Party Payments and Receipts
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute letting a tenant redeem the tenancy by paying before removal, and none that prescribes wording for accepting partial rent. The Civil Code's general rules apply instead. You do not have to accept a partial payment unless the lease or a law says you must, but anyone may pay the tenant's debt for the tenant, so rent paid by a relative, a charity or a government program counts as payment. Receipts matter: if you give a receipt for the latest rent without noting that earlier rent is still unpaid, the law presumes the earlier rent was paid, and a receipt for the principal without reserving interest presumes the interest paid. So, when you accept a partial or late payment, write on the receipt what it covers, what remains due, and, if you have already demanded payment or ended the lease, that the demand or termination still stands. Refusing a full payment without reason can cost you: the tenant may deposit it in court, and the court may sanction you up to 5 percent of the amount plus costs and fees.

title: Rent Into Court and Defenses in an Eviction
bodyText: Puerto Rico's eviction procedure is summary. The hearing is set within ten days after you file, the tenant must raise every defense when answering, and in a nonpayment case the tenant may prove payment only with a receipt or another document showing payment. No statute requires the tenant to pay rent into court to defend the case or to file a counterclaim in it; a tenant's repair complaints are handled separately, for example through a municipal judge's provisional order on urgent repairs. If the tenant claims to co-own the property because of contributions to it, the case moves to an ordinary lawsuit. Rent into court comes in only on appeal: to appeal a nonpayment judgment the tenant must post a bond or deposit the rent owed and each rent as it falls due.

title: False Statements on the Rental Application
bodyText: If a tenant lied on the rental application about something important, Puerto Rico's Civil Code gives you remedies: a lease you were induced to sign by serious fraud can be annulled, lesser fraud gives damages, and the library's Application Accuracy clause makes a material misstatement a breach of the lease that you can act on after a written demand. If you screen criminal history, ask for the official certificate from the Puerto Rico Police (Certificado de Antecedentes Penales). It leaves out convictions that were reversed or eliminated, and it may not show older misdemeanors or felonies; an applicant whose certificate is clean has not misled you about a conviction the law has eliminated. Ask only for information you may lawfully consider under fair-housing law.

title: No Termination Because Repairs Cost Too Much
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no rule letting you end a lease because a needed repair would cost too much compared with the rent or the property's value: your duty to make necessary repairs within a reasonable time after notice continues for the whole lease. The Civil Code's only relief is narrow: if an extraordinary, unforeseeable event outside both parties' control, such as a disaster, makes your performance excessively burdensome, you may ask a court to revise the lease or declare it ineffective, but you must act within six months of the event, and the tenant can keep the lease by agreeing to an equitable adjustment. The library does not offer a clause letting you cancel over repair costs. During a fixed term, plan for repairs; once the lease is continuing on the same terms after the term, you may end it by notice without giving a reason.

title: Retaliation Against Tenants
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no general law barring a landlord from retaliating against a tenant who complains to you or to an agency, for example by raising the rent, cutting services or ending the lease. Three rules still apply. Older adults and people with disabilities have a statutory right to be free from reprisal for exercising their civil rights, which can include a housing complaint. If you operate a long-term care establishment, it is unlawful to retaliate against, discriminate against or penalize a resident for filing a complaint with, or giving information to, the Ombudsman for Older Persons. And the Civil Code does not protect the abuse of a right: ending a lease or refusing to continue it to punish a tenant for asserting rights can expose you to damages and court orders. Federal fair-housing law also bars interfering with or threatening anyone for exercising fair-housing rights. Keep a written, legitimate reason for any non-renewal or rent change that follows a complaint.

title: Seasonal and Vacation Rentals
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no special rules for seasonal or vacation leases: a seasonal rental is an ordinary lease. State the exact start and end dates, because a lease of real property with no agreed term is treated as a one-year lease. And plan the end: when the agreed season ends, the lease continues on the same terms until you or the tenant gives notice ending it, so give written notice before the last day if you need the home back. Rentals of fewer than 90 days are short-term rentals under Puerto Rico's room-occupancy tax law, with registration and tax collection through the Tourism Office, and a hotel-style stay is a lodging contract rather than a lease. In a condominium, check the master deed and bylaws: they may prohibit short-term rentals or set a minimum stay and a special monthly fee.

title: No Self-Help Eviction
bodyText: In Puerto Rico you may remove a tenant only through a court eviction (desahucio) carried out by the court marshal. Changing the locks, removing doors or belongings, or otherwise putting a tenant out without a court order is unlawful even if the lease has ended or the tenant owes rent: a tenant in possession is protected by the Civil Code, can get a fast court order (a possessory injunction) restoring possession with costs against you, and unlawfully dispossessing someone of real property is a misdemeanor under the Penal Code. Cutting off water, electricity, elevator, telephone or another service the lease provides, or willfully interfering with the tenant's peaceful enjoyment, is also a misdemeanor for a landlord, agent, manager or building employee (fine up to $500, up to 90 days in jail, or both). That law stops applying only after three consecutive months of unpaid rent and a certified-mail demand giving five working days to pay and warning that included services will be cut, and even then it does not authorize a lockout. The tenant can also sue you for damages.

title: Military Tenants
bodyText: Two sets of protections apply to military tenants in Puerto Rico. Federal law (the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act) applies here to members on federal active duty: it can stay an eviction and lets a servicemember end a residential lease early on qualifying orders. And Puerto Rico's Military Code protects members of the Puerto Rico National Guard and other Puerto Rico military forces called to state active duty by the Governor's executive order for more than 30 days: such a member who is a party to a civil case, including an eviction, may ask the court to stay it, and gets an automatic stay of at least 90 days on a proper petition with the military orders. The Military Code gives state-duty members early-termination rights for vehicle leases and mobile-phone contracts, but not for a residential lease. If a tenant tells you of a mobilization, ask for the orders and plan for a delayed eviction case; in an eviction, the court also notifies the Veterans Advocate's office if the tenant is a veteran.

title: Late Benefit or Subsidy Payments and Eviction
bodyText: No Puerto Rico statute requires a court to postpone or dismiss a nonpayment eviction because the tenant's Social Security, other government benefit, rent subsidy or voucher payment is late. Two things still matter. If the lease is subsidized under a Puerto Rico Department of Housing program, you must follow that program's eviction regulations, which may require an administrative step before you file (a project in the older adults' rent subsidy program must first go through mediation, at its own cost, and the Department's complaint process). And rent paid by an agency or program for the tenant counts as payment, so accept it. The courts have also run a temporary eviction-prevention program that pauses some cases for 60 days while a rent-assistance application is pending, for unpaid rent that began during the pandemic. When a late public payment is the only problem, a short written payment arrangement is often faster than a lawsuit.

title: Tenant's Statutory Grounds to End a Lease Early
bodyText: Puerto Rico's Civil Code lets a tenant end a lease before the term ends only for your own failures, or by agreement. The tenant may end the lease if you fail to keep the home fit for the agreed use, if you breach the warranties against eviction or hidden defects, or if your improvements deprive the tenant of part of the home (in that last case the tenant may instead take a proportional rent reduction). More generally, either party may end the lease after a written demand, with a warning, if the other fails a principal obligation. A tenant who was tricked into signing by serious fraud can ask a court to annul the lease. Puerto Rico law gives no separate right to leave early for domestic violence, illness or a job move; federal law gives some military members and some federally assisted tenants their own rights. Selling the property does not end the lease.

title: Open-Ended Leases and Occupants Without a Lease
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no common-law tenancy at will. A lease may be for a fixed or an open-ended period, but a lease of a home with no agreed term is treated as a one-year lease, and a lease need not be in writing unless it is for more than six years. When the agreed (or one-year) term ends, the lease continues on the same terms until either party gives notice ending it; the Civil Code sets no notice period, so put one in the lease, and if there is none give written notice of at least one full rental period. Someone who occupies the property without paying rent and without a lease (for example a relative you let stay) can be removed through the same court eviction (desahucio) as a tenant.

title: When a Tenant Files for Bankruptcy
bodyText: Puerto Rico law has no rule of its own for a tenant's bankruptcy; federal bankruptcy law applies here. When a tenant files, an automatic stay generally stops you from starting or continuing an eviction or collecting past-due rent without the bankruptcy court's permission, with exceptions, for example where you already have a judgment for possession before the filing. If a tenant tells you of a bankruptcy filing, stop collection and eviction steps and get advice. Do not confuse bankruptcy with the Puerto Rico eviction rules for a family of proven economic insolvency: those require the court to notify the Departments of the Family and of Housing and to have their officials present at any removal.

title: When the Tenant Causes the Damage
bodyText:
Under Puerto Rico's Civil Code the tenant must take care of and maintain the home and return it in the condition received, except for wear from time and ordinary use, and answers for damage the tenant, the tenant's household, guests or others on the tenant's account cause. You may end the lease if the tenant fails to conserve the property, and you can recover the repair cost and your other losses, including lost rent. The tenant's routes to stop paying or to leave depend on your own failures, so damage the tenant caused does not give the tenant those rights.

The optional Damage Caused by Tenant clause states this in the lease: rent keeps running while you repair tenant-caused damage, and if the lease ends because of the damage the tenant owes your lost rent for no longer than the rest of the term (or the notice period, once the term is over), less what you collect by re-renting. Repair and re-rent with reasonable diligence, and keep records.

title: When a Tenant Dies
bodyText: In Puerto Rico a lease does not end automatically when the tenant dies. The tenant's rights and obligations pass to the heirs, and for a home, family members who lived with the tenant during the six months before the death, or another person who lived there that long, may take the tenant's place under the lease. No statute sets a special procedure, so after a tenant dies, ask in writing whether a qualifying household member will continue the lease, and otherwise deal with the estate's representative or the heirs about ending it, the belongings, the deposit and any prepaid rent. The optional Emergency Contact clause lets the tenant name someone for you to call, but that person gets no right to the home or the belongings unless the law gives one.

title: Assisted-Living Projects: 30-Day Termination Notice
bodyText: If you operate housing certified by the Puerto Rico Department of Housing as an assisted-living project for older persons (Vida Asistida), special rules apply to your residential contracts. The conditions for ending services must be agreed with the resident, and you may never end services without 30 days' written notice; when you give it, you must also notify the Department of Housing and the Ombudsman for Older Persons so they can look for help for the resident. These rules cannot be changed by agreement. They do not apply to an ordinary lease to an older tenant.

title: Squatters and Unauthorized Occupants
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no fast-track procedure for police or the marshal to remove a squatter on your sworn complaint outside the courts. Your remedies are: a court eviction (desahucio), which reaches anyone occupying the property without paying rent, including someone who never had a lease; a possessory injunction, which a court hears within 15 days, if you were dispossessed within the past year; and a criminal complaint, since entering another's dwelling without the owner's consent and acting as owner is the misdemeanor of usurpation. Do not treat a current or former tenant, or a guest the tenant still welcomes, as a squatter: changing locks or removing them yourself is unlawful self-help. If the occupant claims to have contributed to the property as a co-owner, the eviction becomes an ordinary lawsuit.

title: Accepting Rent After a Default
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute saying that accepting rent you know is late waives your right to act on the tenant's default. But receipts can cost you: if your receipt for the latest rent says nothing about earlier unpaid rent, the law presumes the earlier rent was paid. So every time you accept a late or partial payment, write on the receipt what it covers, what is still owed, and, if you have demanded payment or ended the lease, that the demand or the termination still stands. The library does not offer a blanket no-waiver clause: in a form lease a clause that overrides the receipt presumption is likely to be annulled, while a reservation written on the receipt is what the Civil Code expects.

title: Agreed Ways to Give Notice
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no landlord-tenant rule on actual notice, so you and the tenant may agree in the lease on extra ways to give routine notices, such as text messages or e-mail. Electronic notices count only between parties who agreed to deal electronically, a party who agreed may later refuse further electronic dealings, and a message the recipient cannot print or save does not count as a written notice. Notices of default, of the right to cure, or about eviction on a lease of a principal residence are outside Puerto Rico's electronic-transactions law: give them on paper, by hand or by certified mail with return receipt, and treat any e-mail or text copy as a courtesy. If the lease was signed online, accept the tenant's notice ending the lease through the same channel.

title: Proceedings Against the Property
bodyText: No Puerto Rico statute requires you to tell a tenant or applicant that the property faces foreclosure, a tax sale, expropriation or another legal proceeding. The duty runs the other way: the tenant must tell you promptly of any usurpation, disturbance or attempt to impose an easement on the property, and of damage that needs repair. You, in turn, guarantee the tenant's peaceful use against third parties' legal claims, and if a third party's claim takes the home away the tenant may end the lease and claim damages. Telling a tenant early about a proceeding that may affect the lease is still good practice.

title: No Automatic Renewal on Silence
bodyText: Do not put an automatic-renewal clause in a Puerto Rico form lease. A clause that renews or extends a fixed term because the tenant stayed silent is one the Civil Code lists as especially open to annulment in contracts the tenant could not negotiate. What happens instead is set by law: when the term ends, the lease continues on the same terms until either of you gives notice ending it, and either of you may end it by notice. If you want a new fixed term, have the tenant sign a renewal or a new lease. Puerto Rico's statutory bans on automatic renewals cover telephone, pay-TV, microinsurance and condominium supplier contracts, not leases.

title: Arbitration Clauses in Leases
bodyText:
Puerto Rico's Arbitration Act makes a written agreement to arbitrate future disputes valid and enforceable, and bars waiving the right to a lawyer in advance. But no Puerto Rico law is written for arbitration in residential leases, and in a form lease the tenant could not negotiate, a clause that limits the tenant's right to go to court or excludes the Department of Consumer Affairs (DACO) is especially open to annulment. The eviction itself is a fast court proceeding. Keep any arbitration clause mutual and leave the tenant's DACO complaints and court remedies alone.

Federal law also matters here: the Federal Arbitration Act overrides state rules that block arbitration directly or indirectly (for example, a rule against giving up a jury), and the U.S. Supreme Court has held that renting out real estate is activity it reaches.

On that basis the library now offers an optional clause, `arbitration-agreement`: money claims only, with possession, small claims, security-deposit, injury, emergency and government-agency matters kept out, every remedy and the right to a lawyer kept, the arbitration fees above a court filing fee paid by you, a 30-day opt-out for the tenant, and separate initials from both of you.

Because state law points the other way, a court here could still refuse to enforce it; if one did, the dispute would simply go to court.

title: Other Rules Puerto Rico Does Not Have
bodyText: Several protections found in other places do not exist in Puerto Rico law, each covered in its own section of this library: no just-cause rule for ending a lease after its term; no general law against retaliating against a tenant (only residents of long-term care establishments are protected); no landlord's lien on a tenant's belongings; no right to lock a tenant out; no statutory right for a tenant to stop an eviction by paying before removal; no possession bond; no rule on notice fees; no continuance when a benefit payment is late; no early-termination right for illness or disability; and no right to end a lease because repairs cost too much. General Civil Code rules, such as good faith and the bar on abusing a right, still apply.

title: Checked Across All of Puerto Rico Law
bodyText: Three things landlords often ask about, checked across all of Puerto Rico's laws: there is no fast removal of squatters outside the courts (use an eviction, a possessory injunction or a criminal complaint for usurpation); a tenant who pays has the right to demand a receipt, and business landlords should give one for every payment; and no general registration or licence is required before you can win an eviction, except that a student-housing business needs a DACO licence before it may lease at all, and a corporation or limited liability company formed outside Puerto Rico that does business here must first obtain the Department of State's authorization (naming a resident agent) and may not bring any court case, an eviction included, until it is authorized and has paid the fees, penalties and franchise taxes owed for the time it did business without authorization. The missing authorization does not void its leases, and merely owning property is not doing business, so whether renting it out is depends on the facts (Ley 164-2009, arts. 13.01, 13.03, 13.05, 20.02, 20.05 (14 L.P.R.A. §§ 3801, 3803, 3805, 4022, 4025)). Registering a trade name with the Department of State is optional and does not affect your right to sue (Ley 75-1992, art. 4 (10 L.P.R.A. § 225b)).

title: Domestic Violence Order Citations
bodyText: Puerto Rico has not moved or renumbered its domestic-violence protection-order provisions: they remain in Law 54 of 1989 (article 2.1), which lets a court order the abuser out of a shared home and order rent payments on the home to continue while the order is in force. Recent amendments (2025 and 2026) added provisions and re-lettered some definitions, so check the current text before citing a definition by letter. Similar protective orders, including orders to leave a shared home, exist for older adults, people with disabilities and stalking victims.

title: Signing the Lease Electronically
bodyText: Puerto Rico's Electronic Transactions Act lets you and the tenant sign the lease electronically: an electronic signature satisfies a signature requirement and a lease is not invalid because it was formed electronically, provided both parties agreed to deal electronically. Give the tenant a copy the tenant can print or save. Two limits: a lease to be recorded in the Property Registry must be signed before a notary in a public deed, and notices of default, of the right to cure or about eviction on a lease of a principal residence are outside the Act, so give those on paper. A party who agreed to deal electronically may refuse to do so for later transactions.

title: Emergency Contacts
bodyText: No Puerto Rico statute requires you to give tenants an emergency or 24-hour contact number, or to post your contact details. In a condominium, the board must keep an emergency plan and each January register its board's and managing agent's contacts with the police, the municipal emergency office and the fire bureau (DACO's condominium regulation also requires that notice to DACO), but that is the board's duty, not yours. Giving tenants a working emergency number for repairs is still good practice, and the optional Emergency Contact clause lets the tenant name someone you can call.

title: No Energy Data Release Rule
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no energy-benchmarking program for private rental buildings and no law on releasing a tenant's energy-usage data to the owner. If you need a tenant's utility usage, ask the tenant to share it; the library has no clause for it. Electricity charges passed to a tenant are covered in the utilities sections.

title: Entire Agreement and Lease Changes in Puerto Rico
bodyText:
Puerto Rico has no statute that lets you change an existing lease by written notice, whether to comply with a new law or for any other reason, so a clause requiring changes to be made in a writing signed by both parties gives up nothing. Under the Civil Code a change to a lease already made follows the same formalities as the original: a written lease is changed in writing, and an oral lease can be changed orally.

An entire-agreement clause does not shut out the terms Puerto Rico law itself supplies: where the lease is silent, or a clause is ineffective, the lease is completed by mandatory rules, default rules, local usage and good faith (for example, the lease continuing on the same terms after the term ends, and the seven days' notice before an inspection).
