Because a lease you present on your own form is read against the party who drafted it, write any side agreement (a parking space, an approved pet, a rent concession) into the lease or a signed addendum rather than relying on a conversation.

The library clause's words letting you change the lease by notice where applicable law permits have nothing to attach to in Puerto Rico; you may not change rent, the term or another element of the lease on your own.

The clause's statement that the lease binds the parties' heirs and successors matches Puerto Rico law: a lease binds the parties' successors, the landlord's death or a sale does not shorten it unless the lease says otherwise, and certain family members or a person who lived with the tenant for the six months before the tenant's death may take the tenant's place.

title: Puerto Rico Law and Courts Govern a Puerto Rico Lease
bodyText:
A lease of a home in Puerto Rico should name Puerto Rico law, as the Governing Law section does. Puerto Rico is a U.S. territory divided into 78 municipalities, with no counties, so a clause naming a "State of" Puerto Rico or a county is wrong. The Civil Code lets contracting parties choose the governing law and forum unless a law provides otherwise, and where they make no choice it presumes that a contract about rights in real property is governed by the law of the place where the property is.

An eviction must be filed in the Judicial Region where the property is located, before a municipal judge when the rent owed or the claim does not exceed $5,000 a year and before the Court of First Instance otherwise.

Do not choose mainland law or mainland courts in a Puerto Rico form lease: a form lease the tenant must accept as written is an adhesion contract, and a clause that limits the tenant's actions or defenses or moves the tenant's contractual domicile without reason can be annulled. Federal law (fair housing, lead-paint disclosure, servicemember protections) applies in Puerto Rico as it does on the mainland. Municipal ordinances may add rules; check the municipality where the property is.

title: Settling Disputes Before Court in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute that requires, regulates or forbids a lease clause asking you and the tenant to try to settle a dispute informally before going to court. Voluntary help exists: Puerto Rico law authorizes informal dispute-resolution centers, run under Supreme Court rules (the Judicial Branch's conflict-mediation centers), where participation is voluntary, and the Department of Consumer Affairs (DACO) runs a mediation program for complaints filed with it. The library does not offer a Puerto Rico clause making notice and an offer to meet a condition of going to court, and does not offer an arbitration clause. A form lease the tenant must accept as written is an adhesion contract, and a clause that limits the tenant's right to sue or restricts the tenant's defenses or evidence, or that excludes a regulatory agency's jurisdiction, can be annulled. A written agreement to arbitrate future disputes is generally valid under Puerto Rico's Arbitration Act, but in a residential form lease it is exposed to the same challenge; if you want one, have it negotiated and take legal advice first. Nothing stops you from inviting the tenant to raise problems with you first, and from proposing mediation when a dispute arises. An eviction (desahucio) is filed in court and cannot be moved to arbitration or mediation by the lease.

title: Registration and Licenses for Puerto Rico Landlords
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no general landlord registration, rental license or rental registry for long-term residential rentals, and no rule that an individual owner living outside Puerto Rico must hire a local broker or agent. An owner that is a corporation or limited liability company formed outside Puerto Rico is different: before doing business here it must obtain the Department of State's authorization and keep a resident agent in Puerto Rico, and until it is authorized it may not bring an eviction or any other court case (Ley 164-2009, arts. 13.01, 13.03, 20.02, 20.03, 20.05 (14 L.P.R.A. §§ 3801, 3803, 4022, 4023, 4025); see Owners Who Live Outside Puerto Rico). Three registrations or licenses can still apply: (1) Short-term rentals: if you rent a home or room for periods of less than 90 days, Puerto Rico's room-occupancy tax law treats you as a lodging operator; you must register with the Puerto Rico Tourism Company and obtain its tax identification number, and booking platforms must require that registration before doing business with you (see the rent and room-tax rows). (2) Student housing: renting to three or more post-secondary students, or renting rooms to students in a home where you live, requires a DACO license before you sign any lease (see Renting to Students: DACO License). (3) Property managers: a person who, for pay, acts as an intermediary in leasing, renting or administering someone else's property must hold a real estate broker's license; an owner renting or administering its own property for its own benefit does not. Municipalities may impose their own business licenses or taxes on rental activity; check the municipality where the property is.

title: Complete Every Blank Before Signing
bodyText: Fill in every blank in the lease before the tenant signs. Puerto Rico's consumer bill of rights says a consumer may not be required to sign a contract that is incomplete, lacks its proper heading or has blank spaces. Treat it as applying to your leases if you rent homes as a business: the law does not define who is a consumer or exclude leases, though it does not apply to contracts regulated by a special law; the library reads an ordinary residential lease, and a student-housing lease, as outside that exception. Write "None" or "Not applicable" in any space that does not apply, and complete optional sections or strike them. A blank or unclear term in a lease you drafted is read against you, and in a form lease a clause that is not written clearly and completely, in Spanish or English, can be annulled. No Puerto Rico statute makes an unfilled blank a ground for the tenant to end the lease; the risk is that the missing term is supplied by the Civil Code's default rules or read in the tenant's favor.

title: What a Puerto Rico Lease Must Contain
bodyText:
Puerto Rico has no statute listing what every residential lease must contain, and no required statutory lease form.

What the law does require, by situation:
- (1) Every form lease: write it clearly, completely and legibly, in Spanish or English; a form clause that is not can be annulled.
- (2) If you rent homes as a business: give the tenant a copy to read before signing if asked, do not ask the tenant to sign with blanks, and give a signed copy (see Complete Every Blank Before Signing and Giving the Tenant a Copy of the Lease); itemize every mandatory charge with its cost (see the Fees and Charges section); and tell the tenant before signing how the lease can be ended, offering at least the same ways to end it as to sign it (see Ending the Lease at or After the End of the Term).
- (3) Student housing under the DACO license: the certification in the Student Housing Certification section.
- (4) Property inside the Convention Center District or the Science, Technology and Research District: the bold acknowledgment in the Special District Acknowledgment section.
- (5) A tenant receiving a rent subsidy under the older-adult or veterans' program of Ley 173-1996: the conditions in the Rent Subsidy Conditions section.
- (6) A condominium apartment: the Condominium Statement (the landlord's statement that it knows and will observe the Condominium Act, master deed and bylaws, with a copy of the lease to the board).
- (7) A home in an access-controlled community: the Access-Controlled Community Statement.
- (8) Property in a flood-prone zone declared by the Planning Board: the Flood-Prone Zone Notice.
- (9) A lease of real property for more than six years must be in writing.
- (10) Federal law: the lead-based paint disclosure for housing built before 1978, and the HUD tenancy addendum and program rules for federally assisted tenancies (for example Section 8 vouchers).

Municipal ordinances may add requirements.

title: Giving the Tenant a Copy of the Lease
bodyText: Give the tenant a copy of the lease. Puerto Rico's consumer bill of rights says a consumer has the right to know the content and scope of any contract the consumer is asked to sign, to ask for a printed or digital copy before signing with the time the consumer needs to read it or get advice, and to receive a true and exact printed or digital copy once it is signed. Treat this as applying to your leases if you rent homes as a business: the law does not define who is a consumer or exclude leases, though it does not reach contracts regulated by a special law. The Civil Code separately requires that the standard terms of a form contract be accessible to the party who did not draft them. No Puerto Rico statute makes your failure to give a copy a defense to enforcing the lease or to an eviction; the Department of Consumer Affairs (DACO) enforces the consumer bill of rights. If the lease is signed electronically, give a copy the tenant can print or save (see the electronic-signature row). Keep a record of when you delivered the copy.

title: No Initials Requirement
bodyText: No Puerto Rico statute requires a tenant to initial a particular lease term, such as a longer notice period or a fee, for that term to bind the tenant; the signatures on the lease are enough. The one initials rule found is for public deeds: if a lease is executed before a notary as a public instrument (for example so it can be recorded in the Property Registry), every signer initials the margin of every page under the Notarial Act. Initials on key terms are still useful evidence that the tenant saw them, because a form lease is read against the party who drafted it, but initials do not cure a clause Puerto Rico law makes annullable in a form lease.

title: Lease Length Limits in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico sets no minimum or maximum length for a private residential lease. A lease may have a fixed or an indefinite duration; if a lease of a home names no term, the law treats it as a one-year lease, and when a fixed term ends the lease continues on the same terms until either party gives notice. Length still matters in three ways: a lease for more than six years must be in writing; a lease for six years or more (or a shorter one the parties agree to record) can be recorded in the Property Registry, which takes a notarial deed (see Lease Writing and Recording Rules); and in a condominium the master deed or regulations may set a minimum lease term or bar short-term rentals, which binds an owner who leases a unit. Make sure the person signing as landlord may lease the property: the owner, a usufructuary or someone whose administration powers include leasing. One co-owner cannot lease a jointly owned home without the others' consent, although they can ratify the lease later. The ten-year limit in the Civil Code applies to financial leases (arrendamiento financiero), not to ordinary residential leases.

title: No Type-Size Rule for Leases
bodyText: Puerto Rico sets no minimum type size for a residential lease and no penalty tied to print size. The DACO law lets the Secretary of Consumer Affairs require, by regulation, that documents a consumer signs be in Spanish (unless the consumer prefers English) and in type of at least 10 points, but no regulation applying that to leases was found. A form lease clause that is not easily legible can still be annulled, so use a readable type (10 points or larger is a sensible floor) and do not hide key terms in small print. Two narrow rules require bold type: the special-district acknowledgment for property in the Convention Center District or the Science, Technology and Research District (see the Special District Acknowledgment section). Rent-to-own contracts for household goods have their own type-size rules, but they cover movable goods, not homes.

title: Owners Who Live Outside Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico does not require an individual owner who lives outside Puerto Rico to name a local agent in the lease, to register an agent, or to hire a Puerto Rico broker. An owner that is a corporation or limited liability company formed outside Puerto Rico must, before doing business here, obtain the Department of State's authorization and keep a resident agent here; until it is authorized and has paid the fees, penalties and taxes owed for the unauthorized period it may not bring an eviction or other court case, though its leases stay valid; and while it does business here without authorization it is treated as having appointed the Secretary of State to receive service of process in suits arising from that business. Merely owning property is not doing business, so whether renting it out is depends on the facts (Ley 164-2009, arts. 13.01, 13.03, 13.05, 13.13, 20.02, 20.03, 20.05, 20.08 (14 L.P.R.A. §§ 3801, 3803, 3805, 3813, 4022, 4023, 4025, 4028)). Either way, if you pay someone to manage or lease the property for you, that person must hold a Puerto Rico real estate broker's license. Tax withholding matters more. Puerto Rico's Internal Revenue Code requires anyone paying rent to a nonresident individual, tenants included, to withhold 20 percent (if the owner is a U.S. citizen) or 29 percent (otherwise), but only to the extent the rent is taxable Puerto Rico income. Under the Real Property Market Stimulus Act, rent from leasing residential property in Puerto Rico is exempt from Puerto Rico income tax through 2040 for resident and nonresident owners alike, and exempt rent is not subject to withholding; short-term rentals (under 90 days) do not qualify, and to keep the exemption you must report the rent as exempt income on a Puerto Rico income tax return. The exemption does not cover municipal business-license (patente) taxes. If you are a nonresident owner, take Puerto Rico tax advice before the first rent payment and tell the tenant in writing whether withholding applies, so the tenant does not hold back part of the rent.

title: How Lease Notices Are Delivered in Puerto Rico
bodyText:
Puerto Rico has no landlord-tenant statute listing how lease notices must be delivered, so the lease sets the methods.

Four Puerto Rico rules limit what the lease can do:
- (1) Default, cure and eviction-related notices on a lease of a principal residence are outside the Electronic Transactions Act: deliver them on paper, by hand or by certified mail with return receipt, and treat any e-mail copy as a courtesy (see Delivering Default Notices on Paper).
- (2) Routine notices may go by e-mail or another electronic channel only between parties who agreed to deal electronically; a party who agreed may later refuse further electronic dealings, and that right cannot be waived; an e-mail the recipient cannot print or store does not count.
- (3) If a law requires you to give a tenant certain information in writing and you want to give it electronically, the tenant must first receive a clear statement of the right to paper copies and to withdraw consent, and then consent.
- (4) If you rent as a business, the tenant may end the lease the same way the lease was signed (for example online if it was signed online), and the lease cannot require a harder channel for the tenant's notice of ending.

Certified mail with return receipt is the method Puerto Rico law names for the rent demand that must come before cutting services included in the lease, and it is the safest proof of delivery for any important notice. No Puerto Rico rule requires a sheriff or process server to deliver a lease notice; court papers in an eviction are served under the court rules.

title: No Rule on Move-Out Notice Forms
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute on a move-out or notice-to-vacate form you ask a tenant to sign, no required warning if the form adds terms the lease does not contain, and no rule against repairs or alterations while a notice to vacate is pending. Keep any such form to the facts: the address, the date the tenant will leave and how keys will be returned. A new term in it (a fee, a cleaning charge, a release) is a change to the lease, which follows the same formalities as the lease itself, and if it is your pre-printed form it is read against you and may be annulled if it limits the tenant's rights or defenses. Until the lease has ended and the tenant has left, the landlord's duties continue: keep the home fit for its agreed use, and do not carry out works that reduce the tenant's use unless they are repairs that cannot wait. A tenant who has not left after the lease has ended can be removed only by a court eviction (desahucio).

title: The Notices Clause in Puerto Rico
bodyText:
The library's Notices section works in Puerto Rico as written: it sends notices to the addresses in the lease and lets any method Puerto Rico law requires control. Puerto Rico law sets few notice rules of its own, so the lease's addresses and methods do most of the work.

Fill in a street or postal address for each party where certified mail can be received, and keep it current. Give default, cure and eviction-related notices on paper, by hand or certified mail with return receipt (see Delivering Default Notices on Paper); a demand to cure must warn that you will end the lease if the tenant does not comply (see Default by Tenant).

If you rent as a business, the tenant may give notice ending the lease the same way the lease was signed, and you must tell the tenant before signing how the lease can be ended; the Notices and Ending the Lease sections together do that. See How Lease Notices Are Delivered in Puerto Rico for electronic notices.

title: Where Puerto Rico Law Lets Your Lease Decide
bodyText: Many Puerto Rico rules apply only if, or unless, the lease says so; a silent lease gets the Civil Code's default. The main ones, with the library section that makes the choice: (1) Rent is payable in arrears unless the lease says in advance (the Rent section says in advance). (2) A lease of a home with no stated term is a one-year lease (the Term section states the term). (3) The tenant may sublet unless the lease expressly forbids it (No Subletting or Assignment). (4) A sale of the property or the landlord's death does not shorten the lease unless the lease says otherwise (Sale of the Property: Landlord's Right to End the Lease, optional). (5) The parties may agree on early termination (the optional early-termination clause). (6) Penalty clauses, such as a late fee or an agreed holdover charge, are allowed, and a court may reduce one only if it is extremely out of proportion (Late Fee; Agreed Holdover Charge). (7) Co-tenants each owe the whole rent only if the lease says so expressly (Joint and Several Liability). (8) A guarantor can be pursued before the tenant's property only if the guaranty says so or makes the guarantor jointly liable (Guaranty). (9) Interest on late amounts is the agreed rate, or else the legal rate (Interest on Unpaid Amounts). (10) The tenant must not make improvements the lease forbids (No Alterations). (11) Electronic notices work only between parties who agreed to deal electronically (the optional e-mail notice clause). Other optional Puerto Rico clauses: landlord's right to end after a fire or casualty, damage caused by the tenant, landlord's right to cure, collection costs, property left after move-out, utilities in the tenant's name, a designated repairer for urgent repairs, and the principal-residence sales-tax statement. Use only the ones that fit your rental; none is required.

title: No Small-Landlord Exemptions
bodyText: Puerto Rico's lease rules apply the same way to every residential landlord, whatever the number of units owned: there is no small-landlord exemption and no set of duties that starts at a portfolio size. A few regimes turn on numbers about the property or the tenants rather than on how many units you own: student housing needs a DACO license when you rent a unit to three or more post-secondary students, or rent to students in a home where you live (see Renting to Students: DACO License); an assisted-living residence for older adults must have at least five residential units and be certified by the Department of Housing; and short-term rentals of under 90 days fall under the room-occupancy tax (see Registration and Licenses for Puerto Rico Landlords). Whether you rent as a business matters for the consumer-protection laws (copies, no blank spaces, itemized charges, the same way to end as to sign), which the library applies to any landlord who rents homes as a business.

title: Requiring Renter's Insurance in Puerto Rico
bodyText:
Puerto Rico has no statute on requiring renter's insurance in a residential lease: none bars it, sets a maximum coverage you may require, regulates force-placed coverage, or requires a written notice that you will not insure the tenant's belongings. You may require renter's insurance as a lease term, as the library's Tenant's Property and Insurance section does.

Two Puerto Rico rules shape how: the tenant, as an insurance consumer, has the right to choose the insurer and the agent or broker, so do not require a particular company or agent; and in a form lease, do not use the insurance clause to excuse your own liability (a clause that excludes or limits the drafter's liability can be annulled).

The library offers no clause letting you buy insurance for the tenant and charge for it; if you want one, state the cost in the lease as an itemized charge and take advice. A tenant's insurance never replaces your own repair duties under the Civil Code.

title: Selling the Property or Changing Managers
Which Law Governs a Puerto Rico Lease
bodyText: One body of law governs every residential lease in Puerto Rico: the lease chapter of the 2020 Civil Code, which applies to leases of any thing, homes and commercial premises alike, read together with the Code's general contract rules. There is no separate residential landlord-tenant act, no local adoption of a uniform act, and no county layer; the same rules apply in all 78 municipalities, which may add ordinances of their own. Some arrangements are governed by other rules: a lodging (hospedaje) arrangement in which you provide accommodation, often with meals or services, is a separate lodging contract; a financial lease used to finance the purchase of property, and rent-to-own and other leases of household goods, have their own rules; and Puerto Rico has no mobile-home park law. Special laws add rules on top of the Civil Code for student housing (DACO license), condominium units (the Condominium Act and the building's master deed and regulations), assisted-living residences for older adults, government rent-subsidy programs, short-term rentals under 90 days (room-occupancy tax), and federally assisted housing (federal program rules). Federal fair-housing, lead-paint and servicemember laws apply in Puerto Rico. Leases already running when the 2020 Code took effect in November 2020 stay under the 1930 Civil Code (see How a Puerto Rico Lease Continues After Its Term).

title: Severability in Puerto Rico
bodyText:
The library's severability clause works in Puerto Rico as written. The Civil Code allows a court to declare part of a contract invalid while the rest stands, where the remaining part is valid on its own, directs that a contract be read so that it has effect when its effectiveness is in doubt, and fills the gap left by an ineffective clause with mandatory rules, default rules, local usage and good faith.

Puerto Rico statutes that strike lease terms work clause by clause: an abusive clause in a form lease is annullable at the tenant's request without voiding the lease, and a clause contrary to the consumer law on ending adhesion contracts is treated as not agreed, without affecting the contract's validity. No Puerto Rico statute found voids a whole lease because one term is unlawful.

Severability does not save an unlawful clause: the clause still fails, and the Code's default rule takes its place, so draft each clause to be lawful on its own.

title: Lease Writing and Recording Rules
bodyText: A Puerto Rico residential lease needs no special form to be valid: an oral lease is binding, and a lease of a home for six years or less does not have to be in writing. Three rules turn on length: (1) a lease of real property for more than six years must be in writing (Civil Code art. 1343, as rewritten in 2026); (2) a lease of real property for six years or more must be set out in a public or private written instrument for evidentiary purposes, so put a lease of exactly six years in writing too; (3) a lease of six years or more, or a shorter one the parties agree to record, may be recorded in the Property Registry, which requires a public document executed before a notary; recording is what makes the lease effective against third parties who rely on the Registry, such as a later buyer or a mortgage lender at foreclosure. Before the 2026 amendment, the Code's text was read as requiring a written lease for terms of six years or less, which the Legislature called an internal contradiction and corrected; for any lease signed between November 2020 and 2026, put it in writing if it was not, or sign a written renewal. Whatever the term, use a signed written lease: it is your proof of the rent, the term and every agreed charge, and Puerto Rico's consumer rules on copies and blank spaces assume one.

title: No Statutory Lease Form in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico prescribes no statutory residential lease form and no verbatim lease text that every lease must contain. The only model lease the law calls for is DACO's model rent-to-own contract for household goods, which does not apply to homes. Puerto Rico law does prescribe wording for a few clauses in particular situations, and the library carries each one: the special-district acknowledgment (in bold), the student-housing certification, and the rent-subsidy conditions for the older-adult and veterans' programs. The Judicial Branch publishes court forms for eviction cases, which you will meet if you go to court: a pro se eviction complaint (OAT-931), which asks you to attach a copy of the lease and to say whether the rent is subsidized by a Department of Housing program and whether minors, older adults or people with disabilities live in the home; the summons (OAT-972); the tenant's answer (OAT-1801); and a motion for the eviction order (OAT-1742). Keep a signed copy of the lease ready for the complaint.

title: Tenant Portals and Electronic Dealings
bodyText: No Puerto Rico statute addresses tenant portals. You may offer an online portal for signing, notices, maintenance requests and payments, and the lease may name a portal as a payment method (see Acceptable Forms of Payment and Payment Methods and the Card Surcharge Ban). Puerto Rico's Electronic Transactions Act sets the limits: electronic signing and notices work only between parties who agreed to deal electronically; a tenant who agreed may later refuse to deal electronically for further transactions, and the lease cannot waive that right, so do not make the portal the only way the tenant can give you a notice, and accept paper from a tenant who withdraws; documents in the portal must be ones the tenant can print or save; and default, cure and eviction-related notices on a principal-residence lease go on paper, not through the portal. If a law requires you to give the tenant certain information in writing and you deliver it in the portal, first give the consumer statement about paper copies and withdrawing consent and get the tenant's consent. Do not charge a fee for paying rent by card through the portal.

title: Rent Records and Tenant Data in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no rent-ledger statute and no rule requiring you to give a tenant a statement of account on request or with a notice. Your records still decide eviction cases: in a nonpayment eviction the tenant may defend only with a receipt or another document showing payment (the court may also hear evidence that the tenant contributed to the property as a co-owner), so keep a complete ledger and copies of every receipt. A tenant who pays part of the rent may demand a receipt, and if you give a receipt for the latest rent without noting that earlier rent is still unpaid, the earlier rent is presumed paid; write any unpaid prior balance on each receipt (see Rent Receipts in Puerto Rico). Applicant and tenant data: if you keep Social Security, driver's license or bank account numbers of Puerto Rico residents, you must notify the people affected of any security breach as quickly as possible and report it to DACO within 10 days; fines run from $500 to $5,000 per violation. When you discard records with tenants' personal information, shred or erase them so they cannot be read (larger businesses must also document the disposal before a notary). If you collect applicants' or tenants' personal information through a website or online portal, link a privacy policy from the site that names your business, says what data you collect, when you share it, how you announce changes and when they take effect, how the site responds to "Do Not Track" signals, and whether third parties can track users across sites.

title: Renter's Insurance Clause Without a Disclaimer
bodyText:
Use the library's insurance clause that requires renter's insurance without a liability disclaimer. A Puerto Rico form lease the tenant must accept as written is an adhesion contract, and a clause excluding or limiting the landlord's own liability ("Landlord is not liable for loss or damage to Tenant's property") can be annulled; liability for fraud or deliberate bad-faith breach cannot be waived at all.

Stating that your own insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings is a statement of fact, not a disclaimer, and requiring the tenant to carry renter's insurance with a stated liability minimum and to show proof on request is a lawful lease term. Let the tenant choose the insurer and agent: Puerto Rico's insurance consumer bill of rights gives the insured that choice. A tenant's insurance does not shift your repair duties under the Civil Code (see Tenant's Insurance and Your Repair Duties).

title: Changing Lease Terms in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico sets no notice period or form for changing a lease term, whether rent, a fee the lease already provides, a rule, or anything else, and draws no line between rent and other terms. The rule is simpler and stricter: a term of the lease can be changed only by agreement, made with the same formalities as the lease (in writing for a written lease). During a fixed term you may not change a term on your own, and a form-lease clause letting you change the contract's elements unilaterally can be annulled. When the term ends the lease continues on the same terms until either party gives notice ending it, so a continued lease is not a month-to-month tenancy you can re-price or re-write by notice: to change a term, give written notice ending the lease on a date at least as far ahead as the lease requires, together with an offer of a new lease or a signed amendment with the new terms. If the tenant signs, the new terms apply from the agreed date; if not, the lease ends on the notice date and a tenant who stays can be removed only by court eviction. Changes the lease itself schedules (stated rent steps or an index) apply as written. See Raising the Rent in Puerto Rico and Rent Changes During the Lease.

title: No Sunsetting Tenant Laws
bodyText: None of Puerto Rico's core landlord-tenant rules is on a repeal or expiration clock: the Civil Code's lease chapter, the eviction articles of the Code of Civil Procedure, the Condominium Act's leasing rules and the student-housing law carry no sunset date. The Condominium Act amendments of Ley 157-2026 took effect in late October 2026; they changed some board powers and court jurisdiction over condominium disputes, not the leasing articles. Dated items to watch: (1) the income-tax exemption for residential rental income under the Real Property Market Stimulus Act runs through 31 December 2040 (see Owners Who Live Outside Puerto Rico); (2) the 2020 COVID-19 law whose title mentions barring evictions from principal residences is no longer current law. Leases that were already running when the 2020 Civil Code took effect in November 2020 stay under the 1930 Code, which matters only for those older leases.

title: Lease Language: Spanish or English
bodyText: Write the lease in Spanish or English. Puerto Rico's Civil Code makes a form-lease clause that is not written clearly, completely and legibly in Spanish or English especially annullable, and the DACO law lets the Secretary require by regulation that consumer documents be in Spanish unless the consumer prefers English (no such regulation for leases was found). No Puerto Rico statute requires you to translate a lease into the tenant's language, or into a language you used in advertising or negotiation. If your tenant reads only Spanish, offer the lease in Spanish: a tenant who signs a form in a language the tenant cannot read can argue the clause was not clear to the tenant, and a form lease is read against the drafter. If you sign in both languages, say which version controls. (For Puerto Rico laws themselves, the Spanish text prevails over the English unless the law says otherwise; that rule does not decide which version of a private lease controls.) An English-language lease can be filed with an eviction complaint without translation, although the court must order a translation when a party asks or justice requires it. A lease to be recorded in the Property Registry that is not in Spanish or English needs a certified Spanish translation.

title: Notices That Must Be in Writing
bodyText: Puerto Rico's Civil Code requires notice for the key lease steps but rarely says it must be in writing: the notice ending a continued lease, the demand to cure before ending the lease for breach, and the seven days' notice before an inspection have no prescribed form. The lease fills that gap, and the library's lease requires written notice for all of them; treat that as binding on you as well as on the tenant. A few Puerto Rico rules do prescribe the form, and a lease cannot downgrade them to oral notice: (1) before cutting a service the lease includes, a tenant three or more months behind must have received a payment demand by certified mail with return receipt giving five working days to pay, or the cutoff can be a crime; (2) default, cure and eviction-related notices on a principal-residence lease cannot be given electronically under the Electronic Transactions Act, so they go on paper; (3) in a certified assisted-living residence for older adults, ending the residence contract needs 30 days' written notice that cannot be waived; (4) a guarantor's withdrawal of an open-ended guaranty must be by reliable notice. Because the law rarely fixes the form, keep proof of every notice: hand delivery with a signed receipt, or certified mail with return receipt.

title: Animals Left in a Puerto Rico Rental
bodyText:
Puerto Rico gives you no special right to enter a rental to feed, check on or remove a tenant's animal, and no procedure for taking custody of an animal a tenant leaves behind. Your entry right is the ordinary one: justified cause and seven days' notice, with an emergency limb in the library's entry clause (see Landlord's Right of Entry).

Puerto Rico law treats domestic animals as sentient beings that must be treated according to their nature, and abandoning an animal is a felony. If you find an animal left without care, contact the tenant or the tenant's named contact first; a person who keeps a found animal must notify its owner or, if the owner is unknown, the police or an animal shelter. Do not sell, give away or destroy a tenant's animal.

The keeper of an animal is liable for the harm it causes even without fault, which is one reason to require pet liability insurance. The optional Animal Care clause lets the tenant name a caregiver you may let in.

title: Assistance Animals in Puerto Rico Rentals
bodyText:
Assistance animals in Puerto Rico rentals are governed mainly by the federal Fair Housing Act, which applies in Puerto Rico: treat a service or support animal a tenant needs because of a disability as a reasonable accommodation, not a pet, charge no pet deposit or pet rent for it, and ask for reliable documentation only when the disability or the need is not apparent. The library's Assistance Animals section does this and works in Puerto Rico as written.

Puerto Rico's own Assistance Animals Act gives a person with a disability the right to be accompanied by a trained, certified assistance animal on public transportation and in hotels, buildings, premises and other facilities open to the public, with no extra charge, and makes it a misdemeanor to prevent the person from using that right. It is written for places open to the public; whether it reaches the common areas of a private residential building is not settled, so let an assistance animal through lobbies, pools and other common areas.

Puerto Rico has no separate statute on emotional support animals or on verifying a housing request; the Civil Code recognizes animals trained for therapy or assistance as "domesticated" animals. See Disability Accommodations in Puerto Rico Rentals.

title: No Pet Eviction Fact Sheet
bodyText: Puerto Rico requires no fact sheet, notice or lease disclosure about what happens to a tenant's pet in an eviction, and no notice to an animal-control agency when a tenant with a pet is evicted. The general animal-welfare rules still apply when a tenant leaves or is removed: animals are sentient beings, abandoning one is a felony, and you should not sell, give away or destroy a pet left behind; contact the tenant, the tenant's named contact or the police or an animal shelter. If you know a tenant facing eviction has an animal, tell the tenant in writing to take it at the removal and give the contact of the local animal-control service. See Animals Left in a Puerto Rico Rental and The Tenant's Belongings at Removal.

title: Pet Deposits, Fees and Pet Rent in Puerto Rico
bodyText:
Puerto Rico has no statute on pet deposits, pet fees or pet rent: none caps them, defines a pet deposit as a security deposit, or bars a nonrefundable pet fee. The lease decides. Pet rent is part of the agreed rent; a refundable pet deposit is money you hold under the lease, so state that it secures the same obligations as the security deposit and is returned on the same terms (Puerto Rico has no deposit statute); a nonrefundable pet fee should be named as such with its amount.

If you rent as a business, list every mandatory pet charge in the lease with its cost. Do not set a fixed charge for pet damage that the tenant cannot dispute; charge actual repair costs beyond ordinary wear. Never charge a pet fee, deposit or pet rent for an assistance animal a tenant needs because of a disability.

title: Requiring Pet Liability Insurance
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute on requiring a tenant with a pet to carry liability insurance or to name you as an interested party, and none bars it, so the library's pet insurance clause works in Puerto Rico as written. The reason to use it: under the Civil Code the keeper of an animal is liable for the harm it causes even without fault, unless the injured person was at fault, so a dog bite in a common area is the tenant's liability, and a claim against you is likely too. Let the tenant choose the insurer and agent. Puerto Rico's new pet insurance chapter of the Insurance Code (2026) regulates policies covering a pet's own accidents and illnesses; it is not the liability coverage the clause requires. Do not require insurance for an assistance animal.

title: Pet Policies in Puerto Rico Leases
bodyText:
Puerto Rico has no statute limiting pet policies in residential leases: you may allow or forbid pets, approve them in writing, charge pet rent or a pet deposit, and require the tenant to answer for pet damage and claims. Puerto Rico gives no special right to keep a pet to older adults or other tenants, apart from assistance animals a tenant needs because of a disability (see Assistance Animals in Puerto Rico Rentals). Federally assisted rental housing for older adults or people with disabilities must allow common household pets under federal law. Condominium regulations may add pet rules that bind an owner who leases a unit.

Two limits shape the clause:
- (1) in a form lease, do not say you may act "without liability to Tenant" or are not liable for anything concerning the pet; a clause excluding or limiting the landlord's liability can be annulled;
- (2) do not reserve a right to enter and remove a pet on your own: entry needs justified cause and seven days' notice except in a real emergency, and taking a tenant's animal is self-help.

Use the library's Puerto Rico pet clause, which approves named pets, states pet rent and any pet deposit, has the tenant indemnify you except for your own negligence or misconduct, and lets you revoke approval of a pet that becomes a nuisance or danger by written notice.

The keeper of an animal is liable for the harm it causes even without fault, and animals must be treated according to their nature; abandonment is a felony (see Animals Left in a Puerto Rico Rental).

title: Penalty for Denying an Assistance Animal
bodyText: Puerto Rico's Assistance Animals Act makes it a misdemeanor to prevent a person with a disability from using the rights the Act gives: a fine of up to $100 or up to 30 days in jail, or both, and for each later violation a fine of at least $200 or up to 60 days in jail, or both; using force to keep the person out of a public place, causing harm, is a felony. The Act protects the right to travel on public transportation and to enter hotels, restaurants, buildings, premises and other facilities open to the public with a trained, certified assistance animal, at no extra charge. It does not mention private dwellings, so the penalty most clearly reaches the parts of a property open to the public (a leasing office, a lobby, short-term lodging); whether it reaches a residential lease is not settled. The housing rule that clearly applies is the federal Fair Housing Act, under which refusing a reasonable accommodation for an assistance animal is discrimination with federal remedies (see Assistance Animals in Puerto Rico Rentals). Do not refuse or charge for an assistance animal without legal advice.

title: No Penalty for Misrepresenting a Service Animal
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute making it a crime or an infraction to misrepresent a pet as a service or assistance animal, in housing or anywhere else. The Assistance Animals Act protects only a trained animal certified by a qualified trainer, and in places open to the public the person may be asked to show the identifying tag, card or document and a yearly veterinary health certificate. In housing, follow the federal Fair Housing Act: where the disability or the need for the animal is not apparent you may ask for reliable documentation, and you may deny an accommodation supported by false information. A tenant who obtained the accommodation by deceit may be in breach of the lease, and general fraud rules apply; no Puerto Rico penalty specific to animals does.

title: No EV Right-to-Charge Law
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no right-to-charge statute: no law gives a tenant (or a condominium owner) a right to install or use an electric vehicle charger, and none requires you to provide or allow one. Treat a tenant's request as a request to make an alteration, which the lease may forbid or allow with your written consent. If you allow it, agree in writing who installs and pays, that a licensed electrician does the work with any required permit, who pays for the electricity, and what happens at move-out. Bill electricity only through the tenant's own meter at the utility's billed amount: reselling electricity can make you a regulated electric service company (see Utilities in Tenant's Name).

title: No EV Charger Installation Rules
bodyText: Puerto Rico sets no rules on the conditions a landlord may or must impose on a tenant's electric vehicle charger (insurance, licensed installer, registration, cost-sharing). The lease or a signed alteration agreement decides. Require a licensed electrician and any permit the municipality requires, liability insurance if you wish, and payment of the electricity through the tenant's own meter; do not resell electricity.

title: EV Chargers When the Tenancy Ends
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no EV-specific rule for chargers at the end of a tenancy; the Civil Code's rule on tenant improvements applies: a tenant who installed a charger cannot make you pay for it, but may remove it if removal does not damage the property, and must return the home in the condition received except ordinary wear. The lease or the alteration agreement may change that default, for example by providing that an approved charger stays and becomes yours, or that the tenant must remove it and restore the wiring at the tenant's cost. Put the choice in writing when you approve the installation.

title: No Shared-Area EV Charging Rule
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute on tenant EV charging in shared parking: no right to install a charger in a common area, no rule on reserving or charging for a charging space, and no condominium EV-charging article. In a condominium, common-element parking is allotted among unit owners under the Condominium Act, and a landlord cannot give a tenant a common-area space or charger the owners' council has not assigned to the unit. If you offer shared charging, charge only a stated parking or service fee agreed in the lease, not a price per kilowatt-hour: selling electricity to tenants can make you a regulated electric service company.

title: Parking at a Puerto Rico Rental
bodyText:
Puerto Rico has no statute on parking terms in residential leases, so the lease decides whether parking is included, where the tenant may park and what rules apply. Use the library parking clause that has no liability disclaimer: in a form lease, a sentence saying you are not liable for damage to or theft of a vehicle can be annulled, while saying you do not provide security for the parking area is a statement of fact.

Two Puerto Rico laws can reach a rental's parking.
- (1) The Public Parking Areas Act requires a DACO license, posted rates and liability insurance for anyone who lets vehicles park for a fee, treats the operator as the depositary of the parked car, and gives DACO jurisdiction over damage claims; parking run only as a convenience for the customers of a business is exempt from the license but must still carry the insurance. DACO's parking regulation applies the license rule to areas open to the public for a fee and run for profit, which parking for your own tenants generally is not, but the Act's own definition is broader (any area used to let vehicles park for a fee). So if you charge separately for parking, and above all if you rent spaces to non-tenants, check with DACO, and in any case keep liability insurance on the lot.
- (2) In a condominium, common-element parking is allotted among unit owners, and an owner of a separate parking space must give the other owners notice and priority before renting it to anyone else, or the rental is void.

title: No Rule on Delivering Parking Rules
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute on parking or towing rules in a residential lease: no requirement to deliver them before signing, no prescribed heading, no limit on the vehicle information you may ask for, and no rule tying a parking permit to the lease. The lease decides. Attach any parking rules to the lease or a signed addendum so the tenant agrees to them; a rule added later binds the tenant only if the tenant agrees in writing, because a form-lease clause letting you change the contract's terms on your own can be annulled (see Changing Lease Terms in Puerto Rico). In a condominium, the building's parking rules and the council of owners' allotment of common-element spaces apply as well. Municipalities regulate street parking by ordinance.

title: Vehicle Rules and Towing at a Puerto Rico Rental
bodyText:
Puerto Rico has no statute on vehicle rules in residential leases, so you may limit parking to operable, registered passenger vehicles, require registration information, and restrict repairs and washing, as the library's vehicle rules clause does. List any charge for tags, decals or access cards in the lease with its amount.

Towing is the limit. Puerto Rico's Vehicle and Traffic Act gives the power to remove vehicles to the Puerto Rico Police and the Municipal Police: a vehicle left unattended for more than 24 hours on a public road or an adjoining public or private area is presumed abandoned, and if the owner does not remove it within 24 hours of a police demand, the police or the municipality may tow it.

No Puerto Rico statute found authorizes a private landlord to tow, boot or hold a tenant's or visitor's car on its own. So the library clause's towing sentence works in Puerto Rico only through that procedure: call the Police or the municipality; do not tow or immobilize a vehicle yourself. Do not ban a tenant's car only because its registration has lapsed without asking the tenant first to renew or remove it.

title: Storage Space With a Puerto Rico Rental
bodyText:
Puerto Rico has no statute on storage space provided with a residential lease. Puerto Rico's self-service storage law, which gives a storage operator a lien and a sale procedure, applies only to property devoted to renting storage spaces (a storage business), not to a storage room or locker that comes with an apartment, so it gives you no lien or sale right over a tenant's stored belongings; Puerto Rico also has no landlord's lien on a tenant's property (see No Landlord Lien on Tenant Belongings).

List the assigned space in the lease, ban hazardous, flammable or perishable materials, and do not add a sentence saying you are not liable for items stored there: in a form lease such a disclaimer can be annulled.

In a condominium, storage rooms (covachas) are common elements unless the master deed assigns them to a unit, so lease only a space the unit owns or controls. Belongings left in the storage space after the tenancy are handled like other property left behind (see Property Left After Move-Out).

title: Towing Vehicles From a Puerto Rico Rental
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no private-property towing statute for rental properties: no signage rule, no written-authorization form, no rate cap and no procedure letting a landlord have a tenant's or visitor's car towed on its own. Vehicle removal runs through the police: under the Vehicle and Traffic Act, a vehicle left unattended for more than 24 hours on a public road or an adjoining public or private area is presumed abandoned, and if the owner does not remove it within 24 hours of a demand by the Puerto Rico Police or the Municipal Police, the police or the municipality may tow it and store it for the owner, who is notified and has a set time to reclaim it; illegally parked vehicles are removed by the police in the same way. For a car parked in a tenant's space without permission or abandoned in your lot, call the Puerto Rico Police or the Municipal Police; do not hire a tow truck yourself, block, boot or keep the car. If you operate a paid parking lot open to the public, the Public Parking Areas Act applies (see Parking at a Puerto Rico Rental). Municipal ordinances may add rules.

title: Charging Separately for Parking
bodyText: Puerto Rico does not require you to offer parking separately from the rent, and does not regulate a separate parking charge. If you charge for parking separately, state the charge in the lease as an itemized mandatory or optional charge. Two cautions: a parking area used to let vehicles park for a fee may fall under Puerto Rico's Public Parking Areas Act, which requires a DACO license and liability insurance (parking run only as a convenience for a business's customers is exempt from the license but not from the insurance; see Parking at a Puerto Rico Rental); and in a condominium, a separately owned parking space can be rented to someone other than a unit owner only after giving the other owners notice and priority.

title: Medical Cannabis and Puerto Rico Rentals
bodyText:
Puerto Rico allows only medical cannabis, under the Medical Cannabis Act, for registered patients with a photo identification card; recreational marijuana remains illegal. Medical use is allowed only in homes and private places, never in public places.

The Act protects registered patients from discrimination in employment only; no Puerto Rico law protects a patient's cannabis use in rental housing, so a lease may ban smoking, vaping or growing cannabis, or any use or possession, on the property, as the library's optional marijuana clause does. Patients may not grow their own cannabis under the Act; cultivation requires a license.

Cannabis remains illegal under federal law, and federally assisted housing must follow federal rules. If a tenant asks to use medical cannabis as a disability accommodation, get legal advice before answering. See Smoking and Cannabis Rules for Puerto Rico Rentals.

title: Common Areas, Displays and Installations
bodyText:
Puerto Rico has no statute giving a tenant a right that the library's common-area and alterations clause would block: no protected right to flotation bedding (waterbeds), no right to install solar panels or a clothesline or drying rack, and no statute protecting a tenant's display of flags or signs against a lease rule. The clause works in Puerto Rico as written, including its carve-out for any display that applicable law protects.

Puerto Rico's constitutional free-speech guarantee is written as a limit on lawmaking, and whether it reaches a private landlord has not been settled here, so keep any display rule neutral and honor the clause's carve-out for protected displays. Puerto Rico's sign law limits signs in residential zoning districts and lets a temporary political, civic or religious sign go up only with the authorization of the owner, tenant or possessor, so the lease may set the landlord's rule (see Tenant Display Rights); a display rule must be neutral, because refusing to rent for religious or political reasons is barred.

In a condominium, the building's regulations and the Condominium Act's rules on facades and common elements may restrict balconies, signs and installations further. The keeper's duty to conserve the home supports the drilling, weight and candle rules.

title: No Disaster-Displaced Guest Rule
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute on people displaced by a hurricane or other declared disaster who stay in a hotel, a short-term rental or a tenant's home: no rule letting your tenant house them despite the lease's guest or occupancy terms, no rule limiting such stays, and no rule on when a displaced person's stay in a hotel or other lodging becomes a tenancy. The Civil Code treats lodging as its own contract, separate from a lease. For hotels and other lodgings with 15 or more bedrooms, the Hotel Keepers Act counts even a tenant of the hotel as a guest, and lets the operator, after notice and a refund of any unearned prepaid charges, have a person who keeps breaking the hotel's rules leave, with police help; a landlord renting a home must instead go through the court eviction process. If your tenant wants to take in relatives or friends who lost their home, your lease's guest and occupancy terms decide; consider agreeing in writing to a temporary, dated exception rather than enforcing the guest limit during the emergency. When a disaster or emergency is declared, prices of essential goods are frozen automatically until it ends, and the price-control law counts a lease as a sale; whether housing or lodging is on the Department of Consumer Affairs' (DACO's) list of covered goods and services was not checked, so check any DACO price-freeze order before raising a rent or room rate during an emergency.

title: Grills and Fire Safety in Puerto Rico
bodyText:
No Puerto Rico statute regulates grilling, open flames or flammable materials at a rental home, or limits what a lease may say about them, so the lease decides. The Fire Bureau's power to adopt fire-prevention rules reaches non-residential buildings, multi-story commercial buildings and the common areas of multi-story residential buildings, not the inside of homes; those fire-prevention regulations and the building code adopted by regulation were not read, so check them before allowing grills in a multi-story building's common areas.

In a condominium, the bylaws and rules may restrict grills on balconies and terraces, and your tenant must follow them (see Condominium Statement).

The library's Fire Safety and Grilling clause is lawful in Puerto Rico as written: the tenant must keep and maintain the home and answers for damage the tenant causes, and the 15-foot distance is your drafting choice, not a Puerto Rico figure. For building-wide fire-protection duties, see Smoke Alarms and Fire Safety in Puerto Rico.

title: Firearms at a Puerto Rico Rental
bodyText:
No Puerto Rico statute limits what a lease may say about firearms. None protects a tenant's right to keep a firearm in a rental home, none makes a lease restriction on firearms unenforceable against a weapons licensee, and none protects a firearm kept in a vehicle in your parking area.

Puerto Rico's Weapons Act of 2020 does set rules that reach rental homes. Anyone who has, carries or transports a firearm needs a current weapons license, and a licensee must carry concealed. A licensee with five or more firearms must keep 80 percent of them in a secure place, locked and fixed to the building, so a tenant may need to fasten a gun safe to the structure; decide in advance how you will handle that request.

Firing a firearm outside authorized places is a felony except in lawful defense of oneself or others, and a person in possession of the property under a title or right, which includes your tenant, who is present and knows of an unlawful discharge there must alert the Police immediately, and in any case within 48 hours, or face a $1,000 administrative fine. Negligently leaving a firearm within reach of a minor under 18 who then causes serious harm is a crime.

The presence of three or more firearms in a home is prima facie evidence that its owner or possessor, or the people living there, traffic in firearms illegally unless they hold a weapons, gunsmith, shooting-club or hunting-preserve license. The Secretary of Justice may also seek forfeiture of any property where firearms or ammunition are stored or moved in violation of the Act (see Nuisance Complaints and Your Rental on challenging a forfeiture), so act promptly on reports of unlicensed weapons at the property.

Beyond these rules, a firearm term in the lease is a matter of contract. The library offers only the optional Firearm Discharge and Storage clause, which tracks the Act; a broader ban is not barred by statute, but no case law was searched on it, and a landlord who wants one should take advice first.

title: Guests in a Puerto Rico Rental
bodyText: No Puerto Rico statute limits how long a tenant's guests may stay or what a lease may say about guests, and no statute protects a live-in caregiver's stay. Puerto Rico has no mobile-home-lot statute, so lot-rule notice questions don't arise. A guest rule is a matter of contract, but in a form lease the guest period must be stated in the lease itself: a clause that lets you set or change the period later by notice is especially open to annulment as a one-sided change. Use the library's Guest Policy (14-Day Limit) clause, which fixes the period. Two Puerto Rico rules make a guest rule worth having. When a tenant of a home dies, family members who lived there for the six months before the death, or another person who lived there for that time, may take the tenant's place under the lease (see Occupants and Survivors in Puerto Rico). And unless the lease expressly prohibits it, a tenant may sublet, so a long-staying "guest" who pays may in fact be a subtenant; the library's No Subletting or Assignment clause closes that gap. In a condominium, the unit owner answers to the other owners for violations of the building's rules by guests and anyone else occupying the unit, so make sure your tenant's guests follow the condominium's rules.

title: Guest Stay Limits in Puerto Rico
bodyText: No Puerto Rico statute sets a maximum or minimum guest stay, so the number of days in a guest clause is your choice. The library's Guest Policy (14-Day Limit) clause is lawful in Puerto Rico as written: it states the limit in the lease (14 consecutive days, or 14 days in any rolling 6-month period) and requires your written consent before a guest becomes an occupant or tenant. A limit well under six months also helps you keep track of who lives in the home, since a person who has lived with the tenant for six months before the tenant's death may take over the lease. Apply the limit the same way to every household; federal fair housing law bars rules that treat families with children, or people with disabilities who need a live-in aide, less favorably.

title: Guests' and Suppliers' Access in Puerto Rico
bodyText: No Puerto Rico statute gives a tenant's guests or suppliers a right of access to a multi-unit building, and none bars a fee for guest access. Two narrower rules apply. In an urbanization or community with a municipal access-control permit, the gate may never block police, emergency services, water, power, communications, security and garbage providers, or officials on duty; guards may ask a visitor for name, the home being visited, vehicle make, model, colour and plate, and times in and out; and every owner or resident has access to the controlled area on equal terms, which includes your tenant. In a certified assisted-living housing project for older adults, a resident may receive visitors of the resident's choice without supervision (see Assisted-Living Projects: 30-Day Termination Notice). Outside those settings, guest access is a matter for the lease and, in a condominium, the building's rules.

title: Keys and Re-Keying in Puerto Rico
bodyText:
Puerto Rico has no statute on rental keys. None requires a key receipt, limits what you may charge when keys are not returned or must be replaced, bars a rule against copying keys, or requires you to re-key between tenants (see No Security-Device or Re-Keying Statute).

The library's Keys clause is lawful in Puerto Rico as written. Its re-key charge is the actual cost caused by the tenant's failure to return the keys, which follows from the tenant's duty to give the home back as received; charge only the real cost and keep the invoice. Because Puerto Rico's purchase-receipt transparency law, which we treat as covering landlords, requires every non-optional charge to be itemized, also list the re-key charge and any replacement-key charge in the Fees and Charges clause.

Never change the locks to keep a tenant out: that is self-help eviction (see No Self-Help Eviction). After a court judgment, the lock is changed at the removal the court marshal supervises. Puerto Rico has no domestic-violence lock-change statute; see Lock Changes for Domestic-Violence Victims.

title: Police Cooperation and Crime-Free Leases in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no crime-free lease statute. No law requires you, as a landlord, to join a crime-free housing programme, to give police or child-protection investigators access to your tenants' homes, or to evict after police calls, and none limits a lease penalty for a tenant who calls the police or emergency services. But the reporting duties Puerto Rico puts on every person bind you and your staff. Anyone who knows or suspects that a child is being maltreated or neglected, or is at risk of it, must report it immediately to the Department of the Family's maltreatment hotline, to the Police or at a Department office, and a wilful and knowing failure to report is a misdemeanour, or a felony with a fixed two-year prison term where sexual abuse of the child is known or suspected (Ley 57-2023, arts. 6, 51, 51-A (8 L.P.R.A. §§ 1653, 1732, 1732a)). Anyone who knows or suspects that an older adult is being maltreated must report it to the Department of the Family's Special Investigations Unit, the Office of the Ombudsman for the Elderly, the Police and the Bureau of Special Investigations (Ley 121-2019, art. 18 (8 L.P.R.A. § 1528)). And anyone who learns of a death from a crime, an accident, violence, poisoning, suicide or drug intoxication, or of a sudden and unexpected death, as when a tenant is found dead in a unit, must report it immediately to the Police or to a judge or prosecutor, and may not touch or move the body, its clothing or objects near it without written permission; a wilful failure to report, or disturbing the scene, is a misdemeanour (Ley 135-2020, arts. 9, 16 (34 L.P.R.A. §§ 3051, 3058)). Two other rules touch the subject. A person in possession of the property under a title or right, which includes your tenant, who is present and knows that someone has unlawfully fired a firearm there must alert the Police immediately (see Firearms at a Puerto Rico Rental). And in an urbanization with a municipal access-control permit, the gate may never block law enforcement officers. The library's criminal-activity clause does not apply when the tenant or a household member is the victim or calls for police or emergency help, and we recommend keeping it that way (see Criminal Activity at a Puerto Rico Rental). Puerto Rico's Constitution protects homes against unreasonable searches and lets only a judge issue a search warrant, so do not let police into a tenant's home on your own authority without the tenant's consent or a warrant. In federally assisted housing, follow the federal programme's rules.

title: No Candidate or Canvasser Access Rule in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute requiring you to let political candidates, campaign workers, petition circulators or voter-registration volunteers into an apartment building, condominium or gated urbanization to reach tenants' doors, and none requiring a voter-information area. Puerto Rico's Election Code regulates campaign propaganda in public places and near polling centres, not access to private homes. If you allow canvassing, apply the same rule to every candidate and cause. In a condominium or an access-controlled urbanization, the building's or association's rules and guards also decide who enters the common areas.

title: Window and Portable Air Conditioners
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute giving a tenant a right to install a portable or window air conditioner, and none requiring a lease that restricts window units to say so. Whether a tenant may install one is a matter for the lease; the library's alterations rules apply to anything fixed to the building (see Alterations and Improvements Under Puerto Rico Law). In a condominium, an occupant may not change the outside of the façade, including exterior windows, without the consent of two-thirds of the owners holding two-thirds of the shares in the common areas, and may not attach to the walls anything that could endanger people or property, so a through-the-wall or window unit may need the building's approval. If you allow window units, say in the lease who installs them, who pays for any electrical work by a licensed technician, and that the tenant restores the opening when the lease ends.

title: Plug-In Solar and Batteries in Puerto Rico Rentals
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute giving a tenant a right to install a plug-in solar device, solar panels or a home battery at a rental, and none limiting what a lease may say about them, so the lease and your consent decide. The Civil Code does protect an owner's right to the sunlight that ordinarily reaches a property against neighbors who shade it, and voids any agreement limiting that right; that rule protects owners and holders of real rights, not tenants, and we read it as not reaching your lease rules about equipment on your own building (no case law was searched). In a condominium, solar installations serving the building are common elements, and changes to the façade need the owners' approval, so a tenant's panels outside the unit need the condominium's consent as well as yours. If you install a system and charge tenants for the electricity it produces, you may be acting as an electric service company that Puerto Rico's Energy Bureau regulates; charge only for a unit's own meter at the utility's billed amount (see Splitting Utility Bills Among Tenants). If you allow a tenant's equipment, put in writing who installs it, who pays, insurance, and removal and repair at the end of the lease.

title: Recycling at Puerto Rico Rental Buildings
bodyText: Puerto Rico does not require you to tell tenants where or how to recycle. The duties fall on buildings and municipalities instead. Every housing complex, apartments or houses, whose construction began on or after July 1, 2003 must have a designated area for recyclable materials where residents place them in separate containers. Every condominium must have containers for recyclable materials in a common area unless no space is available, in which case the board must notify the mayor in writing (until the 2026 amendment took effect in late October 2026, that notice went to DACO's Secretary). Municipalities are responsible for making residents separate recyclables before collection, through their own recycling programmes and ordinances, which we did not search. If your building has a recycling area, telling tenants where it is and what goes in each container in your house rules is good practice, and a lease rule requiring tenants to follow the municipality's separation rules is lawful.

title: Religious and Cultural Displays
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute giving a tenant a right to display religious or cultural items on a door, doorframe or balcony, and none limiting a lease rule on displays. Two rules still matter. Puerto Rico's Civil Rights Act forbids anyone with the right to rent a dwelling to refuse to rent it for religious or political reasons, or for race, colour or sex, so a display rule should be neutral, written and applied to every kind of item alike; a rule aimed only at religious items invites a discrimination claim. In a condominium, no occupant may decorate or change exterior walls, doors or windows with designs or colours different from the rest of the building without two-thirds of the owners' consent, so a display on the outside of an entry door may need the building's approval. Federal fair housing law may also apply.

title: House Rules Under Puerto Rico Law
bodyText:
Puerto Rico has no statute listing what makes a landlord's house rules enforceable. Your rules bind the tenant as terms of the lease, so attach them or describe them in the lease when it is signed.

You cannot change them alone during the lease: a change to a signed lease needs the same form as the lease itself, so a written lease's rules change only by a written amendment the tenant signs, and a form-lease clause letting you change terms by notice is especially open to annulment. When the term ends and the lease continues, it continues on the same terms, rules included; to bring in new rules, agree them in writing with the tenant or offer a new lease.

Use the library's Rules and Regulations clause, which makes new rules bind only if the tenant agrees in writing or they are part of a renewal. Keep rules reasonable and in good faith: a rule that is unclear in a form lease is read against you.

Other rules apply in some buildings. In a condominium every occupant must strictly comply with the building's deed and bylaws, whatever the lease says (see Homeowner / Condominium Association Compliance). In a certified assisted-living project the residence contract must set reasonable conduct rules and the resident may have a copy of every rule. Student housing licensed by DACO follows DACO's rules (see Renting to Students: DACO License).

title: Smoke From Other Units and Smoke-Free Common Areas
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute on smoke drifting between units and none letting a lease make a tenant accept drifting smoke or give up claims over it. Do not use a drift waiver: in a form lease, a clause that limits your own liability is especially open to annulment, and a tenant's waiver cannot stop the tenant suing the neighbor who smokes for nuisance. Puerto Rico's smoking law does reach parts of apartment buildings. Smoking, including electronic cigarettes, is banned in any workplace with one or more employees, and the law counts as a workplace the common areas of multiple dwellings and residential buildings where any trade, service or business is carried on, so lobbies, hallways and other common areas where your staff or contractors work are smoke-free, except outdoor areas outside the work area. Smoking is also banned in elevators of residential buildings. If your building is covered, post signs reading "prohibido fumar" with a citation of the law (Ley 40-1993), and brief your employees on the law at least every two years. The law does not apply inside tenants' homes, so a smoking rule for units comes only from the lease (see Smoking and Cannabis Rules for Puerto Rico Rentals).

title: Snow Removal: Not Applicable in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Snow does not fall in Puerto Rico, and Puerto Rico law has no snow or ice removal rule for rentals, so the library's Snow Removal clause is not used in a Puerto Rico lease. Yard, walkway and parking-area upkeep, including clearing storm debris after a hurricane, is a matter for the lease (see Yard Upkeep and Irrigation in Puerto Rico and After a Hurricane or Other Disaster).

title: Flags and Signs at Puerto Rico Rentals
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute protecting a tenant's right to fly a flag or post a political sign, and none limiting what a lease or a condominium may say about flags or signs, so the lease decides, subject to three rules. First, Puerto Rico's signs law lets anyone put up a temporary sign for up to 90 days for a political, civic, religious or similar message without a permit, but only with the authorization of the owner, the tenant or the possessor of the property; signs may be no taller than 30 feet or larger than 200 square feet and must come down within five days after the campaign ends. Posting a sign on someone else's private property without the consent of its owner, custodian or person in charge is a misdemeanor, so neither you nor anyone else should post on a rented home without the tenant's agreement. Second, you may not refuse to rent to anyone for political or religious reasons, so keep any sign rule neutral and apply it to every message alike. Third, in a condominium no occupant may change the façade or decorate exterior walls, doors or windows differently from the rest of the building without two-thirds of the owners' consent, so balcony flags and window signs may need the building's approval. Federal law separately bars condominium and cooperative associations from stopping their members (unit owners) from displaying the United States flag, subject to reasonable time, place and manner rules; it does not give a tenant a right against the landlord's lease.

title: Tenant Security Cameras and Video Doorbells
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute giving a tenant a right to install security cameras or a video doorbell, and none limiting what a lease may say about them, so the lease and your consent to any fixture decide (see Alterations and Improvements Under Puerto Rico Law). Puerto Rico's Penal Code sets the outer limits for everyone, you included. Secret video surveillance, with or without audio, of a private place or anywhere people reasonably expect privacy is a crime punished by three years' imprisonment, so a tenant may not aim a camera into a neighbor's home, and you may never put a hidden camera in a rented unit. Recording a private conversation you take part in without the express consent of everyone in it is a misdemeanor, so cameras and doorbells that record sound need care; video-only recording, or clear notice, is the safer course. In a condominium, devices on the façade or in common areas need the building's approval. If you allow tenant cameras, say in the lease where they may point, that they may not record other units or shared spaces where people expect privacy, and that the tenant removes them and repairs any damage when the lease ends.

title: Keeping Non-Tenants Off the Property
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute letting a residential landlord bar a non-tenant from common areas by a trespass warning. The only statutory no-entry notice is for shopping centres. The Penal Code's trespass-type offences are narrow: entering another's dwelling without the express consent of its owner, possessor or person in charge is a crime only when the person also acts as owner, and entering another's land without authorization is a crime only when the person forces a fence, intends to commit a crime, or occupies an authorized construction site. So a warning letter alone does not make a later visit a crime. To keep a disruptive non-tenant away, call the police when a crime occurs, ask the court for an order (see Squatters and Unauthorized Occupants), and in a condominium ask the board, which may sue to stop violations of the building's rules. Remember that your tenant's home is the tenant's: barring a tenant's lawful guest from reaching the unit can interfere with the tenant's peaceful use of the home (see Quiet Enjoyment in Puerto Rico).

title: Waterbeds and Water-Filled Furniture
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute on waterbeds or other water-filled furniture: none lets you ban them, requires a tenant to insure them, or caps a related deposit or fee. The lease decides. The tenant must keep the home and maintain it and is liable for damage the tenant or the tenant's household causes, so a clause requiring your written consent to water-filled furniture, proof of the tenant's insurance and proper installation is a contract term you may use. If you charge anything for it, list the charge in the Fees and Charges clause.

title: Renting a Condominium or Gated-Community Home
bodyText:
If you rent out an apartment in a condominium, the Condominium Act requires the lease to contain your statement that you know and will fully observe the Act, the master deed and the bylaws, and you must give the Board of Directors a copy of the lease no later than the date it takes effect. You stay solely responsible for the maintenance fees and you answer to the condominium for your tenant's compliance. If you skip these steps, the people living in the unit are not recognized as authorized to receive any service from the board, its staff or the management. Use the Condominium Statement clause.
