If the home is in an urbanization or community with a municipal access-control permit, you must notify the residents' association of the lease within 30 days and require in the lease the tenant's statement that the tenant knows and will observe the access-control law and the association's regulation; you stay responsible for the access-control fees and answer for your tenant's breaches. Use the Access-Controlled Community Statement clause.

Neither law requires you to hand the tenant the association's documents, but give the tenant the bylaws and rules at signing anyway: they bind the tenant only if the tenant can know them (see House Rules Under Puerto Rico Law). Municipal ordinances and a condominium's own bylaws may add requirements.

title: No Bed Bug Disclosure Rule in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute requiring you to tell an applicant or tenant about current or past bed bugs or other pests, and none requiring a bed bug information sheet. You must still deliver the home in a condition suitable for its use, so treat any known infestation before the tenant moves in, and never deny one if asked: deceit during the negotiations is a breach of the duties the Civil Code imposes before a contract is signed, and you would owe the tenant's resulting expenses and losses. For reporting, treatment and cost terms during the tenancy, see No Bed Bug or Pest Statute in Puerto Rico and the optional Pest Reporting and Treatment clause.

title: Use Permits and Certificates of Occupancy
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute requiring you to disclose a building's use permit (permiso de uso) or a certificate of occupancy to a tenant, or to attach one to the lease. The permit itself matters: every use of a building in Puerto Rico must be authorized in advance by the Permits Management Office, an autonomous municipality with delegated powers or an authorized professional, and utilities and licences for the use of a building require the applicant to present the use permit. If a use permit is voided, the utilities are told to cut basic services such as electricity and water. So before renting, make sure the home has a use permit for residential use, and keep a copy: a tenant opening utility accounts may be asked for it, and renting space whose use is not authorized (for example a converted garage or added unit) puts the tenancy and the services at risk.

title: No Defective Drywall Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute requiring you to disclose defective (for example, imported sulfur-emitting) drywall or other construction defects to a tenant. You must still deliver the home in a condition suitable for its use and make necessary repairs, and you should not hide a known defect: deceit during the negotiations breaches the duties the Civil Code imposes before a contract is signed, and you would owe the tenant's resulting expenses and losses. If a known defect affects health or the use of the home, fix it before renting or tell the applicant in writing before signing.

title: Electric Submetering in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute on electric submetering in rentals and none requiring a submetering disclosure. The question is answered instead by the energy law and the Energy Bureau's rules: anyone who offers billing or resale of electricity is an electric service company that must hold the Bureau's certification, with no exception for landlords, small properties or charges passed on at cost. So the library never has you charge the tenant for electricity: no submetering, no allocation of a master electric bill and no reimbursement of an electric bill. Either the tenant opens the electric account in the tenant's own name before moving in, or electricity is included in the rent (see Utilities in Tenant's Name and Splitting Utility Bills Among Tenants).

title: Renting in a Flood-Prone Zone
bodyText:
Puerto Rico requires a flood warning in the lease only where the property is in an area the Planning Board has declared a flood-prone zone. There, it is illegal to lease without warning the tenant, in the written lease itself, that any construction, use or development must comply with the Regulation on Flood-Prone Zones; a willful violation is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $500, up to six months in jail, or both. Use the Flood-Prone Zone Notice clause.

Check the Planning Board's flood-zone maps before you rent, and tell the tenant in writing if the home has flooded before: Puerto Rico has no flood-history disclosure statute, no state form or rider and no special tenant termination right, but deceit during the negotiations breaches the duties the Civil Code imposes before a contract is signed, and you would owe the tenant's resulting expenses and losses.

Building, filling or making substantial improvements in a flood-prone zone without complying with the regulation is also illegal, so keep control of alterations. Federal flood-insurance rules may apply to your financing but do not create a tenant disclosure.

title: No Foreclosure Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute requiring you to tell an applicant or tenant that the property is in foreclosure, that you have received a foreclosure complaint, or that a sale is scheduled. The risk to the tenant is real: after a foreclosure sale, the court may order the removal of everyone occupying the property by the owner's order or tolerance, which can include your tenant (see Tenants When the Property Is Foreclosed, which also covers the federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act). So if your mortgage is in default or a foreclosure case has been filed, tell an applicant in writing before signing: hiding it is deceit in the negotiations, and you would owe the tenant's resulting expenses and losses.

title: No Good-Cause Eviction Notice in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no good-cause eviction law for private residential leases, so it has no notice telling tenants whether such a law covers their home and no good-cause notice to include in a lease or renewal. When the term ends, the lease continues on the same terms until either party gives notice of ending it; see No Just-Cause Requirement to End a Lease and How a Puerto Rico Lease Continues After Its Term. Federally assisted housing has its own federal notice and good-cause rules.

title: No Contamination Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute requiring you to disclose known environmental contamination, a cleanup or a recorded environmental use restriction to a tenant, and none requiring a lease to repeat such a restriction. Puerto Rico's environmental agencies regulate cleanups under their own laws and regulations, which we did not search. If you know the property or its soil or water is contaminated, deal with it before renting and tell the applicant in writing: you must deliver a home suitable for its use, and deceit during the negotiations breaches the duties the Civil Code imposes before a contract is signed, and you would owe the tenant's resulting expenses and losses. Federal rules (for example, on lead-based paint) apply separately.

title: Condominium and Homeowner Associations and Your Lease
bodyText:
Puerto Rico's association rules for rentals come from the Condominium Act (for buildings under the horizontal property regime) and from the Municipal Code (for urbanizations with access control). No statute requires or caps an association's approval of a lease or of a tenant, an approval fee, or an association-held deposit; if the building's master deed or bylaws require approval, the library's Association Approval of Lease clause, which makes the lease depend on that approval, is lawful in Puerto Rico.

Short-term rentals (under 90 consecutive days) of a condominium apartment cannot be prohibited unless the master deed or bylaws expressly prohibit them or set a minimum lease term; the bylaws may regulate them and charge the owner a special monthly fee no greater than the maintenance fee, and fines for violations by short-term occupants are doubled.

If you fall behind on condominium fees, the board may sue and the court may order your tenant to deposit the rent in court for the condominium until your debt is paid; the board may also cut water, power and other services that run through common elements to your unit after at least 15 days' notice, which falls on your tenant. In an access-controlled urbanization, a court in a fee suit must order your tenant to deposit rent for the association and deduct it from what the tenant pays you. Stay current on fees: either order disrupts your rent and your tenancy.

title: Association Rules and Fines in Puerto Rico Rentals
bodyText:
In a condominium, every occupant, your tenant included, must strictly comply with the Condominium Act, the master deed and the bylaws, and you answer to the other owners for violations by your family, guests and anyone occupying the apartment. The board may fine you, the owner, up to $100 for each violation by you, your occupant, resident, visitor or supplier (up to $200 when a short-term rental occupant commits it), and an unpaid fine can lead to the same service cuts as unpaid fees. In an access-controlled urbanization you likewise answer to the association for your tenant's breaches.

The library's Homeowner / Condominium Association Compliance clause, which has the tenant follow the association's rules and pay fines the tenant's violations cause, is lawful in Puerto Rico; use it with the Condominium Statement or Access-Controlled Community Statement clause where the property needs one. When you pass on a fine, give the tenant a copy of the association's notice and charge only the fine actually imposed.

Satellite dishes and antennas: federal rules protect a tenant's small dish or antenna in areas within the tenant's exclusive use; check them before enforcing an association or lease ban.

title: Outstanding Inspection or Condemnation Orders
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute requiring you to disclose an outstanding inspection, repair or condemnation order to an applicant or tenant. It goes further for the worst case: if the Secretary of Health has declared a vacant dwelling unfit for residential use, renting it, extending a lease of it, or letting anyone occupy it before making the ordered repairs is a crime, and on conviction you lose all rent from the date of the notice until the repairs are done (see Renting a Home Declared Unfit). For any other open order on the property, tell the applicant in writing before signing: you must deliver a home suitable for its use, and deceit during the negotiations breaches the duties the Civil Code imposes before a contract is signed, and you would owe the tenant's resulting expenses and losses.

title: No Mandatory Landlord Liability Insurance
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute requiring a residential landlord to carry liability insurance, and no municipal rental registration tied to insurance. Two settings differ: DACO's student-housing regulations may require public liability insurance or bonds of a licensed student-housing business (see Renting to Students: DACO License), and a condominium's council may insure the building's common areas, which every owner then helps pay for. Insurance is still wise: you answer for damage caused by your own fault or negligence, and a lease clause cannot remove that liability (see Services You Provide Under a Puerto Rico Lease).

title: Lead-Based Paint in Puerto Rico Rentals
bodyText:
The federal lead-based paint disclosure applies in Puerto Rico exactly as in the states: before renting housing built before 1978, give the tenant the Lead Warning Statement, your disclosure of any known lead-based paint or hazards and any reports, and the EPA pamphlet, and keep the signed acknowledgment; use the library's Lead-Based Paint Disclosure.

The federal rule requires the disclosure elements to be in the language of the lease, so if your lease is in Spanish, give the Lead Warning Statement and your disclosure in Spanish and use the pamphlet's Spanish edition; if an agent is involved, include the agent's statement, and have everyone sign and date.

Puerto Rico adds no lease disclosure of its own, but it does regulate lead work: anyone who inspects for lead, assesses lead hazards, designs lead-paint removal or removes it must be certified or licensed under the environmental agency's regulations, removal needs a permit first, and a violation is a felony with daily fines of $10,000 to $25,000. Hire certified contractors for any work that disturbs old paint.

title: No Lead-Safe Certificate for Puerto Rico Leases
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no lead-safe or lead-free certificate that must be obtained for a rental or attached to the lease. Puerto Rico's lead rules certify people, not homes: inspectors, risk assessors, designers and removal workers must be certified or licensed, and lead-paint removal needs a permit before it starts. The federal disclosure still applies to housing built before 1978 (see Lead-Based Paint in Puerto Rico Rentals), and federal renovation rules may apply to work on older homes.

title: No Puerto Rico Lead Notices Beyond the Federal Disclosure
bodyText: Beyond the federal lead-based paint disclosure, Puerto Rico requires no lead notice, certificate, tenant-rights packet or information sheet at lease signing or during the tenancy, and no repeat notice at renewal. Follow the federal rule for each lease (see Lead-Based Paint in Puerto Rico Rentals).

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute requiring you to tell a tenant whether the building has fire sprinklers, or to describe its fire-protection system in the lease. The building rules apply instead: every multi-story building, including condominiums, must have a working automatic fire extinguisher on each floor and lit, unobstructed escape stairs, and some older high-rise residential buildings must have an approved fire-protection system (see Smoke Alarms and Fire Safety in Puerto Rico). Violations are crimes. Telling tenants where the extinguishers and exits are is good practice.

title: No Drug-Lab Contamination Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute requiring you to disclose that a property was used as a methamphetamine or other drug laboratory, no contamination-testing or cleanup standard for former drug labs in housing, and no duty to report a suspected lab to the police as a landlord. If you know a home was used to make drugs, have it professionally assessed and cleaned before renting and tell the applicant in writing: you must deliver a home suitable for its use, and deceit during the negotiations breaches the duties the Civil Code imposes before a contract is signed, and you would owe the tenant's resulting expenses and losses. Property used in a drug felony can also be subject to government forfeiture (see Nuisance Complaints and Your Rental).

title: No Mold Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute requiring you to disclose mold or water intrusion to an applicant or tenant, and none setting mold standards for rentals. In Puerto Rico's humid climate mold is common, so deal with it as part of your repair duties: deliver the home in a condition suitable for its use, make necessary repairs within a reasonable time after the tenant reports a problem, and fix leaks before renting. Tell an applicant in writing about any known mold problem: deceit during the negotiations breaches the duties the Civil Code imposes before a contract is signed, and you would owe the tenant's resulting expenses and losses. The Department of Health can act on unsanitary conditions (see Health Inspections and Unfit-Dwelling Orders).

title: No Radon Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute requiring radon testing, disclosure or mitigation in rentals, and no radon-resistant construction mandate in its statutes. If you have radon test results for a property, share them with the tenant.

title: No Private Well Testing Rule for Rentals
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute requiring you to test a private well that serves a rental, or to give the tenant well-water test results. If the home's water comes from a private well or a non-public system, you must still deliver a home suitable for its use, which includes safe drinking water: test it, keep the results, and share them with the tenant.

title: No Pesticide Application Notice Rule
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute requiring you to notify tenants before pesticides are applied in or around a rental, or to post a notice of pest-control treatment. Give reasonable advance written notice anyway, especially for treatments inside the unit, and remember that entering a unit to treat it needs justified cause and seven days' prior notice (see Pest Reporting and Treatment and Landlord's Right of Entry).

title: No Sex Offender Registry Notice in Leases
bodyText: Puerto Rico does not require a lease notice about the sex offender registry, and no statute requires you to tell tenants that a registered offender lives nearby or in the building. The registry is public: Puerto Rico publishes it on an internet portal, searchable by name, town and postal code, so tenants can check it themselves. Do not use registry information to exclude applicants without care: decisions based on criminal records raise fair-housing questions (see Criminal Activity at a Puerto Rico Rental).

title: No Military Installation Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute requiring you to disclose that a rental is near a military installation or in an aircraft noise or accident-potential zone, and no related tenant termination right. Puerto Rico's former naval station lands (Roosevelt Roads) are being redeveloped under their own law, which creates no tenant disclosure. If a property is close to an active airfield, range or base, telling an applicant in writing is good practice.

title: No Ordnance, Demolition or Meter Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute requiring a lease disclosure about former military ordnance or unexploded munitions near a property, planned demolition, or meter arrangements. The Navy's former training areas on Vieques and Culebra are subject to cleanup programmes under their own laws, which do not create tenant disclosures. If you rent near a former range or impact area, or plan demolition or construction that will affect the tenant, tell the applicant in writing before signing. For electric meters, see Electric Submetering in Puerto Rico.

title: No Shoreline or Beach-Access Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute requiring a lease to disclose that a property is on or near the maritime-terrestrial zone (the public shoreline) or to describe public beach access. Puerto Rico's beaches are public property, and an urbanization's access-control permit must allow compliance with the beach-access rules. If the home is on the coast, tell the tenant in writing which areas are private and which are public shoreline, and that coastal-zone rules may limit structures and uses.

title: No Required Tenant Rights Guide
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no state-published landlord-tenant rights guide that you must give tenants before signing or at renewal, and no signed acknowledgment of one. The Judicial Branch publishes community guides on the eviction process, and Puerto Rico's Consumer Bill of Rights gives consumers rights to information and copies, which the library applies to landlords who rent as a business (see What a Puerto Rico Lease Must Contain). Giving tenants a copy of the Judicial Branch's eviction guide is optional.

title: No Health-Code Variance Notice Rule
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute requiring you to give tenants, or attach to the lease, a Department of Health variance (dispensa) from sanitary rules that applies to a rental. If the Department grants you a variance or orders repairs, keep the document and tell the tenant in writing what it covers (see Health Inspections and Unfit-Dwelling Orders).

title: No Statutory Landlord-Identity Disclosure
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute requiring a residential lease to state the name and address of the owner or of a manager, and none barring an eviction because the landlord did not disclose that information. Put it in the lease anyway: the tenant must know whom to pay and where to send notices, a notice or payment sent to the address in the lease protects both of you, and DACO's consumer rules favour clear, complete contracts. In a gated community, you must notify the residents' association of the lease within 30 days; in a condominium, the board gets a copy of the lease. A manager who leases or administers property for others for pay needs a real estate broker's licence (see Registration and Licenses for Puerto Rico Landlords).

title: No Meter Conservation Charge Rule
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no energy-efficiency or meter conservation charge that a landlord must disclose to new tenants or offset with a rent deduction. For electricity charges generally, see Electric Submetering in Puerto Rico.

title: No Property-Tax Share of Rent Statement
bodyText: Puerto Rico requires no annual statement telling tenants what part of their rent goes to property tax, and has no renter's property-tax credit tied to such a statement. Property tax on real property is the owner's obligation to the Municipal Revenue Collection Center (CRIM); whether you pass any increase to the tenant is a matter for the lease (see Passing Property Tax Increases to the Tenant).

title: California Proposition 65 Warnings: Not Applicable
bodyText: California's Proposition 65 warnings do not apply in Puerto Rico, and Puerto Rico has no equivalent chemical-exposure warning for rentals. Federal disclosures, such as lead-based paint, still apply.

title: No Font-Size or First-Page Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute requiring a particular disclosure on a lease's first page or in a set type size relative to the rest of the lease, and no single-family-occupancy disclosure. Two narrow rules require bold type (the special-district acknowledgments for the Convention Center District and the Science, Technology and Research District), and any form clause that is not clear, complete and easily legible can be annulled (see No Minimum Type Size for Leases and Special District Acknowledgment).

title: Required Lease Disclosures in Puerto Rico: Situational Ones
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no general list of disclosures every lease must contain (see What a Puerto Rico Lease Must Contain). Beyond the items listed there, three situational statements must appear in the written lease itself: in a condominium, your statement that you know and will observe the Condominium Act, master deed and bylaws (Condominium Statement); in an urbanization with access control, the tenant's statement that the tenant knows and will observe the access-control law and the association's regulation (Access-Controlled Community Statement); and in a declared flood-prone zone, the warning that any construction, use or development must follow the flood-zone regulation (Flood-Prone Zone Notice). Puerto Rico has no just-cause or rent-law coverage notice, no required first-page form, and no rule turning a lease with a purchase option into a sale requiring seller disclosures.

title: Deaths, Crimes and Illness at the Property
bodyText: No Puerto Rico statute says whether you must, or need not, tell a prospective tenant that someone died at the property, that a homicide, suicide or other crime happened there, or that a past occupant had HIV or another illness. Puerto Rico has no stigmatized-property rule for leases or sales. The Civil Code's general rules on deceit apply instead: an intentional act or omission that induces a person to sign a contract they would not otherwise have signed is serious fraud, which lets the tenant annul the lease and claim damages, and deceit during the negotiations makes you liable for the tenant's resulting expenses and losses. So answer a prospective tenant's direct question truthfully, and never hide a defect in the property itself. Don't disclose, and don't ask about, anyone's HIV status: Puerto Rico's HIV Bill of Rights bars any person from seeking information that intrudes on the privacy of a person with HIV, from conditioning a rental on proof of an HIV diagnosis, and from referring to another person's HIV diagnosis without that person's consent. If a prospective tenant asks about registered sex offenders, see No Sex Offender Registry Notice in Leases: no statute requires you to disclose registry information, and the registry is public, so you can point the tenant to it; if you answer, answer truthfully. The library offers no lease clause saying you made no statements about events at the property: in a form lease, a clause that limits your liability is especially open to annulment, and liability for fraud can't be waived. No case law was searched on whether staying silent about a death or crime at the property is a material omission.

title: No Required Tenant Rights Statement
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no state-agency statement or summary of tenant rights that you must give tenants, attach to the lease or renewal, or have tenants sign, and no rule barring an eviction or other suit until one is given (see also No Required Tenant Rights Guide). Two narrow exceptions apply only to special kinds of housing. A student-housing business licensed by DACO must put in every lease a clause certifying that the lodging complies with the student-housing law and DACO's regulation and that the tenant was told those texts are available and worth reviewing at signing (see Student Housing Certification). A certified assisted-living project must use a residential contract that clearly describes all the rights and responsibilities of the resident and the operator. Puerto Rico's Consumer Bill of Rights lists consumer rights, including to see and get a copy of a contract before signing, but it is a list of rights, not a document you must hand out. Giving tenants a summary of their rights is optional; if you do, keep it accurate and don't present it as an official form.

title: No Exemption Notice
bodyText: Some states require a lease statement telling tenants that a property is exempt from a statewide rent cap, just-cause eviction rules or a tenant's right to buy. Puerto Rico has none of those laws for private rentals, so there is nothing to be exempt from and no exemption notice to give or put in the lease: there is no general rent control (see No General Rent Control in Puerto Rico), no just-cause requirement for ending a lease after its term (see No Just-Cause Requirement to End a Lease), and no right for a tenant to buy the property when you sell it (see No Tenant Right to Buy). Rent limits that come with a subsidy, tax-credit or incentive programme are set by that programme's own terms, not by an exemption notice.

title: No Tenant Right to Buy
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no tenant protection act of the kind some states have: no cap on rent increases, no just-cause rule for ending a lease after its term, and no right for a tenant of a private landlord to buy the property or receive an offer before you sell it. No notice about any of these belongs in your lease. The Civil Code's purchase rights (first refusal and redemption) arise only by agreement or where a law grants them, and the laws that grant them reach co-owners, co-heirs and owners of adjoining small rural plots, not tenants. Two laws give an occupant a preference to buy, but only when a government owner sells: a tenant occupying a municipal lot in a town centre that the municipality decides to sell gets a preferential right to buy and at least 30 days' written notice, and a five-year occupant of land the Department of Transportation and Public Works disposes of has a preference too. If you sell a rental you own, the tenant has no purchase right unless the lease gives one; a sale does not by itself shorten the lease (see Selling the Property or Changing Managers).

title: No Truth-in-Renting Law
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no truth-in-renting law. No statute requires you to give tenants a state statement of landlord and tenant rights, to print a notice that the lease must comply with Puerto Rico law, or to warn tenants that some clauses may be unenforceable, and no statute penalizes you simply for offering a lease that contains a void clause. The protection works the other way: a clause that breaks a mandatory or prohibitory law is void, and in a form lease the Civil Code lists kinds of clauses that are especially open to annulment, such as one that limits your liability, lets you change the lease on your own, or limits the tenant's actions or evidence. A court may also read any unclear clause against you as the drafter. So the practical rule is to leave such clauses out, not to warn about them. The one lease statement of this kind is for licensed student housing (see Student Housing Certification).

title: Leasing as a Usufructuary
bodyText:
A usufructuary (someone with the right to use and enjoy a property owned by another, often a surviving spouse or a parent who kept a life usufruct when giving a home to the children) may lease the property, but every lease a usufructuary signs ends when the usufruct ends: on the usufructuary's death, at the end of the usufruct's term, or on another ground the Civil Code lists, even if the lease term has time left. If you lease as a usufructuary without the owner's consent, you answer to the owner for damage the tenant causes through fault or negligence, so get the owner's written consent.

The holder of only a right of use or of habitation, including a surviving spouse's lifetime right of habitation in the family home, may not lease that right at all. A single co-owner may not lease the property without the other co-owners' consent. If the home stands on a parcel the government granted in usufruct under Puerto Rico's Land Law, the usufructuary may not rent or lease it at all: such a lease is absolutely void and forfeits the usufruct to the government without a court order.

No statute requires you to tell a tenant that you hold only a usufruct, but hiding a fact that will cut the lease short can be fraud, so use the optional Landlord's Status as Usufructuary clause. A lease signed before November 28, 2020 is governed by the 1930 Civil Code, which also ends a usufructuary's leases with the usufruct.

title: No Utility Disclosure Attachment
bodyText: Puerto Rico requires no utility disclosure attached to the lease: no form explaining how a shared bill is apportioned, no submeter certificate and no notice of energy-improvement charges. What matters instead is electricity: Puerto Rico's energy law counts anyone engaged in billing or reselling electric power as an electric service company regulated by the Energy Bureau, and its rules have no exception for landlords, so the library never has you charge the tenant for electricity (see Electric Submetering in Puerto Rico). If the tenant will pay utilities, the lease should say which ones, in whose name each account will be, and, for water or gas billed by you, the method, the share and how the tenant can see the bill (see Splitting Utility Bills Among Tenants and No Submetering Disclosure Statute).

title: Accessory Dwelling Units
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute on accessory dwelling units (a second, smaller home on the same lot, such as a converted garage or a backyard apartment): none requires municipalities to allow them, none bars an owner-occupancy requirement, and none regulates renting one. Whether you may build or rent one is a zoning and permits question: every use, construction or alteration of a building must be authorized in advance, and a use permit is not issued for a use that does not comply with the applicable laws and regulations. The detailed zoning rules sit in the Planning Board's regulations and each municipality's land-use plan, which the library did not read. Before renting an added unit, make sure it has its own use permit for residential use (see Use Permits and Certificates of Occupancy), and in a condominium check the master deed and bylaws.

title: No Alarm Tampering Fee Rule
bodyText:
No Puerto Rico statute authorizes, sets or caps a lease fee for a tenant who removes, disconnects or tampers with a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm, and no statute requires such alarms inside a rental home (see Smoke Alarms and Fire Safety in Puerto Rico).

The Civil Code already makes the tenant keep the home in good condition and tell you of any breakdown, and a tenant who fails to conserve the home, personally or through someone on the tenant's account, gives you a ground to end the lease. Destroying, disabling or damaging property that belongs to someone else, such as an alarm you installed, is also a misdemeanor under the Penal Code, and the court may order restitution.

A fixed tampering fee would be a penalty clause, which Puerto Rico allows and a court may reduce only if it is extremely out of proportion; the library does not offer one and instead uses the optional Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors clause, which has the tenant pay the reasonable cost of repairing or replacing an alarm the tenant or the tenant's guest removes, disables or damages. A landlord who wants a fixed fee can add one, keeping it modest and taking advice first.

title: Asbestos in Puerto Rico Rentals
bodyText: No Puerto Rico statute requires you to inspect a rental for asbestos, to disclose known asbestos to a tenant, or to follow special rules for asbestos in a rented home. The only Puerto Rico statute that mentions asbestos in buildings concerns government-funded demolition of disaster-damaged buildings in five southern municipalities, which must follow the asbestos and lead management plan approved by the Department of Natural and Environmental Resources and federal EPA and OSHA protocols. Federal and environmental rules on asbestos removal during renovation or demolition still apply to work on your building, so use licensed contractors for any work that may disturb old insulation, flooring or ceiling material. If you know of damaged asbestos material in the home, tell the tenant before signing: concealing a known hazard can be fraud under the Civil Code, and you must deliver the home in a condition suitable for its use.

title: No Balcony Inspection Rule
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute requiring periodic inspection of balconies, decks, stairways or other elevated elements of a rental building, and none requiring you to give tenants an inspection report. Your general Civil Code duties still apply: you must deliver the home in a condition suitable for its use and make necessary repairs within a reasonable time after the tenant tells you of a problem, and the tenant must tell you of any breakdown that needs repair. In a building where units are owned separately (a condominium), the façade with the exterior coverings of balconies and terraces, and the structural elements, are common elements, so their repair is a matter for the association; report a balcony problem to the board and to your tenant promptly. A loose railing or cracked balcony is a safety hazard: inspect it at each turnover and after storms or earthquakes, and restrict use until it is repaired.

title: Changing the Casualty and Re-Renting Rules by Lease
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no casualty statute for leases and no statute requiring you to re-rent after a tenant leaves early, so a Puerto Rico lease is not waiving a statutory casualty or mitigation right. The Civil Code's general rules apply instead, and they are mostly default rules: if the home is destroyed without anyone's fault the lease obligations end, a partial loss can reduce the rent for the usable part, and the tenant may end the lease if you fail to keep the home fit for its agreed use (see Fire and Other Casualty in Puerto Rico). The Code lets an agreement make a party answer even for unforeseeable events, and lets rights be waived unless the waiver is contrary to law, morals or public order. But in a form lease the tenant signs as presented, a clause that limits your liability or limits the tenant's actions or defenses is especially open to annulment. So the library changes the casualty rules only in the landlord's favor where the Code allows it: the optional Fire or Casualty clause adds your right to end the lease after a serious casualty and keeps every right the tenant has, and the Damage Caused by Tenant clause allocates damage the tenant's side causes. The library does not offer a clause making the tenant keep paying full rent after a casualty that was not the tenant's fault, or giving up the tenant's right to end the lease if the home becomes unfit; between parties who negotiate, such a clause may be lawful, but a landlord who wants one should take advice. On re-renting, no statute requires it, but your damages are limited to what was foreseeable and you must act in good faith, so make reasonable efforts to re-let and credit the rent you receive (see When a Tenant Abandons: Rent and Re-Letting); the library offers no waiver of that.

title: Children in the Household
bodyText: No Puerto Rico statute requires a lease to address occupancy by children. Puerto Rico's Civil Rights Act bars refusing to sell or rent a dwelling for political or religious reasons, race, color, sex, or protective hairstyles and hair textures, but not because of children or family status. Puerto Rico's Real Estate Brokers Act does reach family status: a licensed broker, salesperson or real estate company may not discriminate against any party to a sale, lease or property-management transaction because of familial status, among other grounds, so a broker or licensed manager renting for you is bound by it. Federal fair housing law, which applies in Puerto Rico, is different: it bars refusing to rent to, charging more or setting different terms for a household because of familial status (children under 18 living with a parent or legal custodian, and pregnancy), with an exemption for qualifying housing for older persons. So don't exclude children, steer families to particular units or set rules that single children out, and keep any occupancy limit reasonable and applied the same way to everyone (see Occupants and Survivors in Puerto Rico). List every occupant, including children, in the lease: a family member who lived in the home for the six months before the tenant's death may take over the lease. Children are occupants, not tenants; for tenants under 21, Puerto Rico's age of majority, see Tenants Under 21 and Minors in Eviction Cases.

title: Confession of Judgment
bodyText: Puerto Rico's Rules of Civil Procedure do allow a judgment by consent, entered without a trial or even without a lawsuit, but only on a separate writing the debtor signs under oath, authorizing judgment for a set sum and stating the facts and origin of the debt and showing the sum is justly owed. A lease clause in which the tenant agrees in advance to a judgment, or appoints someone to confess judgment for the tenant, does not meet that form, and in a form lease a clause that limits the tenant's right to sue or defend, or restricts the tenant's evidence, is especially open to annulment. The rule covers money, not possession: there is no confessed eviction, and a tenant who will not leave can be removed only through a court eviction (desahucio). So the library offers no confession-of-judgment clause. If a dispute arises and the tenant agrees to pay what is owed, a sworn consent that meets the rule can be part of a settlement; have a lawyer prepare it.

title: Consumer Protection Law and Your Lease
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no single consumer protection act of the kind many states have, with a statutory list of unfair or deceptive practices and a private damages remedy. Its consumer law is built around the Department of Consumer Affairs (DACO): DACO hears complaints from consumers, issues cease-and-desist orders and fines (each day of a violation is a separate violation), and regulates deceptive practices by regulation. DACO's Commercial Practices Regulation (No. 9158) covers anyone who offers goods or services to consumers, and it defines goods to include real property that is leased, so treat it as reaching a landlord who rents homes. Under it: deliver what you advertise; state the full price in ads without the reader having to calculate it, and disclose relevant facts, including the total price, before the lease is signed; never make a statement that is false or misleading or hide a relevant fact; do not charge a fee for a service that does not exist or cannot be shown, and do not charge separately for basic services needed to use the home; give a receipt for every payment showing the date and time, what it pays for, who received it, the amount and the method; collect personal information only with the applicant's consent and after explaining how it will be used; and do not put in the lease a clause that treats the tenant's silence as accepting a change, or an automatic-renewal clause with a charge, unless the tenant expressly agrees in a separate clause the tenant initials after it is explained. DACO's law also carries a Consumer Bill of Rights: the consumer may see and get a copy of a contract before signing, may not be required to sign a contract that is incomplete or has blank spaces, and must get a copy once it is signed. Fill every blank, give the tenant a copy before and after signing (see Complete Every Blank Before Signing and Giving the Tenant a Copy of the Lease), itemize every mandatory fee (see Itemize Every Mandatory Fee), and never put in the lease a clause that bars the tenant from complaining to DACO or another agency, which a form lease cannot do.

title: Keeping Domestic Violence Information Private
bodyText: No Puerto Rico statute requires a private landlord to keep a domestic violence victim's information confidential, limits what you may record or disclose about a tenant's protective order or abuse, or sets a penalty for disclosure. Puerto Rico's confidentiality rules bind government agencies and victim-service bodies instead: communications between a victim and the Women's Advocate's Office or other public victim-service bodies are privileged, and the Criminal Justice Information System runs a Substitute Address Registry so that agencies can answer public-records requests without revealing a victim's real address, with the substitute address used for the victim's mail. Act as if the duty applied anyway: keep any information about a tenant's abuse, protective order or shelter stay strictly private, share it only with the tenant's written consent or when the law requires, and accept a substitute address for mail and notices other than those that must be delivered to the home itself. Disclosing a victim's whereabouts can put the tenant in danger and expose you to a damages claim. See also Domestic Violence and Eviction in Puerto Rico.

title: Calls for Police or Emergency Help
bodyText: No Puerto Rico statute expressly protects a tenant's right to call the police or emergency services, bars a lease from limiting that right, or bars penalizing a tenant for calls for help, and no Puerto Rico statute makes calls for service a ground for eviction or a nuisance charge against a rental. Even without a statute, never write or enforce a lease term that limits or penalizes a tenant, an occupant or a guest for calling the police, 9-1-1 or other emergency help: a term that discourages calling for help, especially from a victim of domestic violence, is contrary to public order, which Puerto Rico's Civil Code does not let a contract override, and it would expose you to liability if harm followed. The library's criminal-activity clause does not apply when the tenant or a household member is the victim or to calls for police or emergency help (see Criminal Activity at a Puerto Rico Rental).

title: No Eviction Penalty Statute
bodyText: No Puerto Rico statute specifically voids, or specifically allows, a lease clause that charges the tenant a fee or penalty because you served a notice, demanded payment or filed an eviction case. Puerto Rico's general rules decide it. A fixed charge for a breach is a penalty clause, which the Civil Code allows; a court enforces it but may reduce it in a case of extreme economic disproportion, reads it narrowly, and lets you collect both the penalty and full performance only for late performance. In court, the winning party recovers its costs under the court rules (see Attorney's Fees in Puerto Rico Lease Disputes). In a form lease, a charge that punishes the tenant for defending an eviction case or exercising a legal right is especially open to annulment as a limit on the tenant's actions or defenses. So the library has no separate eviction or notice fee: the late fee compensates for late payment (see No Statutory Rule on Notice Fees), court costs come through the court, and actual collection costs are capped in the optional Collection Costs clause. Never charge a fee for the tenant's choosing to contest a case.

title: No "Landlord Is Not Liable" Clauses
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute written specifically against exculpatory clauses in leases, but its Civil Code reaches them. In a contract signed on a form one side drafted, as a landlord's lease normally is, a clause that excludes or limits the drafter's liability is especially open to annulment, and liability for fraud or bad-faith breach can never be waived. You also answer for harm you cause through fault or negligence, and, as owner, for damage caused by a building's collapse from lack of necessary repairs, even without fault. So don't put "Landlord is not liable" sentences in a Puerto Rico lease. The library uses versions of its insurance, parking, storage and utilities clauses without those sentences, and its other clauses allocate risk in ways the Code allows: the tenant answers for damage the tenant's side causes (Damage Caused by Tenant), the tenant may be required to carry renter's insurance for the tenant's own belongings, and the person who controls a unit answers for objects thrown or falling from it. A clause making the tenant indemnify you for your own negligence is not offered.

title: Fair Housing in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico has its own fair housing rules, spread across several laws, and the federal Fair Housing Act also applies. Under Puerto Rico's Civil Rights Act, no one with the right to sell, lease or sublease a dwelling may refuse to rent it because of political or religious views, race, color, sex, or protective hairstyles and hair textures associated with a race or national origin; a deliberate violation is a misdemeanor, and the person harmed may sue for damages plus mandatory punitive damages. The Act has no owner-occupied or small-landlord exemption. Its advertising ban is written for ads about acquiring (buying) homes, but treat rental ads the same way. Licensed real estate brokers, salespersons and companies, including licensed property managers, may not discriminate in a sale, lease or management transaction because of race, color, religion, sex, physical or mental disability, familial status or national origin. A rental may not be conditioned on proof of HIV status. DACO's Consumer Bill of Rights adds that consumers may not be discriminated against because of race, religion, gender, economic situation, nationality, sexual orientation, physical disability or any similar reason; whether it reaches a lease is unsettled, so follow it. Puerto Rico's disability laws also reach housing in general terms (see Disability Accommodations in Puerto Rico Rentals). The federal Fair Housing Act adds national origin, familial status and disability for every landlord, with its own limited exemptions. Asking for sexual favors in exchange for housing, or creating a hostile situation, may also be the crime of sexual harassment where the relationship is one of providing services. Apply the same screening criteria, terms and rules to everyone, keep written reasons for every denial, and train anyone who shows or manages your units.

title: Hunting on Rented Land
bodyText: No Puerto Rico statute gives a tenant of rented farmland or rural property hunting or fishing rights, or reserves those rights to the owner, unless the owner grants them. What Puerto Rico's Wildlife Act does say is that hunting on public or private land without the verifiable consent of the owner, administrator or person in charge is a felony, with fines from $5,000 to $50,000 per animal, and every hunter needs a hunting license. Because the Act does not say whether a tenant in possession can give that consent, put the answer in the lease: if you rent rural land or a home on acreage, either reserve hunting to yourself (the optional No Hunting Without Consent clause) or grant it to the tenant in writing. Fishing in Puerto Rico's waters needs a DNER license; no statute ties fishing rights to a lease.

title: Building and Fire Codes in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico's building and fire codes are not statutes: the Permits Management Office (OGPe) adopts and maintains the construction codes by regulation and must revise them at least every three years. As of 2022, according to a joint resolution's statement of motives, the codes in use were the Puerto Rico Codes adopted in 2018, which follow the International Code Council family, including the International Fire Code (the library did not read them). In 2022 the Legislative Assembly ordered OGPe to adopt a property maintenance code, based on the 2021 International Property Maintenance Code, with a uniform inspection, certification and recertification process for existing buildings larger than 2,000 square feet; whether and when OGPe adopted it was not checked. A condominium must keep a disaster and emergency plan, updated each year, under the 2009 International Fire Code. No 2025 or 2026 law moved or renumbered the code-adoption laws. For a rental, the practical rules are: any construction, alteration or change of use needs a permit and must meet the code in force, and the Fire Bureau's prevention certification is part of getting a use permit (see Use Permits and Certificates of Occupancy and Smoke Alarms and Fire Safety in Puerto Rico).

title: Fire Sprinkler Duties in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no sprinkler duty for ordinary rental homes. Its sprinkler law reaches only large buildings built before 1987: the owner or operator of any building more than 75 feet tall (measured from the lowest Fire Service vehicle access level) used for housing must have one of several fire-protection options, such as full sprinklers, sprinklers in selected high-risk areas plus smoke detectors in common areas, a building-wide automatic detection and alarm system, or fire-resistant compartments with alarms. Pre-1987 assembly buildings and high-rise hotels have their own sprinkler rules, buildings over four floors need emergency lighting and exit signs, and every multi-story building must keep an automatic extinguisher on each floor and clear, lit escape stairs. New buildings follow the construction code in force. The duty falls on the owner or the administrator, not the tenant, and a lease cannot shift it; in a condominium the association handles the building systems. If your unit is in such a building, ask the board for its fire-protection compliance, and tell tenants not to block or tamper with sprinkler heads (see No Sprinkler Disclosure Rule and Smoke Alarms and Fire Safety in Puerto Rico).

title: No Foreign Ownership Restriction
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no law restricting foreign persons, nonresident aliens or entities from foreign adversary countries from buying, owning or leasing land or homes, and no statute of frauds requiring a lease to a nonresident alien to say so or give the alien's address. The rules on nonresidents are tax rules: if you, the landlord, live outside Puerto Rico, a tenant or agent who pays you rent may have to withhold Puerto Rico income tax (see Owners Who Live Outside Puerto Rico). A tenant's citizenship or immigration status is not a ground Puerto Rico law asks you to check (see Immigration Status and Your Rental).

title: Which Code Edition Applies
bodyText: Puerto Rico's statutes mostly leave code editions to the Permits Management Office, which must revise the construction codes at least every three years, so the edition that applies to work on your building is the one OGPe has adopted (see Building and Fire Codes in Puerto Rico). A few statutes name a fixed edition. The one that matters for rentals is the Condominium Act: every condominium must approve and keep a disaster and emergency plan, updated each year, under the 2009 International Fire Code, even though newer editions exist. The cement-quality law names the 1997 Uniform Building Code (the sign law also cites it, but "as amended from time to time"), and the legislature ordered a property maintenance code based on the 2021 International Property Maintenance Code. If a newer national edition conflicts with a fixed edition a statute names, follow the statute's edition for that duty and the adopted code for everything else.

title: Waiving Habitability in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no habitability statute with its own waiver rule, so the question is answered by the Civil Code. Rights may be waived unless the waiver is prohibited or contrary to law, morals or public order, so a specific, negotiated arrangement, such as the tenant taking on listed chores for a lower rent, is lawful (see Changing Repair Duties by Agreement in Puerto Rico). What a lease cannot do: remove the protection of a mandatory or prohibitory law (such as the crime of willfully cutting water, power or another service the lease includes, or the crime of renting a home the Secretary of Health declared unfit before making the ordered repairs), waive liability for fraud or deliberate bad-faith breach, or, in a form lease the tenant signs as presented, exclude or limit your own liability or bar the tenant from going to court or to a municipal judge for urgent repairs, which are especially open to annulment. So the library never has the tenant accept the home "as is" or waive your duty to deliver it fit for use and make necessary repairs; the move-in condition report records the home's condition instead.

title: Immigration Status and Your Rental
bodyText: No Puerto Rico statute bars you from asking a rental applicant about immigration or citizenship status, requires you to ask, or makes it unlawful to rent to someone who is not lawfully present, and no Puerto Rico statute protects immigration status as such in housing. Puerto Rico's own fair housing rules do not list national origin for owners renting directly, but licensed brokers and property managers may not discriminate by national origin (see Fair Housing in Puerto Rico), and federal fair housing law bars national-origin discrimination, with narrow exemptions for some single-family homes rented by their owner and some owner-occupied buildings of up to four units (the advertising ban has no such exemption). Puerto Rico's domestic-violence protections, including the Substitute Address Registry, apply regardless of immigration status, and crime victims may not be questioned about their immigration status when they report a crime. If you screen identity, accept any reliable government ID, apply the same rule to every applicant, and don't ask about status unless a housing programme you participate in requires it.

title: No Jury in Puerto Rico Civil Cases
bodyText: A jury waiver does nothing in a Puerto Rico lease. In Puerto Rico's courts, civil cases, including evictions, rent collection and damages claims, are decided by a judge; Puerto Rico's Constitution guarantees a jury only to a person accused of a felony, and statutes extend it to some misdemeanors. So the library has no jury-waiver clause for Puerto Rico, and none is needed. A case between a landlord and a tenant from different states that is filed in the federal court for the District of Puerto Rico follows federal law on juries; a landlord who wants a waiver for that case should take advice. For the related question of arbitration clauses, see Arbitration Clauses in Leases.

title: No Penalty for Using a Prohibited Term
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute that fines or penalizes a landlord simply for knowingly putting a prohibited or unenforceable term in a lease. A void term is simply void, and in a form lease an abusive term is especially open to annulment when the tenant challenges it. Penalties attach instead to conduct: willfully cutting a service the lease includes, or willfully interfering with the tenant's peaceful enjoyment, is a misdemeanor with a fine of $25 to $500, up to 90 days in jail, or both; refusing to rent for a reason the Civil Rights Act forbids is a misdemeanor and gives the tenant damages plus mandatory punitive damages; and DACO may impose administrative fines and cease-and-desist orders for violations of the laws and regulations it administers, which the library treats as reaching landlords who rent homes as a business. So a "nothing in this lease limits your rights" sentence does not cure a prohibited term, and the library leaves such terms out rather than relying on a savings sentence.

title: Rights a Puerto Rico Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no landlord-tenant code with a single non-waiver section like other states' habitability acts. The Civil Code's general rule governs: a right the law grants may be waived unless the waiver is prohibited or is contrary to law, morals or public order, or harms a third party, and any act against a mandatory or prohibitory law is void. Applied to a lease, a tenant can't give up: protection under the criminal laws on cutting included services or interfering with peaceful enjoyment, and on renting a home declared unfit; the right not to be refused housing for a reason the Civil Rights Act forbids; liability for your fraud or bad-faith breach; the right to end an adhesion contract the same way it was made; the right to a lawyer in an arbitration; and the court eviction process itself. In a form lease, a clause that limits your liability, lets you change terms alone, limits the tenant's actions, defenses or evidence, renews a fixed term on the tenant's silence, or excludes an agency's jurisdiction is especially open to annulment. Many lease rules in the Civil Code are default rules the lease may change, such as rent paid in arrears, the one-year term and subletting; the library makes those choices on purpose (see Optional Lease Terms).

title: Clear Lease Language in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no plain-language statute for leases: no readability test, no required captions or section headings, and no list of words to avoid. The Civil Code supplies the standard instead. In a form lease, a clause not written clearly, completely and in an easily legible way, in Spanish or English, is especially open to annulment; general clauses on a form must be accessible to the person who did not draft them; and any unclear clause is read against you and in favor of the tenant. DACO's law also lets the Secretary require, by regulation, that documents a consumer signs be in Spanish unless the consumer prefers English, in type of at least 10 points; no such regulation for leases was found. So write the lease in Spanish or English (the language the tenant reads best), use plain words, readable type and clear headings, and avoid fine print (see Lease Language: Spanish or English and No Type-Size Rule for Leases).

title: No Plain-Language Lease Statement
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no plain-language consumer statute requiring a residential lease to pass a readability test, to carry a statement listing the rights or remedies the tenant gives up, or to be pre-approved by a government office, and no dollar threshold above which such rules stop applying. The library therefore adds no consumer-restrictions statement. What Puerto Rico requires instead is that a form lease be clear, complete and easily legible in Spanish or English (see Clear Lease Language in Puerto Rico), and the library leaves out waivers a form lease cannot carry rather than listing them.

title: Pools at Puerto Rico Rentals
bodyText: No Puerto Rico statute requires a residential landlord to fence a pool, install a barrier or alarm, post a pool safety notice, give tenants pool rules at signing, or provide a lifeguard. Public pools, spas and jacuzzis are regulated by the Department of Health through a sanitary license under its General Environmental Health Regulation, and whether a pool at an apartment complex or condominium counts as public for that regulation was not settled. In a condominium, the pool is usually a common element run by the association and its rules bind your tenant. If your rental has a pool, keep it fenced and gated, post the rules, keep rescue equipment nearby, state in the lease who maintains it and that children must be supervised, and check the Health Department's regulation before opening it to many residents. Federal pool-drain safety law applies to public pools.

title: Terms a Puerto Rico Lease Cannot Contain
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no single list of terms a residential lease may not contain. The limits come from the Civil Code and a few special laws, and together they are the complete set the library found. In a form lease, the following clauses are especially open to annulment: one not written clearly and legibly in Spanish or English; one letting you change the lease on your own; one limiting the tenant's right to sue or defend, restricting the tenant's evidence or shifting the burden of proof; one excluding or limiting your liability; one changing the tenant's contractual domicile without reason; one renewing a fixed term on the tenant's silence; and one excluding an agency's jurisdiction. In every lease: liability for fraud can't be waived; terms against mandatory or prohibitory laws are void; a clause making an adhesion contract harder to end than it was to make is treated as never agreed; a lease can't make e-mail the channel for default, cure or eviction notices on a principal residence; an arbitration clause can't waive the right to a lawyer; and a confession of judgment can't be built into the lease. A fixed charge for breach is allowed as a penalty clause, which a court may reduce if extremely out of proportion; the library does not use clauses that bar the tenant from proving a smaller loss. No Puerto Rico statute bars passing a home-warranty deductible to the tenant or charging for repairs the tenant did not cause, and no statute fines a landlord for using a prohibited term (see No Penalty for Using a Prohibited Term); charge only for damage the tenant's side caused.

title: Questions You Should Not Ask Applicants
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no general rule barring a landlord from asking applicants about protected characteristics, or from keeping records of them, separate from the ban on discriminating. One specific inquiry ban does reach landlords: no person may seek information that intrudes on the privacy of a person with HIV, and a rental may not be conditioned on proof of an HIV diagnosis. Other Puerto Rico inquiry bans protect immigration status in hospitals, schools and crime reports, not in housing. Even so, asking about race, religion, political views, sex, disability, national origin, family status or similar traits invites a discrimination claim under Puerto Rico's Civil Rights Act, the brokers' law and federal fair housing law (see Fair Housing in Puerto Rico). Ask only what you need to apply your written screening criteria, and ask every applicant the same questions.

title: Sex Offender Residence Limits
bodyText: Puerto Rico restricts where some registered sex offenders may live, but the duty is the offender's, not the landlord's. A registrant convicted of a specific crime against a minor may not establish a residence 500 feet or less from an elementary, middle or high school or a certified or licensed child-care center, for as long as the person's information is in the Registry; a violation is handled under the registry law's own penalties. No Puerto Rico statute requires you to check the registry, bars renting to a registrant, makes it a crime to rent to two registrants who live together, or gives you a safe harbor for a lease statement. If you learn that an applicant is a registrant and the home is within 500 feet of a school or child-care center, the applicant may be barred from living there; a decision based on that fact should rest on the statute, not on a general ban, since criminal-record screening raises fair-housing questions (see Criminal Activity at a Puerto Rico Rental and No Sex Offender Registry Notice in Leases).

title: No Rental Limit in Single-Family Zones
bodyText: No Puerto Rico statute limits renting a home in a single-family or residential zone, requires the owner to live on the lot, or caps the number of rentals in a neighbourhood. Zoning districts and their permitted uses are set by the Planning Board's regulations and each municipality's land-use plan, and every use of a building needs a use permit consistent with its zoning (see Use Permits and Certificates of Occupancy). Two narrower rules can matter: renting to three or more post-secondary students in a home you do not live in can make it a student-housing business that needs a DACO license (see Student Housing Certification), and a condominium's master deed or bylaws, or an access-controlled urbanization's rules, may restrict rentals, especially short-term ones.

title: Housing Vouchers and Source of Income
bodyText: No Puerto Rico statute requires a private landlord to accept a housing voucher (such as Section 8) or other rent subsidy, or bars refusing an applicant because of the source of the applicant's income, and none requires a lease statement about it. Two broader rules could be argued to reach the question, and neither has been applied to it in the statutes: DACO's Consumer Bill of Rights says consumers may not be discriminated against because of their economic situation or any similar reason, and Puerto Rico's Constitution bars discrimination for social condition. The cautious course is to judge every applicant by the same written income and screening criteria, counting a voucher's payment as income toward the rent, and to explain any refusal in writing. If you do accept a voucher, the programme's own lease addendum and rules apply (for Puerto Rico's own older-adult and veterans rent subsidies, see Rent Subsidy Conditions (Older-Adult and Veterans Programs)).

title: Steam Radiator Covers: Not Applicable
bodyText: Steam radiator covers are not an issue in Puerto Rico: its tropical climate means rental homes are not heated by steam radiators, and no Puerto Rico statute requires radiator covers, a radiator rider in the lease, or covers on request. Puerto Rico has no space-heating requirement for rentals either (see Heating: Not Applicable in Puerto Rico). If your building has any hot surface or equipment a child could touch, such as an exposed water heater or generator, guard it as a matter of ordinary care.

title: Voucher Program Inspections
bodyText: No Puerto Rico statute addresses refusing a voucher or other subsidized tenancy because the programme will inspect the unit, or a subsidized tenant's refusal of an inspection. Because Puerto Rico also has no rule requiring you to accept vouchers (see Housing Vouchers and Source of Income), the decision whether to join a programme is yours; apply the same criteria to every applicant and give your reasons in writing. If you join a federal or Puerto Rico subsidy programme, its inspection rules, lease addendum and rent rules bind you as a programme condition. A tenant's general duty to allow your own inspections, for justified cause and on seven days' prior notice, comes from the Civil Code (see Landlord's Right of Entry).

title: Keeping Tenants' Information Private
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute that lists what tenant or applicant information a landlord may not disclose, or sets a consent form for sharing it. Several rules still protect it. Privacy and the inviolability of the home are essential personality rights under the Civil Code, which a person may enforce against private parties as well as the government, so careless disclosure of a tenant's personal information can lead to a damages claim. If you provide lodging rather than a lease (a room with services, like a guest house), the Civil Code makes you respect the guest's privacy and keep discreet what you learn through the lodging. No one may refer to another person's HIV diagnosis without consent. If you keep Social Security, driver's license or bank account numbers, Puerto Rico's data-breach and disposal laws apply (see Rent Records and Tenant Data in Puerto Rico), and revealing personal data obtained by unlawfully intercepting communications or altering files is a crime. Share tenant information only with the tenant's written consent, with your own agents who need it, or when the law or a court requires it.

title: Housing an Employee
bodyText:
Puerto Rico has no statute requiring a landlord who houses an employee to give a signed occupancy disclosure or to offer a lease when the job ends. The Civil Code and the eviction law decide how such housing works. A lease is the temporary use of property for a certain price, so if the employee pays a stated rent the arrangement is a lease and the ordinary lease rules apply.

If housing is simply part of the job and no rent is paid, it may not be a lease at all: the eviction law expressly reaches caretakers, guards and others the owner placed on the property, and anyone occupying by tolerance without paying rent, so you can recover the home through a court eviction (desahucio), never by lockout.

A live-in domestic employee must have a separate, private, furnished room, and you may deduct reasonable lodging and meal costs from wages only as the written employment contract states, within the Labor Department's limits.

A lease may end on the end of employment: Puerto Rico allows leases of determinate or indeterminate length and lets the parties agree to early termination, but a term tied to an uncertain event is safest written as a fixed term plus the optional Employer-Provided Housing clause, which lets either side end the lease on written notice when the employment ends.

title: Tenant Organizing and Meetings
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no statute giving residential tenants a specific right to form a tenants' association, meet in the building or organize against the landlord, and none bars a private landlord from interfering, with two general rules to keep in mind. DACO's Consumer Bill of Rights says consumers have the right to organize consumer groups to defend themselves when acquiring goods and services; whether it reaches residential leases is unsettled, so treat it as if it does. And breaking up a lawful, peaceful meeting by force, intimidation or violence is a crime whatever the meeting is about. Puerto Rico's Constitution protects the freedom to associate and organize for any lawful purpose; it binds the government, and no Puerto Rico statute applies it to private landlords. Public-housing residents' councils are a government programme and do not apply to a private rental. The cautious course: do not put a clause in the lease forbidding tenants to organize or meet, do not threaten, cut services or refuse to continue a lease because a tenant organized (see Retaliation Against Tenants), and apply the same building rules for common-area use to every group.

title: Screening Applicants in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no tenant-screening statute: no rule on screening criteria, when you may check criminal history, look-back periods, minimum-income tests, portable screening reports or a liability shield for renting to someone with a record. A few rules shape how you screen. Anyone may request an applicant's Criminal Record Certificate from the Puerto Rico Police on paying the fee. The certificate leaves out reversed and eliminated convictions: misdemeanors are removed automatically once 30 days pass after the sentence was served with no new offense, and a felony may be removed by court order after five years (registered sex offenders and some others excepted). Puerto Rico's Credit Reporting Agencies Act adopts the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act but by its terms covers credit bureaus and those who report to them; if you report tenants' payments, see Reporting Rent to Credit Bureaus. When you use a credit or background report, the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act applies directly: have a lawful purpose, and if you deny an applicant or impose worse terms because of the report, give the federal adverse-action notice. Puerto Rico bars employers, not landlords, from using credit reports. Screening must also respect fair-housing law (see Fair Housing in Puerto Rico and Questions You Should Not Ask Applicants). Write your criteria down, apply them to every applicant the same way, and keep the reports private.

title: Unfair Bargains and Unconscionable Terms
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no unconscionability statute by that name and no lease-specific one, but the Civil Code gives courts several tools that do the same work. A contract is open to annulment or revision if one party fraudulently took advantage of the other's need, inexperience, cultural condition, economic dependence or advanced age to gain a disproportionate, unjustified advantage; a disproportion of more than half the value of the promised performance is presumed to be advantage-taking, and if you offer a fair readjustment the case becomes one for readjustment instead of annulment. Because a lease is performed over time, a party whose obligation becomes excessively onerous through an extraordinary, unforeseeable event can ask a court to revise or end it, but must act within six months of the event. In a form lease the tenant had to accept as written, a list of one-sided clauses is especially open to annulment, and unclear clauses are read against you. Rights must be exercised in good faith, the law does not protect the abuse of a right, and a court can reduce an excessive penalty clause. Puerto Rico has no rule that declares any particular lease clause enforceable regardless of fairness. Keep charges proportionate, explain the lease to an applicant who is elderly, inexperienced or in urgent need, and don't use the form lease's one-sided terms to gain an advantage the tenant could not have understood (see Terms a Puerto Rico Lease Cannot Contain).

title: Renting to Veterans
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no tax credit, payment, deposit guarantee or other incentive for a private landlord who rents to a veteran, and no rule requiring a private landlord to prefer veterans. Veterans' rights in housing run against the government: veterans and qualifying surviving spouses get preference, on equal terms, when the Government of Puerto Rico, its agencies or municipalities lease or sell their own property or run social-interest housing and rent-subsidy programmes. Puerto Rico's two veterans' rent subsidies pay toward rent in collective housing for veterans, such as Puerto Rico's veterans' home in Juana Díaz, not in ordinary private apartments. Veterans' property-tax exemptions cover the veteran's own home. If you rent to a veteran and the eviction court rules against the veteran, the court notifies the Veterans Advocate's office (see How Eviction Works in Puerto Rico and Military Tenants). Veteran status is not a protected class in Puerto Rico's own fair-housing rules for private landlords.

title: No Water Heater Temperature Rule
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no rule setting a maximum water-heater temperature or requiring you to set a unit's water heater to a given temperature before each new tenant moves in, in its lease law, its energy laws or anywhere else in its statutes. Puerto Rico's adopted plumbing and building codes may set limits for new installations. If the lease includes hot water, willfully cutting it off to pressure the tenant is a crime (see Heating: Not Applicable in Puerto Rico). As a safety practice, check the water heater at each turnover, set it to a moderate temperature (120°F or 49°C is a common recommendation, not a Puerto Rico rule), and note the setting on the move-in checklist.

title: No Window Guard Rule
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no window-guard law: nothing requires you to install guards or child-fall protection on windows, to ask tenants whether children live in the unit, or to put a window-guard notice in the lease. Security bars (rejas), common on Puerto Rico homes, are not required either (see No Security-Device or Re-Keying Statute). Puerto Rico's adopted building and fire codes may set rules for new installations, such as emergency escape openings. If you install or replace bars or guards, make sure at least one window in each bedroom can still be opened from inside without a key, and in a condominium follow the type and design the council of owners has adopted for replacements.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Puerto Rico's Commercial Transactions Act follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on payments offered in full settlement (pago en finiquito; Sección 2-311, 19 L.P.R.A. § 611). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, in good faith gives you a check or other instrument in full payment of a claim that was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, with a conspicuous statement that it is offered in full payment, and you cash it, the claim is settled, the unpaid balance included. The claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount within 90 days after the instrument is paid, but it is settled if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before collection that it was offered in full settlement. The Supreme Court of Puerto Rico also requires that the debtor's offer be free of oppression or undue advantage over the creditor. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Puerto Rico's Civil Code imposes a general duty of good faith: rights must be exercised, and duties performed, according to the requirements of good faith (P.R. Civil Code 2020, art. 15), and debtor and creditor alike must act in good faith in performing an obligation (art. 1062). A lease creates obligations on both sides, so this binds you and the tenant alike. The text read is the 2020 Code as enacted (Ley 55-2020); no later law amending either article was found in the Legislature's records. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.

title: No Communal or Native Land Approval Rule in Puerto Rico
bodyText: Puerto Rico has no communal, tribal or native land system of the kind that makes a lease wait for a government officer's approval. Under the Civil Code a lease needs no special formality to be valid, except where it is of real property and is meant to be recorded in the Property Registry to bind third persons (P.R. Civ. Code art. 1342), and nothing in the Code's lease articles requires an official's approval of a private residential lease. A lease of real property for longer than six years must be in writing (P.R. Civ. Code art. 1343, as amended by Ley 122-2026). Some land in Puerto Rico is held under special programs with their own restrictions (for example, community land trust land and farm parcels granted under the Land Law); this library hasn't read those laws, so if the property is on such land, check its restrictions with the program before you lease it.

title: Recording a Lease in Puerto Rico's Property Registry
bodyText: You don't have to record a residential lease in Puerto Rico, and an unrecorded lease is valid between you and the tenant: the lease needs no special formality for its validity, except where a lease of real property is to be recorded in the Property Registry so that it has effect against third persons (P.R. Civ. Code art. 1342). Recording is what makes a lease bind people who rely on the Registry, such as a later buyer or a mortgage lender. Length matters. A lease of real property for six years or more must be set out in a public or private instrument for evidentiary purposes (P.R. Civ. Code art. 1245(b)), and a lease of real property for longer than six years must be in writing (P.R. Civ. Code art. 1343, as amended by Ley 122-2026, in effect on approval in 2026). The Legislature's statement of reasons for that amendment explains that under the Property Registry Act it is leases of six years or more that may be recorded, unless the parties agree otherwise (Ley 122-2026, Exposición de Motivos, describing Ley 210-2015, art. 5). No Puerto Rico rule found ties notice to a relative's lease the way Nebraska's does. Practical step: an ordinary one- or two-year lease needs no recording; for a lease of six years or more, or one you want to bind a future buyer or lender, use a written lease and ask a notary about recording it. See also `edu-statute-of-frauds-pr`.
